items.text:
Pakistan minister to visit India, but no breakthrough expected
November 19, 2026
Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Masood Malik will travel to India from November 20 to 22 to participate in the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Civilizational Dialogue in New Delhi.
It marks the first India visit by a Pakistani federal minister since the two nuclear-armed archrivals fought a four-day war last year.
The fighting erupted after armed gunmen killed over two dozen tourists, mostly Hindus, in India-administered Kashmir in April 2025. New Delhi accused Islamabad of backing the attack, a charge Pakistan denied.
Since the military confrontation, diplomatic tensions have remained high, leaving little room for official engagement between the two sides.
The SCO Civilizational Dialogue was proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the SCO summit in Tianjin in September 2025.
As the forum's host, India has invited all member states to participate in the event.
The SCO is a political, economic, and security alliance established in 2001. Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan are its current members.
A 'good sign'
Ajay Bisaria, a former Indian ambassador to Pakistan, sees significance in the fact that neither side sought to avoid the engagement. "The real takeaway is that the relationship isn't so broken that India won't invite Pakistan, or that Pakistan won't come. That alone is a good sign," he told DW.
But Bisaria cautions against assuming that the invitation followed a diplomatic breakthrough.
"The trigger was procedural. This forum grew out of Modi's proposal at the 2025 SCO summit in Tianjin, and as host, New Delhi invited every SCO member. I see no evidence of a back channel or outside mediation, and I wouldn't read much into that either way," he said.
'Being pragmatic'
The multilateral setting serves both countries, though for different reasons.
Pakistan wants to retain its influence within the organization. It currently holds the chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for 2026–27 and is due to host the next leaders' summit in Islamabad in August 2027.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, argues that Islamabad's decision to send a senior minister should be understood primarily in terms of its position in the grouping.
"Pakistan is keen to maintain its position and influence within the SCO and does not want to relinquish its role in the organization. The minister's visit should therefore be seen primarily in the context of Pakistan fulfilling its commitments under the SCO Charter, rather than as a gesture towards India," Siddiqa told DW.
T C A Raghavan, another former Indian ambassador to Pakistan, shares a similar sentiment.
"Both India and Pakistan attach importance to the SCO, and Pakistan currently holds its chairmanship. This visit should be seen primarily in the context of the SCO, rather than as a development in India-Pakistan bilateral relations," Raghavan told DW.
"Islamabad is also being pragmatic in keeping channels open during its SCO chairmanship by participating in an initiative championed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. There will be no real impact on the India-Pakistan bilateral."
The bilateral freeze
Since the April 2025 attack, India has maintained that terrorism and talks cannot go hand in hand.
"Post the Pahalgam attack, we have a Pakistan policy. That Pakistan policy remains in place. There has been no change," Randhir Jaiswal, spokesperson for India's Foreign Ministry, said at the end of October.
Pakistan, meanwhile, continues to raise the issues of Kashmir and the Indus Waters Treaty, which New Delhi placed "in abeyance" following the attack.
Malik, the climate change minister traveling to India, has been a prominent voice in Pakistan's campaign over water rights. In June, he warned: "We will protect ourselves... if anyone lays a hand over our share of water, we'll cut off that hand."
Sanjay Kumar Bhardwaj, professor at the Center for South Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the SCO is part of India's "multi-aligned foreign policy."
He noted that the forum "doesn't provide any space to normalize relations with Pakistan."
Unofficial channels, no formal dialogue
The absence of official talks, however, does not mean all bilateral communication has stopped.
Since the May 2025 confrontation, Indian and Pakistani former diplomats, strategic experts, parliamentarians and retired military officers have reportedly taken part in a series of informal or semi-official back-channel meetings.
Such exchanges allow participants to assess the other side's thinking, keep informal lines of communication open and reduce the risk of miscalculation.
But they do not amount to formal negotiations. New Delhi has said retired officials attending such meetings do so in their personal capacities.
An assessment by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in November said both governments appeared reluctant to resume secret talks, despite the role earlier back-channel contacts had played in stabilizing relations.
Bisaria described the visit by a Pakistani minister to India as "a modest step forward, not a breakthrough."
What happens next, he said, "depends on Pakistan."
"If it avoids grandstanding in Delhi and offers credible assurances on terrorism, publicly or quietly, it becomes more likely that Indian leaders will attend next year's SCO summit in Islamabad. That will be the real test."

Tens of thousands of women were forced to work in South Korean state-sanctioned brothels used by American soldiers based in the country after the Korean War. They were raped, physically abused and forcibly confined. Now, after decades of silence, some of these women are speaking out.
The women accuse the US and South Korean governments of abuse and are demanding compensation for their ordeal. In May of this year, 117 of them – who are now mostly in their 70s – launched legal action that targets the US for the first time. Back in 2022, the South Korean Supreme Court ruled that the government had illegally operated the brothels for American servicemen.
FRANC 24's Chloé Borgnon, Constantin Simon, Aruna Popuri and Justin McCurry report.

items.text:
What to know about Xi, Putin and Trump's historic trilateral summit
China's Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump met for a historic summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, where they agreed on a "peace declaration". The three leaders pledged to reform the UN, increase supplies of refined petroleum products and uphold the immunity enjoyed by officials in international courts.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US and Russian counterparts Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin agreed on a "peace declaration" at their unprecedented three-way meeting on Thursday, in which they reaffirmed that a nuclear war should never be fought, China and Russia said.
The declaration capped Trump's three-day diplomatic swing through Asia that produced few tangible victories, despite his repeated boasts about making history and brokering peace.
Read more
Historic trilateral summit live: Trump, Xi and Putin agree that a nuclear war must never be fought
Instead, the trip raised fresh questions among US allies about his increasingly close relationship with Putin, who continues to wage war with Ukraine.
In the declaration, the three leaders also pledged to advance reforms of the United Nations, to increase supplies of refined petroleum products for all countries and to uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.
The International Criminal Court in The Hague has issued arrest warrants for Putin and five other Russian officials.
Putin and Russia's children's commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, are accused of the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children, while the other warrants relate to alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Moscow rejects the allegations.
"The pushback against international norms and courts is the most interesting aspect. The big powers dictate, the small powers suffer," said Jonathan Eyal, international director at the RUSI think tank in London.
Eyal added that Putin "gained credibility and escape from pariah status", while Trump "gained a photo opportunity he didn't need".
The document was released by Chinese state news agency Xinhua and by the Kremlin. Trump departed on his flight back to the US without making any comment after the meeting.
Earlier, the leaders of the world's biggest nuclear powers, sitting at a round table in a villa nestled among wooded hills beside a lake in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, described their meeting as historic.
"We are really making history," Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting before journalists were sent away. "No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement."
Differences over Ukraine, Iran and trade
Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three countries had "numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine".
The meeting was a diplomatic coup for Putin, with Russia’s economy barely a 10th the size of China’s and most of its businesses barred from trading with the West by sanctions.
The meeting ended a few hours before Ukraine and the leaders of its main European allies were due to meet Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Berlin.
Unlike Trump and Putin, Xi did not make a direct reference to Ukraine, but said: "History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace. When major powers clash, the world falls into turmoil."
The three countries have deep differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade, casting doubts about a durable outcome.
Their meeting on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit has unnerved smaller countries that fear their interests might be disregarded.
The Kylin Villa where they met has a long history of sensitive diplomatic encounters. Its past visitors include former North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, Xi's father Xi Zhongxun, and envoys of the Dalai Lama.
Before the trilateral, Trump met Xi and Putin separately, referring to both as friends.

Fanfare and pageantry
Speaking to Fox News earlier, Trump highlighted the pomp surrounding his arrival for the summit, which contrasted with the more muted greeting of other leaders, including Putin.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi landed without any welcoming ceremony.
Japan's relations with China have soured since Takaichi's remarks in 2025, when she said Japan could deploy its military if a Chinese move on Taiwan also threatened its territory.
Takaichi, who cut an isolated figure throughout the summit, said Tokyo's position on Taiwan had not changed since 1972.
On Taiwan, Xi told Trump the US must "do the right thing" to avoid major setbacks in their relationship.
Xi greeted Trump at the airport, the first time he has done so with any visiting leader since becoming president, reciprocating his counterpart's gesture at Joint Base Andrews in September, when they last met. The leaders also briefly hugged.
"This is a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he's never gone to the airport to meet somebody," Trump said, calling that a "win" for both China and the US.
"And not only that, the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people, the young children, the soldiers, the whole thing."
Tough nuclear arms discussion
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit, despite China's repeated objections in the past to joining talks with Washington and Moscow, which have far larger nuclear arsenals.

items.text:
Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
- Published
Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.
In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week.
A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic.
But at a press conference after historic talks with his Chinese and US counterparts in Shenzhen, Russian president Putin said Moscow's response would be even more significant.
Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.
Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.
Commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors."
The collapse of the Crimean Bridge's arch was the worst damage to be inflicted onto the structure in several years.
The bridge had long been in Ukraine's sights because it represents Moscow's pretensions over sovereign Ukrainian land, and because of its logistical importance in supplying Russian troops in the occupied Ukrainian southern regions.
It was built and unveiled to great fanfare in 2018, four years after Russia illegally annexed Ukraine's Crimea.
Thursday's strike was carried out with Neptune cruise missiles, Ukraine said. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. Train services on the bridge were suspended but resumed in the afternoon.
Car traffic, however, will be prohibited for the foreseeable future as a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was dragged below into the sea when missiles hit the arch on Tuesday.
President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
The seven-stage operation first required the destruction of air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets which protected the bridge. Missiles and drones then dealt the structure the final blow.
In response to Tuesday's hit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
But the operation to repair it could take a long time, and it will likely have to be carried out under frequent Ukrainian fire.
Russia has regularly targeted Ukrainian civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
This week alone, as the Crimean Bridge was being hit, Moscow targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

APEC summit: Trump, Xi, Putin talks end with 'peace declaration'
Published November 17, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
What you need to know
- Three-way talks between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping have finished
- The talks took place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit held in China's Shenzhen
- Trump was greeted by Xi at the airport before greeting Putin in their first face-to-face in over a year
- Trump held bilateral talks with 'friend' Putin as well as separate talks with Xi ahead of the main event
- The wars in Ukraine and Iran, as well as nuclear arms controls, were on top of the agenda for the trilateral talks
Here are the biggest headlines from the APEC summit and Trump's Asia tour on Thursday, November 19:
What do we know about agreements at the trilateral summit?
The highly anticipated three-way talks between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday have ended.
Ahead of the talks, Trump said they would be about "all problems that are being discussed in the world"
Here are quotes from the leaders and from a joint statement on the topics they addressed:
Nuclear arms
- Trump: "The United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used."
- Xi: "A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. Every effort must be made to prevent nuclear war, adhere to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, and maintain global strategic stability."
International Criminal Court and UN
- In a joint statement reported by Chinese state media and the Kremlin, the leaders agreed that "the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction."
- The leaders also "acknowledged the vital importance of the principle of state consent and the respect for (diplomatic) immunity enjoyed by state officials."
- The statement added that all three countries were "committed" to advancing reform of the United Nations.
Energy
- The joint statement said the countries "plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products."
- It reaffirmed "the importance of the stable flow of energy."
Neither the war in Ukraine nor the conflict in Iran were directly mentioned at the talks, according to the Russian and Chinese accounts.
China and Russia report on 'peace declaration' from trilateral summit
Chinese state media and Russian officials have been summarizing a declaration issued by the US, Chinese and Russian presidents at their trilateral summit, which US President Donald Trump billed as history-making.
According to the accounts of what was dubbed a "peace declaration," the three leaders reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
The three presidents of major nuclear powers are quoted as saying they would hold a dialogue on the reduction of nuclear risks and the prevention of nuclear proliferation.
The three men also "reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows," saying they plan to up the production and supply of refined petroleum products, according to the Chinese Xinhua news agency.
In addition, Chinese state media said the three had agreed that the International Criminal Court (ICC) — of which neither the US, China nor Russia are signatories — and similar institutions should not abuse their jurisdiction.
Putin himself is subject to an ICC arrest warrant for suspected war crimes in Ukraine.
The summary of the meeting did not mention the wars in Ukraine, triggered by Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion, or Iran, which began in late February with US-Israeli attacks on the country.
Both conflicts were expected to feature in the discussions.
WATCH: US; Russian, Chinese leaders in historic summit
US President Donald Trump has met with his Russian and Chinese counterparts for an unprecedented meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China.
Trump said they were "making history" with the talks, which lasted around an hour and 20 minutes.
Watch here to see how the meeting began:
Historic Trump-Xi-Putin summit comes to an end
An unprecedented three-way meeting of US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has ended after more than an hour of discussion.
Trump reportedly left the venue of the talks in Kylin Villa for the airport in the southeastern city of Shenzhen directly after the talks ended.
We will be bringing you details on anything concrete that emerged from the talks in further entries.
Xi calls for nuclear-free world
Chinese President Xi Jinping has told his US and Russian counterparts at the three-way that nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, the state-run Xinhua news agency said.
It quoted Xi as saying nuclear war should be prevented by all means and a nuclear-free world created.
"A nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. Every effort must be made to prevent nuclear war, adhere to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, and maintain global strategic stability," the agency cited Xi as saying.
Ukraine war being discussed at trilateral meeting — Trump
US President Donald Trump said that the war in Ukraine would feature in the talks with his Russian and Chinese counterparts in China on Thursday.
"We are going to discuss the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said as the historic summit in Shenzhen got underway.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said all three countries had a shared "interest" to resolve the war in Ukraine, triggered by Moscow's 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbor.

Was it worth it?
I let Apple’s always-listening AI summarize my life for two weeks
Apple’s Siri Recaps make a lot of tradeoffs to protect privacy. But I’m not convinced the benefits outweigh the costs.
I let Apple’s always-listening AI summarize my life for two weeks
Apple’s Siri Recaps make a lot of tradeoffs to protect privacy. But I’m not convinced the benefits outweigh the costs.
I’ve been asking myself this quite a bit over the last month or so while testing both the Amazon Bee Frontier and Siri Recap on the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Both enable a wearable to ambiently listen to your conversations and, using AI, summarize them for you. Why? So you can remember better and, hopefully, stay more present.
The main difference is that Amazon’s Bee takes a maximalist (and frankly reality-bending) approach, whereas Apple is going for a more minimalist, privacy-first take. Both, however, require explicit disclosures to the people around you about recording what they say, and potentially follow-up explanations about how exactly this all works. This past week, I’ve been testing the Siri Recap beta to see if Apple’s is a less dystopian experience.
Apple presents Siri Recap as a sort of backup notetaker. As a college student, perhaps you’re less concerned about writing down what a professor says and can just take in the lecture. Say you attend a parent-teacher conference solo. You can focus on the discussion and then whip out your phone later to reference what was said when explaining it to your spouse.
These are fairly innocuous scenarios. But given the discourse around privacy and surveillance gadgets this year, it’s easy to imagine how always-listening devices could be misused. Apple has taken great care to create a version of this that at least considers that bystanders may feel uncomfortable knowing someone else’s Apple Watch may be taking notes on what they say.
The feature isn’t turned on by default — you have to opt in. Users can then program when the feature turns on. For example, only at the office between the hours of 1 to 2PM on weekdays. Unless saved, all recaps are also set to self-destruct after your choice of one, three, or seven days. Within the summaries, there’s no viewable transcript detailing who said what and when. That makes these recaps more difficult to use as “receipts” for arguments, court cases, or blackmail. There’s also no raw audio file that’s ever saved. Not to get too into the weeds, but the audio gets processed and then immediately deleted through a secure exclave within the 2026 Apple Watch’s S11 chip that’s inaccessible to Apple and other third parties. The vast majority of the processing is also done locally. Whatever does get sent to the cloud is done through Apple’s Private Cloud Compute. Because the feature requires this hardware, it’s impossible to use on older Apple Watches.
It’s not perfect. Unlike Live Rewind, another audio intelligence feature, there’s no outward indicator or audio chime to signal recording intent. So, if you do decide to ethically disclose your usage, you have to be prepared to explain everything I just described if someone asks questions.
Maybe that’s worth it — if Siri can be trusted to be truly helpful.
The reality is that better privacy often means a less useful AI product. The more AI knows about you, the better the summaries from these devices tend to be. To preserve privacy, Apple prevents Siri from learning everything about you and the people in your life. For example, Siri Recap doesn’t train on your voice. Excellent for privacy! But that also means Siri has a much harder time discerning when you’re actually having a conversation. That leads to some funny but ultimately unhelpful recaps.
For instance, I was watching a TikTok in which a chronically ill creator was updating their followers about being sent to the emergency room because of sepsis. Siri recapped that video as if I, or potentially someone I knew, had been sent to the ER. Another TikTok weighing in on an AITA Reddit thread got summarized as if I had discussed a shady homewrecker named Dana trying to seduce her bestie’s husband by wearing a glittery blue bikini top at a concert. Because attribution was stripped, the summary could read as if I were the guilty spouse returning between 2 and 3AM, covered in Dana’s glitter. In both instances, the lack of attribution also made the resulting summaries hilarious and confusing.
Also, neither video was something I wanted or needed to remember. I suspect Siri summarized them because I was playing the audio out loud on my phone, which sits pretty close to my Apple Watch. There’s an easy workaround here. Siri Recap automatically turns off if you use headphones, meaning I could just eliminate recaps from podcasts, audiobooks, TV shows, etc., by always wearing my AirPods. But that’s me adjusting my behavior to accommodate Siri’s inability to discern when I’m talking.
Another quirk: Siri doesn’t know what I want to remember or find memorable from a given conversation.
I turned on Siri Recap during my briefing and demos for the new smart glasses from Google, Samsung, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker. When I sat down to write, the resulting recap helped me remember the main topics discussed. I also found it useful that a handful of interview recaps were linked to a corresponding Voice Memos file. The thing is, Siri Recap heavily prioritizes restating the facts. That means bullet points tend to emphasize statistics, factoids, and dates. That’s useful in straightforward planning meetings, but less useful for what you might personally find to be a salient takeaway. For example, in an interview with a source, what I found most interesting was a personal anecdote and some strong opinions about RFK Jr. My Siri Recap from that interview omitted it in favor of more concrete details.

items.text:
US consortium wins huge Kenya mining deal, beating Chinese rivals
- Published
A US-led consortium, Frontier Minerals, has won the tender to develop Kenya's Mrima Hill mining project, beating seven bidders, including companies from China and Australia.
The site is estimated to hold deposits of critical minerals worth more than $60bn (£45bn), including niobium, used in electric vehicles, aerospace and defence technology.
Frontier Minerals says its proposal aims to keep more of the economic benefits in Kenya through "processing and refining of minerals in-country".
The deal comes as Washington seeks greater access to Africa's minerals, aiming to strengthen US supply chains and compete with China.
Frontier Minerals brings together three US companies - Bunker Hill Mining Corp, American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation. The consortium combines expertise in mineral resource development, critical materials supply chains and advanced refining technologies.
A central part of its proposal is to develop mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya. Brad Marnett from Frontier Minerals said the company wanted the country to capture more value from its mineral resources.
Mrima Hill is located in Kwale County, near Kenya's Indian Ocean coastline. The site covers about 390 acres of forest.
The prospect of mining in the area has raised concerns among local residents, who fear the project could damage the forest and threaten their ancestral heritage.
There are also questions over whether communities living near the site will benefit from the investment.
Marnett was keen to reassure Kenyans that they would benefit: "We intend to create lasting opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy through capacity-building and targeted investment, while prioritising environmental management and performance."
The consortium must still obtain a prospecting licence and meet the necessary regulatory requirements before the project can proceed.
The tender decision has drawn objections from competing bidders.
Reuters news agency reports that two rival companies intend to challenge the selection, with Australia's RareX alleging that Frontier Minerals missed an earlier submission deadline.
Kenya's government has maintained that the process was open and transparent.
The project comes as US strives to secure alternative sources of critical minerals and reduce dependence on China, which dominates the processing of several key minerals.
Washington has been pursuing partnerships with mineral-rich African countries, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, as it seeks to strengthen supply chains for industries ranging from electric vehicles to defence technology.
Kenya's mining ministry says the sector is an important part of its plans to diversify the economy beyond traditional sources of revenue such as tourism, agriculture and financial services.

items.title: Nairobi forum puts Africa’s voice at centre of global AI governance debate
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 19 – Scholars and legal practitioners from several countries have called for stronger international cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) and data governance, warning that the rapid growth of digital technologies risks deepening inequalities if countries and communities are
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 19 – Scholars and legal practitioners from several countries have called for stronger international cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) and data governance, warning that the rapid growth of digital technologies risks deepening inequalities if countries and communities are excluded from shaping the rules.
The experts said fair digital governance must go beyond technological development to address data privacy, national sovereignty, accountability and equitable access to the benefits of the digital economy.
The concerns featured prominently at the inaugural Global Forum on Digital Intelligence, Rule of Law and Interdisciplinary Governance, hosted by the University of Nairobi’s Faculty of Law on November 17, bringing together participants from Kenya, China, South Africa, Japan, the United States and other countries.
Held under the theme “Law, Innovation and China–Africa Cooperation in the Intelligent Age,” the forum examined how countries can develop common approaches to regulating emerging technologies while protecting individual rights and ensuring that digital partnerships deliver shared benefits.
A key focus was the need to give African countries greater influence over the rules governing data and artificial intelligence, particularly as cross-border digital trade and the use of personal information expand.
Sindile Mazibuko, founder and Chief Executive Officer of SkyVerse888 Foundation and co-founder of Circle-AI Venture Lab, argued that data sovereignty requires more than establishing local digital infrastructure.
She said African countries also need technical expertise, accountable institutions and meaningful community participation to ensure they have control over how their data is collected, processed and used.
The question of balancing individual rights with the commercial value of data was also examined by Professor Yun Zhao, Henry Cheng Professor in International Law at the University of Hong Kong.
Zhao proposed an approach that protects personal information while recognising the interests of those investing in data processing and developing products and services.
His presentation explored the competing interests of individuals, data processors and purchasers, including questions of consent, the purpose for which information is collected and access to remedies when rights are violated.
The debate has particular relevance for Kenya, which has established legal safeguards under the Data Protection Act, 2019.
Section 37 of the law requires express consent for the commercial use of personal data, or authorisation under written law accompanied by notice when the information is collected. It also requires anonymisation where possible.
Africa’s role in digital governance
The forum also examined how African countries can strengthen their negotiating position in international digital cooperation, particularly in partnerships involving China.
Professor Congjing Ran of Wuhan University outlined proposals for a trusted cross-border data space between China and Africa, anchored in compatible rules, reliable technology and effective institutions.
Ran, who is also executive dean of the Hubei Data Element Innovation Institute, presented research on a data sovereignty index and a white paper on China–Africa data cooperation.
He also discussed artificial intelligence tools designed to help compare regulatory frameworks and assess compliance, with important decisions remaining subject to human supervision.
The discussions extended to the challenges of regulating digital platforms and ensuring that technological advancement does not undermine fundamental freedoms.
Victor Ndede, head of programmes at Amnesty International Kenya, examined concerns surrounding surveillance and civic freedoms, while Florence Ogonjo, a research fellow at Strathmore University’s Centre for Intellectual Property and Information Technology Law, addressed the protection of fundamental rights in AI governance.
Other contributors examined the implications of AI-generated content for ownership and intellectual property, the digital divide and the responsibilities of technology companies.
Dr Mugambi Laibuta, chairperson of the Data Privacy and Governance Society of Kenya, explored questions of ownership when machines generate content, while Tianjie Lin, a senior partner at JunZeJun Law Offices in Hangzhou, argued for making some responsibilities to address the digital divide enforceable through law.
Cross-border rules and accountability
A second session focused on cross-border data governance and digital trade, highlighting the difficulties businesses and individuals face when operating across jurisdictions with different legal requirements.
Professor Zheng Tang of Wuhan University examined competing claims to regulate data beyond national borders, while Dr Ting Liao of Kyoto University’s Graduate School of Law considered how digital platform contracts determine the rights and interests of users.
The discussions highlighted challenges including overlapping regulatory obligations, suspended accounts, withheld payments and disputes handled by courts in distant jurisdictions.
Kenya’s experience in digital governance also featured through contributions by Dr Ken Obura of the University of Nairobi, who examined cross-border data transfers and the balance between regulatory safeguards and business needs.
Al Kags, principal of Kags Advisories, addressed the role of open data, civic participation and public accountability, while Victor Kapiyo, head of programmes at the Kenya ICT Action Network (KICTANet), examined China–Africa digital partnerships.
Quincey Otieno, a legal officer at the Parliamentary Service Commission, discussed accountability in the intelligent state, linking the adoption of digital technologies to questions of public power and institutional oversight.
The forum was conceived by Professor Haiying Huang during her visiting appointment at the University of Nairobi’s Faculty of Law.

items.summary:
Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield on Sunday for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start.
United are 18th in the Premier League and Liverpool fourth but the head coach
items.text:
Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield on Sunday for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start.
United are 18th in the Premier League and Liverpool fourth but the head coach will not accept nerves. Pochettino is known for being attack-minded and will bring those ideals, but will have had only three days with the players since replacing Michael Carrick.
“We are going to go there to Anfield with the idea to win and be brave and to be Manchester United,” Pochettino told the club’s website. “The history talks for us, and what we need to expect, and we are going to expect in Manchester United. We need to be sure that we are brave and we are protagonists and go there with no fears and challenge a very good team like Liverpool.”
Pochettino arrived in Manchester on Wednesday after an overnight flight, having taken charge of his final USA match against Haiti. He toured the training ground and held meetings with senior staff and players not on international duty. Members of Pochettino’s staff were in place earlier in the week as they seek to revitalise a team with one league win.
“We need to go little by little, step by step,” Pochettino said. “We cannot go too fast but also we need to, at the same time, attack the priorities to build something.”
He said it was important he and his staff adapt to the culture of the club. “And then, with this sense of knowing the history of the club, try to create all together, because we are all different, a culture, a philosophy that can respect that identity, the history of the club. But at the same time, performing. If we don’t perform, the responsibility is mine.”
Pochettino has coveted the United job and is a keen admirer of Sir Alex Ferguson, who he describes as “the best coach in history”. Since the Scot’s retirement in 2013, United have failed to match his success but Pochettino said he was looking at “the potential of the club”. The weight of past achievements has hindered individuals over the past 13 years.
“The players need to express their talent,” Pochettino said. “We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now: it’s to work with them and try to take the pressure.
“Pressure needs to bring energy, responsibility needs to bring energy. Because if not, it’s too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back. When you connect with the game, you connect through your talent when you feel freedom, when you feel happy, when you want to play for your teammates, when you want to play for your family, when you want to play for your club, your fans.”
He sounded an upbeat note, saying: “With the power of this club and the fans supporting us, I think we will get in the place that we deserve to be.”
United on Thursday reported a quarterly net loss of £18.1m, compared with £6.6m in the same period a year earlier. Revenue rose 4% to £146m in the three months to the end of September.

items.text:
Will this be the tightest Championship promotion race ever?
- Published
Many supporters often like to label the Championship "the best league in the world".
It might be a throwaway comment, but it is one founded on the premise that the level of unpredictability and drama is unmatched.
And there is a case to be made that the Championship is living up to its unofficial tag more than ever this season.
We have seen astonishing comebacks, goals galore, unexpected results - and one third of the way through the 2026-27 campaign, you could throw a blanket over the top half of the table.
With just one point between the top five sides and eight points separating leaders Birmingham City down to Blackburn Rovers in 13th after 15 games, is this shaping up to be one of, if not the best promotion and play-off contests ever in the second tier?
'A brilliant start to the season'
"This is going to be fun," said 72+ EFL podcast host Aaron Paul.
Jobi McAnuff, who won the Championship with Reading in 2011-12, agrees.
"It's been a brilliant start of the season. I think there's such a lovely open nature to the league so far," McAnuff said.
"You certainly wouldn't have expected West Brom right up there. Stoke... Mark Robins again doing brilliantly, and Birmingham sitting top of the table."
Former Bromley manager Andy Woodman described it as "anyone's league".
"This Championship is relentless," Woodman said. "I'm looking at all the clubs in there and Scott Parker's record of getting out of the league. He's now at West Ham sitting just behind them ready to come up.
"It is going to be an unbelievable finish to the season and if we were to call it, I don't think we could."
The final game before the two-week international break epitomised just how close the race is, and gives us plenty of reason for excitement when the Championship returns this weekend.
It is usually a rare and precious moment when football fans are able to serenade their heroes with 'We are top of the league' on the terraces.
But no less than four sets of supporters were able to do so in the space of a few hours on the afternoon of Saturday, 7 November.
The name at the top of the table changed eight times between 12:54 GMT and 16:51 GMT that day, with Birmingham eventually securing pole position.
That was only after Wolves, Stoke and Middlesbrough had led the way, however briefly, earlier in the day.
Only been this tight once before
The table after 15 games is as tight as it has been since Opta started compiling statistics in 2004, although there is one other season in which just one point separated the top five sides beyond this point in a campaign, and boy, was it a doozy.
In early March 2015 Roy Hodgson was still England manager and Prime Minister David Cameron led a Conservative/Lib Dem coalition in Westminster.
Meanwhile, 36 games into the Championship season, this is what the title race looked like...
Bournemouth went on to pick up 24 points from their final 10 games to win the title and promotion to the top flight for the first time with 90 points, one ahead of Watford, who also went up.
Norwich and Middlesbrough had to settle for the play-offs, finishing third and fourth on 86 and 85 points respectively, while Brentford and Ipswich sneaked into the play-offs on goal difference, with Wolves missing out after also finishing on 78 points.
Derby ended up in eighth after taking only 17 points from their final 10 games to miss the play-offs by a point.
The table only tells half the story, however.
The Hornets would have been champions had they not conceded a late equaliser against Sheffield Wednesday on the final afternoon while the Rams had just needed to avoid defeat to secure a top-six finish, only to go down 3-0 at home to lowly Reading.
We can only hope 1 May 2027 provides us with half as much drama on the final day of the regular season.
With eight play-off places now up for grabs, the odds are it might even exceed it.
And we can all take heart from the fact the table now is slightly tighter than the one in 2014-15 was after 15 games, while it's worth noting that only one of those top five fell away in the run-in.
Does that suggest our three promoted sides will come from the current top five?
The most entertaining league in Europe?
If you want lots of goals and a tense battle at the top, then look no further than the Championship.
No other league in Europe is as tightly contested right now.
The Dutch Eredivisie comes closest with three points separating the top five, compared to just one point in the Championship.
However, the season is only nine games old in the Netherlands, as opposed to 15 in the English second tier.
Only two points separate the top four in the Belgian Pro League after 11 matches but there is a nine-point gap from first to fifth.
And it is not just the promotion race delivering so far this season - the entire division is coming up with the goods in terms of entertainment.
The last time goals were banged in at a higher rate in the second tier, England were about to win the World Cup for the first and only time to date.
This season's ratio of 2.96 goals per game is the highest in the 60 years since there were 3.08 per game across the 1965-66 campaign.
With 532 goals already netted in the Championship, we are on course for a total of 1,633 should the trend continue.
That would be the highest number of goals achieved at this level since 1957-58 when there were 1,637.
The highest number of goals ever in the second tier was in 1926-27, when there were 22 teams in the division and fewer games played overall (462) compared to today (552).
Who will win promotion from the Championship?
Predicting the completely unpredictable might be a futile task, particularly this season.
But Opta's Supercomputer has tried to do just that by crunching the numbers to estimate the likely outcome of every remaining match using its power rankings tool and betting odds.

items.title: Canva adds an AI ‘off’ button
items.summary:
Canva will now allow you to turn off its generative AI features. With this change, you can disable the graphic design platform’s array of AI tools, such as its AI photo-extending Magic Expand feature, as well as turn off the ability to generate images with its Canva chatbot.
Canva adds an AI ‘off’ b
items.text:
Canva will now allow you to turn off its generative AI features. With this change, you can disable the graphic design platform’s array of AI tools, such as its AI photo-extending Magic Expand feature, as well as turn off the ability to generate images with its Canva chatbot.
Canva adds an AI ‘off’ button
You can also select an option to see less AI-generated content in Canva’s library.
This toggle doesn’t turn off every AI-powered feature on Canva, however. That includes Canva’s background remover and its Magic Grab tool, which lets you select an object in an image and move it somewhere else. Canva says these tools will stay on because they “make everyday tasks faster without generating anything new.”
The toggle still turns off many of Canva’s other AI features, including Magic Write, Magic Design, Magic Layers, Magic Edit, Dream Lab, Canva Code, AI Shapes, and more.
Since Canva’s big push into AI in 2023, some users have expressed frustration with the influx of AI features and asked for ways to turn them off. Canva has only continued to expand on its AI-powered image-editing suite since then, by rolling out a prompt-powered editing update in April and launching its first in-house AI model, Canva Craft, last month.
You can also now switch a toggle to see less AI content in Canva’s content library. Switching this option on means you’ll see human-created content first when searching through Canva’s library for templates, graphics, and other design elements. Canva says a “small portion” of its library consists of AI-generated content, and that any design that uses one of these elements will have an AI label in its metadata.
To turn off Canva’s AI features, head to Profile > Settings > Permission, and then toggle off Enable generative AI features. You can choose to see less AI-generated content by going to Profile > Your account > AI personalization, and then turning on the option to show less AI content. These switches are available to both free and paid users.

items.text:
Top U.N. court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during its 2017 military operations in northern Rakhine State.
Delivering the judgment, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said the scale and nature of the military's actions went "well beyond what would be required to punish the population" and were instead "characteristic of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group."
The judges estimated that around 815,000 Rohingya lived in northern Rakhine State before the operations, and concluded that around 10,000 were violently killed during the 2017 clearance campaign.
The court found that Myanmar's security forces "acted with genocidal intent." Judge Iwasawa said the operations were preceded by an atmosphere of anti-Rohingya hate speech, with the community portrayed as "sub-human" and "a violent threat."
This is a developing story that will be updated.

items.title: Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden
items.summary: It’s injury time at the Emirates on the 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Spurs. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and on to the post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the
items.text:
It’s injury time at the Emirates on the 29 October 2008, Arsenal are 4-3 up against Spurs. Tom Huddlestone cushions a ball to Luka Modric, whose strike takes a deflection. It loops over Manuel Almunia and on to the post into the path of Aaron Lennon, who prods it home and starts skipping towards the Spurs fans before diving on to the ground and being enveloped by Modric, Benoît Assou-Ekotto, Darren Bent and a couple of pitch-invading fans. Pandemonium, for once, seems the apt way to describe it.
But the real entertainment is happening in a radio studio at 18 Hatfields, London SE1; the old home of TalkSport. As the goal goes in, a guttural voice makes an indecipherable but very loud noise. It’s hard to transcribe – perhaps “ERRRRRAAAARRRGGHH”, or maybe “OOEEERRAAGGH”.
It’s just a noise, but it’s unmistakingly Danny Kelly. He regains the power of speech and follows it up with: “Gooooaaaal … Goalll Stan Goalll at the Emirates.” Reporter Ian Abrahams and Stan Collymore join the excitement, before Danny comes back: “I LOVE FOOTBALL, STAN, I LOVE IT.” It is such a brilliant piece of radio. From one of the absolute greats.
Danny died last week. In a beautiful tribute on the Spurs podcast he hosted – A View From The Lane – Charlie Eccleshare pointed out the irony that for someone so articulate and erudite and able to do so much more than just “the football”, his most iconic moment is so simple. Even the opening noise – not even a real word – is perfect in that context.
Words such as pioneer and trailblazer often get thrown out in moments like this. But Danny really was. I first met him at BBC London more than 20 years ago. As someone who’d listened to him and Danny Baker as a teenager, I couldn’t really believe I was in the same office as them.
His career was ridiculous, editing the NME and Q magazine, setting up Football365, but it was radio where I knew him. He understood the absurdity of life and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living by talking about football.
I remember at TalkSport one World Cup – 2018 perhaps – wandering in and he was hosting a live match, watching a game on the TV just marvelling at the fact that this was a job, and that this was his job.
And he was funny. Blimey he was funny – what an ability to be blessed with. I listened to a best of Baker and Kelly Upfront from the old Radio 5 on YouTube the other day; amazing calls about Arthur Cox locking a disgruntled fan in his office for two and a half hours, a man playing football with a pig’s head in a sausage factory in Peckham: “I used to like the volleys when the eyes used to pop out.” Anyone who has tried to make funny football content, of any kind – radio, TV, podcasts, social media – owes a debt of gratitude to him.
Last Wednesday afternoon Charlie Baker and I had to try to do him justice on TalkSport. Afternoon UK time, midnight til 3am for me in Australia. I was asleep when my phone rang and instantly presumed I’d slept through my alarm and missed the show. A millisecond of internal panic surged through me as I jumped up and cracked a shin on the bedside table. Danny would appreciate the ridiculous scene of me hopping around in the dark trying not to wake the kids while one of the bosses gave me the incredibly sad news.
If you’ve broadcast for any amount of time, you will be confronted with having to host shows just after someone has died. Jack Charlton, Terry Venables, Jimmy Greaves – but never before have I had to pay tribute to a friend.
Paul Hawksbee’s voice cracks and we all go. There are West Ham and Chelsea fans calling admitting they listen to his Spurs podcast because it’s him. There are all manner of texts recounting hilarious stories they heard on his shows over the last 30 years: the man who took a TV to a game in Northern Ireland so they could watch the FA Cup final, having to move around holding the aerial to keep the signal.
There’s a moment I think Danny would have found so funny, when I’m being sad – because it is sad, and I am sad – and into the break I read the sponsor’s lines: “This show is brought to you by Toolstation, first stop Toolstation” in such a maudlin way it’s as if I’m delivering a eulogy, just one sponsored by a hardware store. I catch myself just in time.
But most importantly there are so many messages from people who never met Danny, who never knew him, but who felt as if they knew him. We believed he would have wanted a bit of fuss made of him.
He definitely knew the enduring power of radio, even as the broadcasting landscape changes so quickly. It connects in a way nothing else can. And nothing said that more than messages we received from listeners who at one time or another were struggling and going through incredibly hard times and Danny’s energy, wit and joy were an escape and a tonic.
There will be a million people more important in Danny’s life than me. Our paths crossed a great deal, but never for very long. I was a minuscule cog in his world – but Danny had so much love to give. Voice notes about how to broadcast remotely or celebrating Spurs’ win in Bilbao; the tributes showed he had almost infinite time for others.
It always feels such a bland cliche to say it’s impossible to consider someone so full of life not being there – we all know that we have a sell-by date. At the start of October he had been given a choice: to ebb away slowly over a couple of years or have a big but very risky operation. Danny never ebbed.
He sent a big group WhatsApp voice note to many friends and colleagues, and I don’t think he would mind me writing what it said.
“I want you to know that I’ve enjoyed being around you, I’ve learnt from you, I’ve enjoyed working with you, you know how much I love my work – the fact I’m pretty good at it is secondary to how much I enjoy it, but look I’m very much hopeful that the boffins and my own determination will get me through this and we can all laugh about this message. But know how I care about you, how much you have meant in my life and on Thursd

items.text:
Yahoo for the loo! An ode to the commode! Dotty for the potty! It's World Toilet Day!
Twenty-five years ago, Jack Sim was flush with excitement. (Please pardon the pun.)
The Singapore entrepreneur was looking for a meaningful project and came upon this thought from the prime minister: "He said we should measure our graciousness according to the cleanliness of our public toilets," Sim recalls.
Thus was born World Toilet Day. The goal was more than cleanliness. It was access, too — billions of people do not have a safe and sanitary toilet to use.
Enshrined as an official U.N. day in 2013, World Toilet Day aims to get people talking and thinking about a topic that maybe is a taboo in polite conversation.
Let's eschew the euphemisms
World Toilet Day is all about peeing, pooping and addressing menstrual hygiene in a clean and safe manner — followed by the "conveyance" of excreta to a sanitary disposal system, notes Kate Olive Medlicott, the sanitation and waste team leader within the WASH team at the World Health Organization. Human diseases are shed in sewage, so a top-notch sanitation system is critical, says Medlicott. Cholera is linked to sewage. Polio is, too.
This year's World Toilet Day theme is "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures." Even though everyone suffers when they can't find a toilet, the menstrual cycle creates additional complications. If schools or offices lack a safe and sanitary place to attend to period needs and to dispose of period products, girls and women may opt to stay home.
There is another gender issue. Sofia Calltorp, the U.N. Women global head of humanitarian action, says: "When women and girls do not have access to safe toilets," they leave their home and look for a public toilet or a secluded space to do their business, often venturing into unsafe areas. "There is a huge impact in terms of being exposed to harassment or violence," Calltorp says. She points to refugee camps as a place where this issue often arises, with unlit toilets that aren't differentiated by gender.
Now you might well ask: Has World Toilet Day made a difference?
The toilet titans we interviewed say yes, it has, just by talking about toilets in the public arena. The U.N. has stated that access to safe sanitation is a human right. And in just about every country, progress has been made in improving access to sanitary facilities. Since 2015, 1.2 billion people have become part of the world of safely managed sanitation systems.
What are the next steps? Kellogg Schwab, who specializes in water and wastewater contaminants of public health concern at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, stresses that governments should be a force for change but that it shouldn't be top down. It should also be … oh, forgive me again … bottom up. Schwab suggests giving money to communities to figure out what solutions they can come up with to improve the toilet and sanitation situation. There will be flops. But there will be successes that can be scaled up.
So maybe one day — Medlicott of WHO thinks in 50 years or so —- Earthlings will look back and say, How curious that in a world of wealth there were not enough safe and secure toilets.
A toast to toilets
Let's end by reflecting on the present day.
"World Toilet Day is my favorite day of the year," says Medlicott. "People find it fun and funny but it's really important to celebrate and act on something we take for granted."
If you're among the population where toilets are plentiful, she suggests pausing to think of a moment — it's happened to all of us — when you needed a bathroom and couldn't find one. Maybe that incident has turned into a funny story you share with friends. Now imagine if it were to happen every day.
I am deeply thankful that all I need to do is walk down the office hallway to find a clean and private loo.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has received the House Democrats' nomination to become speaker when the party regains the majority in the new year. This nomination, confirmed by a closed-door vote of 251 to 11, marks the start of the formal selection process for speaker. It will culminate in a House floor vote on Jan. 3, at the start of the new Congress. If successful, Jeffries will make history as the first Black Speaker of the House. Jeffries said after the closed door vote that he is committed to addressing cost-of-living issues, pledging to fight for lower costs in groceries, gas, housing and healthcare.
- 🎧 Jeffries, who has served as the top Democrat in the minority since 2023, ran unopposed for the speaker position. But that is not the case in the Senate, NPR's Elena Moore tells Up First. Current minority leader Sen. Chuck Schumer faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen for majority leader. Van Hollen has positioned himself as an anti-status quo, progressive leader. Both Van Hollen and Schumer have served in Congress for decades. The vote for that Senate position is set for early December.
- ➡️ Rep. Robert Garcia, poised to chair the House Oversight Committee, sent document-preservation letters to more than a dozen of President Trump's allies and family members in preparation for investigations starting in January. These letters focus on four main areas: "Trump family corruption, corporate corruption, DHS misconduct and the White House Epstein cover-up."
Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping met today in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Xi and Putin met separately the night before the trilateral meeting. Trump also had one-on-one meetings with Putin and Xi. It's the first time the three leaders have held a summit together.
- 🎧 The three leaders had different agendas as they went into their meeting, NPR's Jennifer Pak says. Trump aimed to prioritize nuclear arms control. He said that they had a unique opportunity to reduce nuclear weapons, a stance Beijing has typically resisted due to its smaller stockpile compared to the U.S. and Russia. Putin sought discussions to end the war in Ukraine, but on Moscow's terms. The complexity of these issues makes substantial outcomes unlikely, Pak says. Xi aimed to position China as a stabilizing global force by bringing together Russia, its old ally, and the U.S., its direct competitor.
Anthropic is set to debut on the Nasdaq exchange today. The company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued the company at around $1.5 trillion. The company sold 956 million shares at $83 each, surpassing its initial target range of $70 to $78. The seven founders sold over 23 million shares as part of the IPO, and the company's prospectus outlines plans to introduce an extra $26 billion in shares through private placements with Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
- 🎧 In its IPO filing, Anthropic was optimistic that AI would have a bigger impact on the economy than industrialization, electricity, semiconductors and the internet, NPR's John Ruwitch says. The company's paperwork suggested that the addressable market for Anthropic's products could be as big as $40 trillion annually, exceeding the GDP of the United States. But CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the danger of losing control over AI. The prospectus flagged some political risks, including the company's current dispute with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. Issued on:
PRESS REVIEW – Thursday, November 19: An historic trilateral summit takes place in Shenzhen between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. But is it more optics than substance? Also, a highly awaited decision from the International Court of Justice could redefine genocide. Finally, a huge cultural moment: "Grand Theft Auto VI" is out and the reviews are ecstatic.
Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen this Thursday for an historic trilateral gathering on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Libération, the French left-wing paper, calls them the "infernal throuple" and wonders if this is an historic meeting or a meeting about optics. Arend van Dam, a Dutch cartoonist, thinks Putin and Xi are just paying lip service to Trump in a front-page cartoon published by Le Monde. British daily the Guardian evokes a "new world order" while La Repubblica, the Italian daily, calls the summit "global disorder."
In Asia, the South China Morning Post notes that Trump received an unprecedented welcome when he touched down on Wednesday. Xi greeted him at the airport – the first time in seven decades that a China leader has done so, the paper reports. The Taipei Times says Taiwan is closely watching the talks. Relations with China are extremely tense – Beijing has ramped up military pressure on the island to which it lays claim and Russia sent two military aircraft down Taiwan's east coast recently, the paper reports. The US is Taiwan's most important international backer.
Elsewhere, the International Court of Justice will deliver a verdict this Thursday on whether Myanmar is guilty of genocide in the persecution of the Rohingya people, a Muslim minority group. According to the UN, some 10,000 Rohingya have been killed and dozens of villages destroyed by the Myanmar government. Since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948 after the Holocaust, individuals have been successfully prosecuted for genocide in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia. But if convicted, Myanmar would become the first country to be found guilty of genocide and such a ruling would also define what constitutes the intention of committing a genocide and what proof is needed to show that it has occurred. The verdict is even more crucial as South Africa in 2023 accused Israel of violating the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. That decision will not be handed down before the end of this decade.
Finally, we end with the biggest cultural event of the year, at least for gamers: "Grand Theft Auto VI" has been released, to huge accolades. The Guardian evokes a "tonal shift" for the game famous for its "violence, misanthropy and pitch-black humour." The new romance is a Bonnie and Clyde-style love story. For those who fear the romance might tone down the grittiness of the game, rest assured, GTA is still "absurdly foul-mouthed, filthy and over-the-top offensive", the paper says.
Variety magazine reports that the game already has a score of 99 on Metacritic, tying it for the highest-rated game of all time with the original 1998 Nintendo 64 version of "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time". With reviews like that, it is no surprise that many workers around the world will be mysteriously calling in sick this Thursday. Parents, teachers, schools and HR departments will be managing a flood of sick calls and unexcused absences. According to The New York Times, there is even a term for it: "GTA flu". One Silicon Valley company has offered a floating day off – since studies show that playing video games improves productivity and reduces anxiety. But one Scottish man has taken it a step further. The Scottish Sun reports that he paid his wife and daughter to sign a "non-interference" contract – and stocked up on snacks so that he can game uninterrupted for the next seven days!
You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday.

items.title: Frontier Minerals eyes local refining of Mrima Hill rare earths to boost Kenya’s mineral value
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 19 – A US-led consortium selected to develop the mineral-rich Mrima Hill deposit in Kwale County has pledged to establish mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya, in a move aimed at retaining more value from the country’s strategic mineral resources.
Frontier Minerals C
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 19 – A US-led consortium selected to develop the mineral-rich Mrima Hill deposit in Kwale County has pledged to establish mineral processing and refining capacity in Kenya, in a move aimed at retaining more value from the country’s strategic mineral resources.
Frontier Minerals Consortium, comprising Bunker Hill Mining Corp., American Resources Corporation and ReElement Technologies Corporation, said its proposal would prioritise in-country processing, Kenyan employment, local supplier opportunities and technical skills development.
The consortium’s selection by the Government marks the next phase in efforts to develop Mrima Hill, which contains deposits of niobium, rare earth elements and other minerals considered important to global industrial and technology supply chains.
However, the selection does not grant the consortium an immediate licence to prospect or mine, with the company required to complete statutory licensing procedures, community consultations and environmental assessments before undertaking exploration activities.
Brad Barnett, Managing Member of Frontier Minerals, said the consortium intended to maximise the economic benefits of the mineral deposit through local value addition.
“We will undertake a thoroughly studied and respectful approach to optimising the value of this critical mineral deposit, with a focus on delivering value chain capture for Kenya, including processing and refining of minerals in-country,” Barnett said.
He said the consortium would also invest in capacity-building and opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy.
“We intend to create lasting opportunities for Kenyan workers, businesses and the wider economy through capacity-building and targeted investment, while prioritising environmental management and performance.”
The proposed approach would involve developing processing and refining facilities in Kenya rather than exporting mineral concentrates for processing elsewhere, potentially creating additional economic opportunities through the mineral value chain.
Frontier said its consortium members brought together expertise in mining, critical mineral supply chains and advanced refining technologies, with ReElement Technologies providing proprietary separation and purification technology for producing high-purity critical minerals.
The company said its refining technology had been validated across 15 rare earth and critical minerals and was already being used to produce multiple high-purity materials for customers.
It cited its refining facility in Marion, Indiana, in the United States, as a potential reference model for deploying advanced processing capacity in Kenya, subject to the necessary approvals.
The consortium said a full feasibility study would determine the most appropriate mining and processing methods, infrastructure requirements, project costs and commercial viability.
The study would also assess environmental, social and cultural heritage considerations, alongside opportunities for Kenyan participation in the project.
Community consent
Frontier acknowledged the environmental, cultural and social significance of Mrima Hill, saying meaningful engagement with host communities would be central to the project’s development.
The company said it would undertake environmental and social assessments to identify potential impacts and establish mitigation measures in line with Kenyan laws and regulatory requirements.
“Frontier recognises the environmental, cultural and social significance of Mrima Hill and the importance of ensuring that local communities are meaningfully involved as the project progresses,” it said.
“The consortium is committed to engaging openly and transparently with local communities and the relevant authorities.”
The consortium said its selection marks an “important milestone in the development of Mrima Hill and the beginning of the next phase of work.”
Its selection follows the Government’s conclusion of a competitive tendering process for strategic mineral development projects across the country.
Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs Cabinet Secretary Hassan Ali Joho announced that the Ministry had issued Notices of Intention to Award to the highest-scoring responsive bidders after completing the evaluation and statutory procurement reviews.
Besides Mrima Hill, a joint venture between Fangda Special Steel Technology Co. Ltd and Sinohydro Corporation was selected for the Kang’ura Chromite Development Project in Samburu County and the Kamacabi Copper Development Project in Tharaka Nithi County.
The tendering process, however, did not produce qualifying responsive bids for the Lali Hills Manganese Project in Tana River County and the Kiritiri Coltan Project in Embu County.
Joho said successful bidders would be required to engage host communities, landowners, county leadership and other stakeholders and obtain the necessary consents under the Mining Act before applying for prospecting licences.
“An award at the end of a tender process is not a licence to immediately break ground; rather, it is the gateway to meaningful local partnership and strict regulatory compliance,” he said.
The prospecting licence applications will be submitted through the Ministry’s Online Mining Cadastre portal and subjected to scrutiny by the Mineral Rights Board, which will make recommendations before the Cabinet Secretary grants the licences.
Frontier said it was ready to begin the licensing process, which will include securing a Prospecting Licence, obtaining the required community consents and an Environmental and Social Impact Assessment licence from the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA).
Exploration and the full feasibility study can only proceed after the necessary approvals have been secured.
A subsequent Mining Licence application would be supported by the feasibility study and a Community Development Agreement.

The ancestral home of the former interim leader of Bangladesh and Nobel Peace Prize winner, Muhammad Yunus,
items.text:
Home of Bangladesh’s former leader Muhammad Yunus set on fire
The blaze broke out during heightened violence in the country in advance of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s planned return.
The ancestral home of the former interim leader of Bangladesh and Nobel Peace Prize winner, Muhammad Yunus, was set on fire in the port city of Chittagong, police have said.
The fire broke out before midnight on Wednesday in the city, about 300km (185 miles) southeast of the capital, Dhaka, authorities said on Thursday.
The arson was followed by protests by supporters of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on Thursday, as violence swept parts of the country.
Yunus served as interim leader of the country for 18 months after a mass uprising forced Hasina to quit. She was flown out of the country by the military on August 5, 2024.
An abandoned ground-floor room in Yunus’s house was set on fire, and a police patrol spotted it and immediately doused the flames, officer Mozammel Haque told local media.
It was not immediately clear who was behind the blaze.
“Criminals set fire to the eastern side of the house. The area was being used as a storeroom,” Chittagong Metropolitan Police spokesman Aminur Rashid said, adding there were no casualties.
Authorities are investigating, and additional details were not immediately available.
Yunus has faced hostility from supporters of Hasina’s Awami League party, which has since been banned.
Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, said 22 of its branches have been subject to arson attacks in the last few days. Police have also reported explosions of crude bombs and roadblocks in Dhaka and other locations throughout Bangladesh in recent weeks in advance of Hasina’s planned return.
The 79-year-old politician, who has been living in India since fleeing Bangladesh, announced she would return to the country in December despite facing a death sentence. She told The Associated Press news agency earlier this month that even death could not prevent her from returning to Bangladesh.
Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia last year after a court convicted her of crimes against humanity over the deadly 2024 crackdown on protesters. The government has rejected her request for a new passport and identity card that would allow her to return.
Thursday’s protests were held after a call by the Awami League for a national “lockdown” to mark the anniversary of Hasina’s sentencing last year.
Earlier this week, protesters set fire to a police station and the home of a lawmaker in Gopalganj.
Clashes there killed two members of the governing Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), police said on Thursday, adding that 107 arrests have been made since Wednesday.
