A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the lo
items.text:
Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
- Published
Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62.bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.
Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.
The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.
Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.
The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.
The firm's $1.5tn valuation makes it more valuable than Walmart and Samsung and on almost on a par with Tesla and Meta.
But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.
One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.
Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.
But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.
Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".
Crucial test for AI
In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.
Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.
The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.
While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.
Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.
Rapid rise
Anthropic was started by seven former OpenAI employees, led by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei.
Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the risks posed by AI, amounting in his view to a possible threat to human existence.
The company has called for a slowdown in the development of AI, and a greater focus on safeguards while forging ahead with plans to grow quickly and boost its financing through the public markets.
OpenAI has voiced similar sentiments and delayed its plans to list on the stock market in order to address AI safety concerns.
Technology stocks have lost value in recent weeks following the US midterm elections. Democrats, who now control of both chambers of Congress, are expected to be tougher on AI regulation. Some Democrat candidates opposed the rapid build of data centres required to run AI.
But Anthropic went ahead with its market listing, despite the market volatility, because it needed to tap into additional funds, said Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton told the BBC. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more and so the time has come."
Broader anxieties about the AI industry remain.
Competition from low-cost rival models is growing.
Expensive computer chips, necessary for the industry to operate, are in short supply.
And the US Federal Reserve is concerned about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss interest rates, as well as the high concentration of AI exposure among a small number of firms.

items.title: How 'sleeping giant' Everton are exceeding expectations
items.summary:
Everton: How Premier League's 'sleeping giant' are exceeding expectations ahead of Brentford test
After a difficult summer, Everton are proving greater than the sum of their parts with another European push and some battling performances; watch Brentford vs Everton live on Sky Sports Premier League
items.text:
Everton: How Premier League's 'sleeping giant' are exceeding expectations ahead of Brentford test
After a difficult summer, Everton are proving greater than the sum of their parts with another European push and some battling performances; watch Brentford vs Everton live on Sky Sports Premier League and Main Event from 6.30pm on Monday Night Football; kick-off 8pm
Thursday 19 November 2026 11:14, UK
Everything felt a bit gloomy at Everton after the closure of the summer transfer window. 'Disappointment' was the buzzword used by David Moyes - especially after a Deadline Day move for Folarin Balogun fell through.
Moyes has said for some time that the Toffees need more bodies, but for all of his public declarations, Everton have been left with just 18 senior players and one recognised striker until January.
Coming so soon after a late-season collapse saw them miss out on European football, it is understandable why Moyes was left frustrated and some tipped them for relegation form.

- Everton fixtures & scores | FREE Everton highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
"My expectations changed during the window," the Scotsman said recently. "I don't think Everton are ever going to spend hundreds and hundreds of millions to improve so all I can do is take a small progression, get a bit better every year and that felt it was going to be much harder, but the players are doing a brilliant job with their league position."
Any expectations have been exceeded. Everton are mounting another European push, currently sixth in the Premier League - just two points from the top four. They are also into quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup, facing Fleetwood in the final eight next month.
"It's a massive club, a sleeping giant of the English game," Everton midfielder Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall told Sky Sports. "I really want to do something with this club or win some silverware and give the fans something to scream about."
While it remains early in the season, the belief and confidence is clear. The Toffees are proving greater than the sum of their parts as their upward trajectory under Moyes continues.
Everton don't know when they are beaten
It hasn't all been easy points for Everton - they have had to work hard for them. In two draws against Bournemouth and Manchester United, they did not score before the 83rd minute. They needed an 80th minute goal from Charly Alcaraz to beat Wolves in the third round of the Carabao Cup.
The Toffees also went behind to Coventry in their last Premier League match before the international break, going on to win 3-1. Admittedly, that game came with its own dose of luck for Everton, but fans might argue that it is about time they were on the right end of things.
After that game on Friday Night Football, Dewsbury-Hall said: "Our mentality this year has gone from strength to strength... we just never know when we're out of the game. Every time we have gone behind this season, we've reacted in a positive manner."
And just as importantly, they have seen out games when needed. There have been wins and clean sheets against Crystal Palace, Ipswich and Newcastle. They also swept the Magpies aside in the Carabao Cup fourth round with a convincing 3-1 win.
They have only lost twice - at home to Chelsea and away to Premier League champions, Arsenal. Neither result was disastrous.
In-form players boosting attacking output
After beating Newcastle in the Premier League, Moyes said: "We're creating chances. That's the big thing for me. We want to be a side that creates more chances. If we could be more offensive, that's the way I'd like it to be."
And Moyes is getting his wish. Everton are largely matching or exceeding their numbers from last season. While the number of goals scored per games is roughly the same, they are registering more shots and have a higher xG.
A big part of that is down to the form of their only recognised striker Thierno Barry. "He's come back off the summer like a different player," team-mate Dewsbury-Hall said.
He is playing far more centrally than last year - where he spent more time on the right wing - and is close to surpassing most of his attacking numbers from the entirety of last season with only ten games played. He has also scored in three successive games for Everton for the first time. Suddenly, the Frenchman is discovering a taste for goals that even the most optimistic Evertonian would have struggled to predict.
However, he has missed more big chances than any other Premier League player this season (16) - twice as many as the player in second, Bournemouth's Rayan (8). It suggests he has actually been anything but clinical, and if he had a better finishing touch, he could be an early frontrunner for the Golden Boot. His continued improvement in that part of his game is going to be vital for Everton.
Another in-form playing having a huge influence is Dewsbury-Hall himself.
Sky Sports pundit Jamie Redknapp was full of praise for the midfielder after his display against Coventry, especially in the No 10 role, running forward with and without the ball to push Everton up the pitch.
"I'm really enjoying it," the former Chelsea and Leicester man said of his role in that game. "I've got a really good hybrid role in this team where the gaffer has given me license to pop up all over the pitch.
"I feel like I'm getting a good relationship with Thierno now and I'm buzzing he keeps getting the goals because he deserves it so much... as long as he keeps performing, I'll keep trying to help him as much as I can."
The Moyes factor
Moyes is the Premier League's most experienced manager. Monday's game at Brentford will see him overtake Harry Catterick's record of the most Everton games managed, moving on to 493.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid will be chall
items.text:
FIFA confirms Diallo, Tashima as Infantino’s challengers at 2027 election
French football chief Philippe Diallo and Japan’s Kozo Tashima will be the only candidates to run for FIFA presidency next March when Infantino seeks re-election.
FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid will be challenged by the French and Japanese federations’ presidents, Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima, football’s global governing body has confirmed.
Former Swiss defender Ramon Vega, who announced his intention to run last month, was not among the candidates FIFA mentioned on Thursday.
The election, set to be held in March 2027, will be the first time Infantino faces a challenger after being re-elected without opposition in 2023.
French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo announced his candidacy on Monday, with the support of UEFA member associations represented on the executive committee and the FIFA Council.
Tashima, the Japanese Federation’s Association president, declared his bid earlier this month and formally submitted his nomination on Wednesday.
“The candidatures have been forwarded to the electoral committee for examination and for passing a decision on the admission of the candidates,” FIFA said in a statement.
“Member associations will be notified of the names of the proposed and admitted candidates no later than 18 February 2027.”
Infantino has faced repeated calls for his resignation since his FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, a bid to sell stakes in the World Cup and other major competitions, failed.
But the 56-year-old Swiss native, who has been the FIFA president since 2016, maintains that he has enough support from member associations around the world to get him re-elected.
Diallo, who took over as FFF president in 2023, played a leading role as France and other European associations withdrew their support from Infantino this year over the FFE controversy.
“Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of FIFA, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community,” UEFA said on Monday.

items.text:
Gianni Infantino 'is not eligible' for FIFA presidency, Sepp Blatter says
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
In an interview with FRANCE 24, former FIFA president Joseph (Sepp) Blatter claimed that Gianni Infantino "is not eligible" to run in the upcoming election for FIFA president because he's running for the fourth time, which is forbidden "according to the existing statutes of FIFA". Blatter also accused Infantino of buying votes and of "using FIFA's money to go from one country to the other to decide them to sign for him".
Gianni Infantino is seeking a third term as head of world football's governing body, with the election for FIFA president scheduled for March 18, 2027. In addition to the former president of the Japan Football Association Kozo Tashima, a last-minute candidate has officially entered the race: the president of the French Football Federation, Philippe Diallo, who is backed by the powerful European confederation UEFA.
"I think this is a candidature that has been well prepared because it's the candidate of UEFA and they have had time to study where is the candidate who would have a chance to win the presidency," Blatter said. "France are used to winning on the field of play. So I do hope also that this time, on the sports political side, that France will be le vainqueur (the winner)."
Read moreInfantino to face France's Diallo and Japan's Tashima in FIFA presidential election
A total of 211 football federations get a vote in the election, and Infantino has promised the federations up to $25 million each over the next four years. "It's not his money. It is the money of the organisation FIFA", Blatter reacted, accusing Infantino of "using FIFA's money to go from one country to the other to decide them to sign for him".
Pressed on these accusations against Infantino, Blatter said: "Everywhere he's going, also from the sports side or political side, he takes with him signed documents (...) That's why the solution to change the presidency of FIFA now is to make sure by all means that the actual president is not eligible for this Congress."
Infantino 'is not eligible'
Indeed, Blatter claimed that "according to the existing statutes of FIFA", Infantino "is not eligible now because it will be the fourth time" and a president can only be elected three times.
Up until the 2026 World Cup and the subsequent revelation of his plan to create a commercial subsidiary involving private investors close to US President Donald Trump, including the brother of his son-in-law Jared Kushner and even Kushner himself, nobody dared to criticise Infantino. "This has been done by his own decision," Blatter reacted. "There was no committee which has been together to do so. And therefore, now when the whole FIFA will come together, they have to be informed about that," he said.
A number of ties have been revealed between Infantino and Trump, such as FIFA renting office space that's nearly unoccupied in a Trump Tower in New York for over $4 million in rent over seven years. Democrats, who now have a majority in the US Congress, have vowed to investigate the issue. For Blatter, this is "a matter of the football organisation and not of a political organisation", adding that FIFA "should just rely on the activities he has had against the statutes and the laws of the game".
Asked about how he judges Infantino today compared to when he succeeded him, Blatter said that the worst thing Infantino has done "is (to) change the rules, the laws of the game" when he decided to nullify a red card after Trump personally intervened during this year's World Cup.
Blatter also claimed that Infantino "denied contact" with him and "didn't want to meet because I think he is not very comfortable to speak with me".

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – At least 155 people have been arrested in Kirinyaga County following a three-month security operation targeting illicit alcohol and drug trafficking.
County Commissioner Shufaa Omar Mwijuma said the arrests were made during a crackdown conducted between August and October 2026 under the Rapid Results Initiative (RRI).
Presenting the operation’s report, Mwijuma said 73 cases had been taken to court, with 58 resulting in successful prosecutions.
The operation saw security agencies seize hundreds of litres of illicit brews, including 384 litres of makabo, 60 litres of chang’aa and 51 litres of muratina.
Officers also intercepted 16 litres of dangerous ethanol before it entered the market, with the commissioner warning that its consumption could have resulted in loss of lives.
“We have no personal issues with business owners. Our concern is drinks that kill people. As County Commissioner, I have a responsibility to protect people and their property,” she said.
Authorities also confiscated 185 crates of assorted alcoholic drinks suspected to be uncertified, alongside other products that allegedly failed to meet Kenya Bureau of Standards requirements.
On narcotics, security agencies seized 15 kilogrammes of bhang, 1,373 rolls, 7,485 grammes and 10 brooms of the substance.
Mwijuma said the operation involved security teams across all five sub-counties, with the county government supporting efforts to streamline licensing of entertainment establishments.
She noted that the crackdown had helped restore order in bars and other drinking establishments, some of which had allegedly become hideouts for illicit activities.
The commissioner vowed to sustain surveillance and enforcement operations to curb the sale and distribution of illicit brews and narcotics.

items.text:
'I'm very healthy' - Kompany to return to dugout after health scare
- Published
Bayern Munich boss Vincent Kompany says he is "very healthy" and grateful for all of the support he has received as he prepares to return to the dugout on Friday.
The 40-year-old former Manchester City captain was taken to hospital after falling ill while watching the club's second team train last month.
Kompany was diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
Speaking at a news conference on Thursday he thanked the club, medical staff, players, coaches and fans for their support.
"It was very intense," he said.
"At the time, it was a new experience. Looking back, everything went perfectly. I received support right away, from the club and the doctors. I'm very grateful.
"You try to stay calm and wait until you have the results. It was a positive process, all the tests were positive.
"I have to say, I'm very healthy. We did a lot of tests, and they all came back fine. In those quiet moments, you also try to learn.
"Now I feel very good again and I'm happy to be back with the team."
While he has been recovering Kompany's assistant Aaron Danks has led the side to four wins and a draw.
Bayern, for whom England captain Harry Kane has been in fine form, are top of the Bundesliga, level on points with Borussia Dortmund.
Defending champions Bayern face Cologne on Friday after the end of the two-week international break.

DJ lag, one of South Africa's best-known electronic
items.text:
'It's a dream come true' – South African DJ celebrates featuring in GTA 6
- Published
South African DJ Lag says it is a "dream come true" to have his music featured on Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), the hugely popular video game released on Thursday.
DJ lag, one of South Africa's best-known electronic music producers, is among several African stars to feature, alongside Nigerian singers Burna Boy and Asake.
"I can't explain the feeling. I started playing the game last night and it's amazing," DJ Lag told the BBC's Newsday programme, adding that he had been playing GTA since he was about 10 years old and could hardly believe he was now part of the latest edition.
Many players have already had a chance to play the game following its worldwide launch.
The game, which lets players explore a fictional American city, features a dedicated African music radio station playing Afrobeats, amapiano and other sounds from across the continent.
The release of GTA 6 ends a 13-year wait for a new edition of the game.
Rockstar Games, the developer behind the franchise, has revealed details of the game's soundtrack and some in-game radio stations, but has yet to release a complete list of songs featured in the game.
Rockstar says AfroBank FM features everything from 20th Century African classics to contemporary amapiano and 3-step, giving the continent's music a prominent place in the latest edition.
Burna Boy co-hosts the station alongside British DJ and producer Palms Trax, while Asake's hit song Joha is among the tracks players can listen to as they drive around the game's virtual world.
DJ Lag, whose real name is Lwazi Asanda Gwala, is regarded as one of the pioneers of gqom, a genre of electronic dance music that emerged in the port city of Durban in the early 2010s.
He posted on Instagram: "God did."
Ghanaian highlife legends Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor also feature, alongside South African artists Robot Boii and Kamo Mphela, bringing a mix of classic and contemporary African music to one of gaming's biggest franchises.
Rockstar has also announced a 34-track official soundtrack album, released in partnership with Atlantic Records, featuring an original Burna Boy song titled Bigger.
For African fans, the inclusion of familiar music adds another dimension to the experience, allowing players to hear some of the continent's biggest sounds while exploring the American setting.
The series allows players to roam through sprawling fictional cities, drive vehicles and complete missions involving crime, police pursuits and other adventures.
The latest instalment takes players to Vice City, a fictional version of Miami, and the surrounding US state of Leonida, inspired by Florida.
Its story follows two criminals, Jason and Lucia, who become caught up in a wider conspiracy after a robbery goes wrong.
The launch has generated enormous excitement among gamers around the world.
Some fans downloaded it in advance so they could begin playing as soon as it became available, while others have booked leave from work.
The previous edition, GTA 5, was one of the best-selling video games of all time, selling more than 200 million copies worldwide.
The new release is expected to be another major commercial success, although it remains to be seen whether it will match its predecessor's extraordinary sales.

items.text:
UN top court convicts Myanmar of ‘genocidal intent’ against Rohingya
In case filed at the ICJ in 2019, The Gambia accused Myanmar of breaching the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The United Nations’s top court has found Myanmar guilty of “genocidal intent” in massacres that killed 10,000 Rohingya in its military operations in 2017.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague delivered its judgement on Thursday over the military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 mainly Muslim Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.
Evidence shows Myanmar forces killed some 10,000 Rohingya, ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said during a three-hour readout of the verdict.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh,” he added.
In specific cases that he referred to, he said Myanmar had acted with “genocidal intent”.
The case was brought by the West African nation of The Gambia, which in 2019 accused Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people. It asked the ICJ to rule that Myanmar has breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order the nation to put an end to any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished.
Myanmar, meanwhile, has claimed its crackdown was in response to attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) on police posts.
The ICJ said that the “only reasonable inference” from evidence of widespread atrocities by Myanmar security forces is that they had the intent to destroy a “substantial part” of the Rohingya minority.
It said Myanmar should have known that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians participated in the military campaign. “Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” it added.
More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in sprawling refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh, according to the United Nations.
Conflict, shrinking humanitarian aid and dangerous sea crossings continue to leave many members of the community displaced and vulnerable.

items.summary:
Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers confirmed?
- Published
Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.
World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take pla
items.text:
Will Infantino feel he's already won as Fifa challengers confirmed?
- Published
Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima will take on incumbent Gianni Infantino in next year's Fifa presidential election.
World football's governing body has confirmed the three candidates for the election, which will take place at the Fifa Congress in Morocco on 18 March.
European football's governing body Uefa only identified its candidate Diallo fewer than 48 hours before Wednesday's deadline.
French Football Federation (FFF) president Diallo, 63, received the unanimous support of Uefa's executive committee.
Japan Football Association honorary president Tashima, 68, announced his intention to stand against Infantino, 56, earlier this month.
Tashima is a member of the Fifa Council and a former international footballer and coach.
Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega had also said he intended to stand but was not named as a candidate by Fifa on Thursday.
A late and surprise choice, Diallo said: "I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative...I'm entering this campaign not just to provide a different voice, but to win."
But he is not the Frenchman some believe Uefa really wanted, as it tries to remove Infantino in the wake of his failed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.
Senior figures in European football had hoped to persuade Arsene Wenger - Fifa's head of global development - to stand against his own boss. Some felt that only he possessed the credibility to pose a serious threat to Infantino's plans for a fourth term.
But after the former Arsenal manager chose not to proceed, Uefa had no choice but to seek an alternative.
So just how credible a challenger is Diallo? Does Infantino's position appear unassailable? And how could he still be stopped from winning another term?
- FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on 
  - Published14 hours ago
- Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino 
  - Published3 days ago
- Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency 
  - Published5 November
'A fantastic advocate for change'
An administrator who has worked in French football since 1992 and became FFF president in 2023, Diallo is not a household name. But he has already shown he is prepared to stand up to Infantino.
In September, Diallo claimed he had "seriously damaged the image and unity of football", and said "trust has been broken" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) sell-off plot.
According to Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister, Diallo is a "candidate who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform" within the governing body.
"We've always made it very clear that our objectives and motivations are driving culture change. That means wide-ranging, systemic reform of football governance rather than simply the replacement of an individual leader," McAllister told BBC Sport.
"I've known Philippe since we were both elected to Uefa's executive committee, and he's an intelligent, honest, sharp-minded football person with an impressive experience of governance in one of the world's football power-houses. Most importantly, he is a person of integrity... Philippe is a fantastic advocate for the change agenda that football needs, and I know his campaign will reflect that."
Infantino remains the favourite to win a majority of the 211 votes, and is thought to have the support of most of Africa (54 members), Asia (47) and South America (10).
However, Uefa hopes that Diallo - whose father was a Senegalese boxing champion who represented France in the 1960 Olympics - could enjoy support in parts of Africa and beyond. He claims he already has the backing of countries beyond Europe.
Has Uefa lost momentum?
While most of Europe's national associations are expected to vote for Diallo, it is clear that he was not Uefa's first choice. "I wasn't initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer," he admitted.
Uefa only approached Diallo about standing in the past week, and senior officials at some European national associations have also told BBC Sport they are frustrated with the failure to find a higher-profile candidate sooner.
Speaking anonymously, one said they only learned about Diallo's potential candidacy on Sunday, and that while they were supportive of him, "it would have been helpful if we'd had someone much earlier" and "a lot of eggs were put in the Wenger basket."
They also made the point that Diallo was yet to publish a manifesto, and questioned whether he could really win.
Another expressed similar sentiments, saying Diallo was a good man, but "not seen as a heavyweight". They claimed that Uefa had "lost the momentum. The process hasn't been great. I really hope they've got a rabbit to pull out of the hat."
McAllister is optimistic: "I have no doubt whatsoever that we will collectively mount a powerful campaign with the objective of winning the election next March". she said.
"The really critical period comes next, once candidate nominations close and eligibility checks are complete."
Infantino win inevitable?
Despite high-profile critics like Germany manager Jurgen Klopp - who this week said "the opinion is unanimous that a change would make sense" - Infantino does appear to be in a position of strength.
As recently as August it all seemed very different. Fifa's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour strongly criticised Infantino for the FFE scheme, while a senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned. The heads of three confederations - Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America - then signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".
Amid an increasingly acrimonious civil war, Infantino seemed vulnerable. But the revolt against him then suffered a series of setbacks.

- Published
An Ecuadorian footballer has been banned for eight years for throwing a rock at an assistant referee, leaving him requiring surgery to his face.
Jhon Perlaza was playing for Club Ciudad de Yantzaza against Club Rio Aguarico FC in a third-tier match in October when the incident took place.
The stone struck assistant referee Lenin Giovanni Ojeda Nunez in the face in the 96th minute of the game, which was subsequently abandoned.
A video on social media shows Perlaza standing up in the team's dugout to throw the stone, with Nunez instantly falling to the floor and holding his face after the object hits him. He then receives medical attention.
"The assistant referee suffered serious injuries that required surgery and a 60-day recovery period," the Ecuadorian Football Federation (FEF) said.
"The disciplinary committee found the player responsible for physical aggression against a match official and suspended him for eight years from all football-related activity, until 19 October, 2034.
"In addition, the FEF will ask Fifa to extend this sanction worldwide."
The FEF also fined his club Yantzaza $2,000 (£1,521) and ordered them to pay Nunez's medical fees of $4,369 (£3,323).
In a statement released on 20 October, three days after the match, Yantzaza apologised to the refereeing team and the fans, and confirmed Perlaza had been sacked as a result of the incident.
"As an institution, we categorically reject all acts of aggression, whether verbal or physical, both inside and outside sporting venues. We firmly believe that football should be a space of respect, coexistence, and fair play," they said.
"Once the person responsible for this regrettable incident was identified, the institution made the decision to remove him immediately, and he is therefore no longer part of our club."

items.title: Ruto Rejects Politics of Exclusion, Pledges Equal Development
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – All parts of Kenya have an equal right to development, President William Ruto has said.
The President criticised leaders advocating for politics of exclusion based on a community’s voting numbers or population.
He said no part of the country or community would be left behind
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – All parts of Kenya have an equal right to development, President William Ruto has said.
The President criticised leaders advocating for politics of exclusion based on a community’s voting numbers or population.
He said no part of the country or community would be left behind in the Government’s ambitious transformation agenda, adding that all Kenyans would be treated equally.
“Do you want to be told about shares? Do you want to be told you come from a small community or you are few?” he posed.
He was speaking on the first day of his development tour of Western Kenya, where he presided over the opening of the Kakapel Iteso Cultural Centre in Teso North Constituency, Busia County.
The facility is dedicated to preserving and promoting the rich cultural heritage of the Iteso community.
President Ruto announced that the Government would allocate additional funds to expand and enhance the centre’s capacity to attract visitors from across Kenya and beyond.
He was accompanied by Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula, Busia Governor Paul Otuoma and several Members of Parliament, among other leaders.
The President reiterated his commitment to uniting the country and eradicating politics of discrimination, hatred and tribalism.
He said this informed his decision to join forces with the Orange Democratic Movement and other political parties to form the Broad-Based Government.
“We want every Kenyan to feel like they belong in Kenya and enjoy equal rights,” he said.
President Ruto urged Kenyans to carefully scrutinise leaders seeking elective positions and elect those with proven track records and clear development agendas, while accusing the opposition of lacking a vision for the country.
Earlier, the President laid the foundation stone for the Akichelesit General Service Unit (GSU) Camp in Teso North Constituency, a project expected to strengthen security in the region.
He also announced that the Government would invest KSh100 million in housing for police officers deployed to the camp to provide them with decent living conditions as they serve and protect the public.
He said the Government was committed to providing security officers with adequate housing and equipment to enable them to effectively discharge their constitutional mandate of protecting the lives and property of Kenyans.
Mudavadi said President Ruto was keen on developing critical infrastructure in the Western region to facilitate trade with neighbouring Uganda.
He said the President’s leadership was anchored on equality and ensuring that no region was left behind in the country’s development agenda.
“Let us, therefore, as a community and as a region, join forces with President Ruto to secure victory in 2027,” he said.
Speaker Wetang’ula described the Malaba-Mombasa highway as a critical transport corridor that had suffered years of neglect.
He said the President would soon unveil plans for the construction of a dual carriageway from Mombasa to ease congestion, boost trade and improve livelihoods.
Governor Otuoma said Busia County had been left behind for a long time but expressed confidence that its transformation was now on course under President Ruto’s leadership.
“After 10 years of President Ruto, you will not recognise Busia County,” he said.
Public Service Cabinet Secretary Geoffrey Ruku [confirm the speaker’s identity/title if this is the intended reference] said the President was delivering on his commitments, citing the proposed Malaba Smart City project, which he said would put the county on the path to transformation.

Denmark's parliament on Thursday ratified a security deal involving Greenland and the United States. The vote comes months after the US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement to end a standoff with the Trump administrati
items.text:
Denmark ratifies Greenland security deal after months of pressure by Trump
Denmark's parliament on Thursday ratified a security deal involving Greenland and the United States. The vote comes months after the US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement to end a standoff with the Trump administration over the Arctic island's future.
Denmark's parliament on Thursday unanimously ratified a security agreement with US President Donald Trump covering Greenland, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island's future that has rattled transatlantic relations.
The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September to resolve tensions after Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory that is home to 57,000 people.
Read moreUS, Denmark and Greenland sign security deal to bolster Arctic security
The deal was backed by 109 Danish lawmakers and none voted against, the parliamentary tally showed.
It is not subject to a vote by the US Senate.
The executive agreement will, following Thursday's vote in Copenhagen, enter into force once the Danish foreign ministry informs the US in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete.
The deal expands the US military's role in Greenland, including permission to establish a "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.
Trump's refusal to rule out military or economic force to acquire the island triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO in January and forced Denmark and Greenland into months of intensive negotiations.
Greenland's parliament ratified the deal this month.
Last week, it passed a first reading in Denmark's parliament with backing from all parties, and lawmakers expressed relief and hope that the deal will normalise the situation in Greenland.
"However, there are many indications that this is not an end, but rather a beginning," said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen.
"With the treaty in hand, the US will be able to demand greater influence on decisions that have security policy implications and on part of the extraction of strategic resources," he said. Other experts say the new agreement does not add much US military access to Greenland.
The shortest route from Europe to North America runs via strategically located Greenland, where the northernmost US military base is already located.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

A year after the UN-backed ceasefire, 2 million Palestinians are confined to an area of less than 130sq km as Israeli territorial expansion and aid blockades deepen the crisis.
One year after the United Nations Security Coun
items.text:
‘Displacement by design’: Trump’s Gaza peace plan a failure, aid groups say
A year after the UN-backed ceasefire, 2 million Palestinians are confined to an area of less than 130sq km as Israeli territorial expansion and aid blockades deepen the crisis.
One year after the United Nations Security Council endorsed the Trump administration’s 20-point Comprehensive Plan to end the Gaza Conflict, a coalition of five prominent international aid organisations has issued a damning assessment.
As Israeli forces launched a new ground offensive in central Gaza this week, advancing with tanks west of its “Yellow Line”, and issued new forced evacuation orders, in violation of the peace plan, the Danish Refugee Council, Norwegian Refugee Council, Oxfam, Refugees International and Save the Children, released a humanitarian scorecard which grades the plan at just four out of 26 possible points. The plan scored a zero on humanitarian access and earned just one point for civilian protection.
Israel’s expanding military footprint
Despite the Gaza Peace Plan’s explicit prohibition against territorial occupation in Gaza – and its requirement that Israeli forces withdraw – the Israeli military “Yellow Line” has moved further west, expanding control of Gaza territory from 58 percent at the start of the ceasefire 13 months ago, to 65 percent today, according to OCHA. Israel itself has said it controls 70 percent of the territory, a UN official told the UN Security Council in June this year.
Palestinians are not allowed to cross the line, so this expansion has confined roughly 2.1 million Palestinians to just 128sq km (49 sq miles), according to OCHA last month, squeezing 16,000 people into each square km. More recent analysis suggests it may be even smaller. Recent map analysis by US news group NPR found the confinement area is now just 109sq km (42 sq miles), creating a population density of nearly 19,300 people per sq km.
Ramy Abdu, founder and chairman of the Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, warned that Israel is carrying out unlawful acquisition of territory by force.
The human cost has been devastating, agencies say, with at least 1,650 Palestinians killed and 5,975 wounded since the “ceasefire” was declared in October last year.
Earlier this week, Shaun Hughes, World Food Programme (WFP) country director for Palestine, told journalists: “When you’re in Gaza, it does not feel like a ceasefire. Israeli military control across nearly 70 per cent of Gaza means that people have almost no space to grow their own food. Fishing in the sea is prohibited and also life-threatening. Unemployment is over 80 per cent, so without humanitarian assistance, people have little or no alternate means of survival.”
Lilu Thapa, executive director for the Middle East, Asia and Europe at the Danish Refugee Council, said: “Palestinians in Gaza are being confined as the “Yellow Line” expands. This is displacement by design, and a ceasefire that allows it is a ceasefire in name only.”
A ‘political shield’ for genocide
The diplomatic framework overseeing this crisis, specifically the Board of Peace and International Stabilization Force (ISF) established by United States President Donald Trump, has drawn intense scrutiny from human rights experts who accuse the body of abandoning its mandate.
“Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor believes that, from the moment of its establishment, the Board of Peace represented a serious infringement on the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination, both in its composition and in the powers entrusted to it,” Abdu told Al Jazeera.
The Board, chaired by the US, operates without any meaningful Palestinian representation, Abdu said.
“Instead, it has effectively become a political shield for Israel’s occupation and its crimes, contributing to the perpetuation of genocidal conditions while providing political cover for grave violations of international law,” Abdu told Al Jazeera. “The available evidence supports describing the Board’s role as a form of functional normalisation of genocide and starvation.”
Mohsen Abu Ramadan, a board member of the Palestinian NGOs Network, said: “Regretfully, the Board of Peace failed the international community and continues to provide political cover for ongoing genocide and atrocities.”
Aid blockade deepens
The peace plan announced last year stipulated that a minimum of 600 UN-coordinated humanitarian aid trucks would be allowed to enter Gaza daily. In reality, an average of just 49 UN-coordinated trucks entered the Strip each day in September.
Only two percent of these limited convoys carried medical supplies, leading to critical shortages and deaths from treatable illnesses.
Instead, Israeli authorities have increasingly prioritised the entry of commercial trucks carrying expensive goods that the impoverished population cannot afford to buy.
During the week of October 12, of 315 commercial trucks which entered Gaza, 223 carried food and 51 carried non-essential items. Only 12 carried hygiene and shelter materials and just a single truck carried medical supplies.
Israel has cited “dual use” restrictions, which restrict the entry of products and goods which have a military as well as a civilian purpose.
Jan Egeland, CEO of the Norwegian Refugee Council, said that the crisis stems from political decisions. “The suffering of Gaza’s 2.1 million people is not inevitable. The world must stop accepting it,” Egeland said. Oxfam America President Abby Maxman noted that the reality on the ground is a “direct result of policy choices made in Israel, the US and at the UN.”
Mounting winter crisis
As Gaza enters its fourth winter of displacement, the shelter crisis has reached breaking point.
While donors have pledged about $18bn for Gaza via the Board of Peace, more than a year after the ceasefire was declared, reconstruction has yet to begin and nearly 1.4m Palestinians are living in makeshift shelters.

items.summary:
Five return for Wales' World Cup play-off final
- Published
Ceri Holland has been named in the Wales squad for next month's Women's World Cup play-off final against Norway despite being out since September through injury.
Olivia Clark, Hayley Ladd, Rhiannon Roberts and Ella Powell are also included
items.text:
Five return for Wales' World Cup play-off final
- Published
Ceri Holland has been named in the Wales squad for next month's Women's World Cup play-off final against Norway despite being out since September through injury.
Olivia Clark, Hayley Ladd, Rhiannon Roberts and Ella Powell are also included after fitness issues, but Ffion Morgan, Laura Hughes and Scarlett Hill are among those who miss out with injuries.
The versatile Holland, arguably Wales' most influential player, has been out with a muscle problem, though she is thought to be close to returning to action for club side Liverpool.
Her involvement is a major boost for Wales as they attempt to reach the Women's World Cup for the first time.
Rhian Wilkinson's side face Norway at the Cardiff City Stadium on Tuesday, 1 December, before the return leg in Oslo four days later.
Wales v Norway
Women's World Cup qualifying play-off final first leg
Tuesday, 1 December at 19:15 GMT
Cardiff City Stadium
Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.
Leicester goalkeeper Clark and Sunderland defender Roberts are also included even though they have not played since September, but the loss of promising Manchester United defender Hill is a blow given her impressive displays against Albania.
Crystal Palace's Ladd and Powell, of Bristol City, have played for their clubs since missing Wales' World Cup play-off semi-final games against the Albanians last month.
Winger Morgan had returned to action for West Ham after not being involved against Albania, but she is back on the sidelines after suffering a knee injury while playing for the Hammers last weekend.
Like Southampton midfielder Hughes, Mia Ross – who is without a club after leaving Charlton in September - is missing again, while Fulham full-back Charlie Estcourt is another absentee.
There is also no place for Sunderland defender Tara Bourne, who has switched allegiance from England to Wales but is injured.
There is a recall for once-capped teenager Gwen Zimmerman, who plays for American side Northwestern NCAA, while Newcastle youngster Casi Gregson is included again after winning her first cap against Albania.
- Wales start Nations League with home double-header 
  - Published5 days ago
- Wales in fight to retain rising female stars 
  - Published1 November
Wolves midfielder Chloe Williams keeps her place having been a late call-up for the semi-final, while the only uncapped player in the squad is third-choice goalkeeper Soffia Kelly.
Wales are hoping to cause an upset as they bid to reach the Women's World Cup for the first time, though beating former champions Norway may not be enough to guarantee a place in Brazil next summer.
The complex nature of the qualification process means that Wales may have to negotiate inter-confederation play-offs next February to secure a World Cup place, even if they triumph over Norway.
Wales squad
Olivia Clark (Leicester City), Soffia Kelly (Aston Villa), Safia Middleton-Patel (Watford – on loan from Manchester United), Hannah Cain (Everton), Mayzee Davies (Manchester City), Gemma Evans (Newcastle United), Olivia Francis (Wolverhampton Wanderers), Casi Gregson (Newcastle United), Mared Griffiths (Manchester United), Ceri Holland (Liverpool), Elise Hughes (Sunderland), Sophie Ingle (Bristol City), Angharad James (Seattle Reign), Lois Joel (Newcastle United), Carrie Jones (IFK Norrkoping), Hayley Ladd (Crystal Palace), Esther Morgan (Bristol City), Mary McAteer (Ipswich Town – on loan from Charlton Athletic), Phoebie Poole (Watford), Ella Powell (Bristol City), Rhiannon Roberts (Sunderland), Rachel Rowe (Nottingham Forest), Tianna Teisar (Watford), Lily Woodham (Liverpool), Chloe Williams (Wolverhampton Wanderers), Gwen Zimmerman (Northwestern NCAA).

items.text:
AI giant Anthropic raises more than $100 billion in record-setting IPO
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Anthropic shares are about to make their market debut after the company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued it at around $1.5 trillion.
It's a remarkably rapid ascent for the five-year-old artificial intelligence powerhouse, and a sign of strong investor appetite despite growing concern about a possible AI bubble.
Anthropic sold 956 million shares — far more than originally planned — at an IPO price of $83 per share, it announced on Wednesday. That price exceeded its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share.
The company's seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO. On top of that, Anthropic's prospectus included plans to put an additional $26 billion worth of shares into the market through private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
The total haul is more than $107 billion.
Anthropic valuation could rise or fall later on Thursday, when its shares start trading publicly on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.
The amount of money raised makes Anthropic's IPO the biggest in history, after Elon Musk's mega-conglomerate SpaceX landed $75 billion when it listed in June.
A breakaway beginning
Anthropic's rise has been meteoric.
"We've never seen a company that's able to grow this fast [and] be this dominant," said Andrew Rocco, a stock analyst at the financial research firm Zacks.
Anthropic got its start in 2021 as a breakaway group of researchers who once worked for ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. Led by now-CEO Dario Amodei, the Anthropic founders were concerned that OpenAI, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.
Amodei and the others quickly raised hundreds of millions of dollars and set out to develop AI models in a way that the company said focused on safety and "alignment," or the idea that AI should be harmless and act in ways that jibe with human values and intent.
Anthropic launched Claude in early 2023, just months after OpenAI released ChatGPT. Ever since, the two companies have been neck-and-neck competitors in cutting-edge artificial intelligence, known as "frontier AI." The Claude family of AI models, including the Claude chatbot and Claude Code, are among the most popular and powerful in the world, and have helped transform everything from online search to software engineering.
They are also the San Francisco-based company's main source of income, according to its IPO prospectus, which said revenue in the first half of the year skyrocketed 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, versus a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
Opportunities and risks
The IPO comes at a time when shares in tech companies linked to the AI boom have been volatile. Investors have vacillated between enthusiasm for what many believe will be a revolutionary technology and concern that the vast sums of money being poured into it may be hard to justify.
"It's going to be a test of investor sentiment towards the AI trade," said Janice Quek, an equity analyst at the investment research firm CFRA. "We've seen in recent weeks that there has been a lot of pressure and really market sell-offs on the AI ecosystem just because a lot of people are worried about the AI bubble, for example, or the concerns around AI financing and whether there's a return on investment on AI."
The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down more than 11% since early October.
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, an early Anthropic investor, told a Semafor conference on Monday the IPO is one of the best ways to invest in AI applications. He said his firm had trimmed its exposure to AI infrastructure — companies involved in things like manufacturing semiconductors and building data centers — but that Altimeter had requested an allotment of Anthropic stock worth $5 billion.
"I've been waiting for it," he said of the IPO. "We put in for the largest request in the 20-year history of our firm."
There is indirect evidence in Anthropic's prospectus that businesses, rather than individual subscribers, are its biggest source of revenue. Malik Ahmed Khan, an equity analyst at Morningstar, says the company's long-term success may hinge on those companies' pace of adoption of AI technologies, but it's unclear how fast that will be.
"Radios went from like 10% penetration to 90% penetration in the U.S. within a decade. Washing machines, to reach that level of penetration, took a multi-decade period," he said. "So when we're thinking about Anthropic and broadly AI in the enterprise setting, what does that adoption curve look like?"
Conflict with the Pentagon, and "pacing the frontier"
Anthropic has not been without controversy. Earlier this year it became embroiled in a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. The Pentagon wanted the military to be able to deploy Anthropic's models without restriction, but Amodei drew a line at fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon subsequently labeled Anthropic a "supply chain risk," a designation previously reserved for foreign adversaries.
And skeptics have criticized Amodei's rapid push to develop AI despite his own dire warnings about the technology's risks. In September, Amodei wrote an essay urging his AI competitors to "pace the frontier," or to slow down development of the most cutting-edge models and make sure that safety incidents are being reported and scrutinized by third-party auditors.
That essay followed a summer when AI agents from Anthropic's lab, as well as OpenAI and other competitors, were revealed to have hacked other companies, setting off a frenzy of concern about the risks of rogue agents. This week, California sued OpenAI over its agents that hacked into Hugging Face, an open-source software

items.text:
Malaysian weightlifting champion Roslin loses arm after motorbike crash
Muhammad Hafizuddin Roslin, who won a gold medal at the Commonwealth Games 2026, had his arm amputated after an accident.
Malaysia’s Commonwealth Games gold medal-winning weightlifter Muhammad Hafizuddin Roslin had his right arm amputated after a motorcycle accident but is in a stable condition in hospital, a Malaysian sports official said.
Roslin was “awake and smiling,” following a seven-hour-long surgery at Kuala Lumpur Hospital, Malaysia Weightlifting Federation president Ayub Rahmat told the AFP news agency on Thursday.
The 21-year-old was conscious and in a stable condition in hospital, three days after the crash, the country’s top weightlifting official said.
Roslin reportedly lost control of his motorcycle while riding on the expressway on Monday night and sustained injuries to his right leg and arm, a haematoma – pooled blood – in the neck, as well as minor head injuries, according to Malaysian media.
Doctors amputated Hafizuddin’s arm above the elbow, local media reports said.
“Physically, his condition is improving but this incident has had a great impact on his future,” Rahmat said. He called it “a shock and a huge loss” for weightlifting in the country.
The Malaysian government said it would cover all treatment costs.
“The government, through the [National Sports Council], is fully covering the costs of treatment and medical care related to the incident, including follow-up treatment and hospital accommodation until he is discharged,” the ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
It added that Roslin’s training allowance would also continue at the current eligible rate.
Malaysian’s Sultan Idris Education University (UPSI) also offered psychological support and sports psychology intervention for Roslin as part of his recovery, Malaysian media reported.
“In this critical situation, an athlete’s greatest challenge is not merely the physical healing process, but also how to cope with emotional shock, the denial phase and the sudden loss of sporting identity,” said Dr Jaffry Zakaria, associate professor of the Faculty of Sports Science and Coaching (FSSK) at UPSI.
Hafizuddin won gold at this year’s Commonwealth Games in the men’s 88kg category and set a games record with a total lift of 345kg. His attempt of 162kg in the snatch category set a national record as well as a games record.
He was a prospect for the country at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.

items.text:
Nov 19 – A machine weighing 28 kilograms once intimidated Rekha Devi. Today, she is among a growing number of rural Indian women using agricultural drones to spray crops, earn livelihoods and challenge the belief that operating sophisticated technology is a man’s job.
Rekha’s journey reflects a wider transformation taking place under India’s Namo Drone Didi initiative, which is equipping women from rural communities with skills to operate drones for agricultural purposes.
The women, popularly known as ‘Drone Didis’, are combining technology with farming expertise to improve crop management while changing perceptions about women’s roles in agriculture and rural enterprise. Didi, the Hindi word for elder sister, is a term of respect and affection commonly used for women in communities.
Their experiences, including those of Sabina Khatoon from Ayodhya, Sita Devi from Karnal, Rekha Devi from Agra and natural farming advocate Kanta Devi from Ambedkar Nagar, show how agricultural innovation is opening new opportunities for women.
For decades, crop spraying has involved farmers walking through fields carrying heavy tanks to apply fertilisers, pesticides and liquid nutrients such as Nano Urea. The work is physically demanding, takes considerable time and often requires large amounts of water.
Drones are changing that process by allowing farmers to apply agricultural inputs more quickly, uniformly and efficiently.
Sita Devi is among the women who have embraced the technology. Before beginning her journey, she had limited knowledge of the wider world, including where Delhi was located. She subsequently completed pilot training in Gurugram and began offering drone-spraying services across five districts.
She has now covered about 5,000 acres and travelled to Delhi to share her experience on a national platform, illustrating how rural women are gaining confidence and expertise in technology-driven agriculture.
The path to becoming a drone operator, however, has involved overcoming unfamiliar technology, personal sacrifices and resistance from communities.
When Sabina Khatoon enrolled for training at Droner Aviation in Motihari, Bihar, she had only encountered drones used to film weddings and movies. She initially imagined that if agricultural work did not materialise, she could use the equipment to film local weddings.
The prospect of operating a large agricultural drone was intimidating. Rekha Devi was similarly taken aback when she encountered the 28-kilogram machine after completing three months of training in Hyderabad, Allahabad and Bihar.
Her training was further complicated by a language barrier in Hyderabad, where lessons were initially delivered in English. She struggled to follow instructions, relying on hand gestures until Hindi-speaking trainers were arranged.
The programme required five to six hours of classes each day. Rekha also had to leave her three-year-old son behind during training, a decision she made with the support of her husband and in-laws.
Despite these difficulties, both women gradually gained confidence as they learnt to operate the drones.
Returning home presented another challenge. In many communities, drone operation was viewed as a male occupation, with women questioned about their ability to handle expensive machinery.
Rekha recalls men mocking her and boasting about their driving licences while doubting her credentials.
She responded that although they were licensed to drive two- and three-wheelers on the ground, she was the only person in her district licensed to fly in the air.
To convince a farmer who was initially reluctant to allow her to spray his crops, Rekha offered a free demonstration. The results helped persuade him to trust her services.
Sabina Khatoon also faced hostility in Chaudhara Gram Panchayat, where a male drone operator reportedly encouraged a crowd and local children to ridicule her as she prepared to work.
She told her colleague, Sheila Didi, to disregard the heckling and concentrate on the flight. Sabina carefully manoeuvred the drone around overhead power lines before spraying a banana plantation.
The demonstration changed the mood, with the women winning applause and securing orders to service 40 acres of farmland.
The initiative is also helping create a network of women with the skills to train others, extending its impact beyond individual operators.
Organised through village Self-Help Groups (SHGs), the programme encourages trained women to become trainers, enabling communities to build their own capacity to operate drone-based agricultural businesses.
Sabina has trained 80 women farmers, while Rekha works with 15 of the 20 women’s groups in her village. She is preparing between five and 10 backup operators in each group to ensure that services remain available when a pilot is unable to work.
Alongside the adoption of technology, women such as Kanta Devi are promoting more sustainable agricultural practices.
Kanta, from Roshan-garh village in Ambedkar Nagar, leads a network of more than 500 women farmers who advocate chemical-free farming using natural inputs derived from cow dung and cow urine.
She promotes beejamrit, an organic microbial preparation used to treat seeds before planting to protect them from soil-borne diseases, and jeevamrit, a fermented liquid bio-fertiliser used to improve soil fertility and encourage beneficial microbial activity without synthetic chemicals.
The growing influence of the Drone Didis is extending beyond the fields. Through their work, women are earning incomes, developing businesses and gaining recognition within their communities, where they are increasingly addressed as Sabina Didi or Drone Didi.
Their success is also helping shift attitudes in households and villages. Men who previously expected women to remain confined to domestic duties are increasingly seeing them as examples of what their daughters and wives can achieve.

items.text:
Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
SHENZHEN, China and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday – capping two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even as the men who led them had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.
"History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," said Xi in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."
Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."
"In that sense and I think in lots of other ways, we are making history," said Trump, who called it a "special responsibility" for the three countries to work together.
Yet, they offered few solutions toward peace, with the leaders offering divergent agendas going in:
Trump wanted to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and his mission to keep Iran from obtaining them; Putin was looking to push for an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow; Xi was signaling he hoped to avoid wading too deep into either topic — preferring to showcase China's growing global clout with more general statements promoting peace and economic stability.
There were also topics to avoid: Trump refused to engage with journalists' questions over China's alleged role in an espionage plot to steal high end Nvidia chips.
In the end, the summit's key deliverable was arguably the image itself: the president of the United States gathering with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia for the first time in American history.
Summit speed dating
Despite being billed as a summit of "groundbreaking significance" by the Chinese hosts, sit-down talks between Trump, Xi, and Putin were relatively brief — with some of that time taken up by interpreters delivering simultaneous translation.
Trump's meeting with Putin lasted 42 minutes. His talks with Xi went about an hour. The trilateral group session went on for an hour and a half.
Still, it was enough time for familiar Trump bonhomie to emerge.
"Who's he? He's my friend," said a smiling Trump upon seeing Putin ahead of their bilateral meeting.
"We've known each other for a long time," added Trump after he and the Russian leader warmly shook hands. "And I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this. Or at least start."
Similarly, Trump told Xi "as long as you and I are in charge of things, we're never going to have a problem."
Both statements were tacit admissions the clock is ticking on Trump's remaining two years in office — with change coming even sooner to Washington when Democrats take control of Congress come January.
Getting there
The China gathering was first proposed by Putin during an October phone call with Trump — an offer to meet together with President Xi when China hosted the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in China that November.
For Putin in particular, the meeting was always going to be a coup: the latest sign that — with Trump and Xi's help — he has effectively chipped away at Western attempts to isolate him politically over his invasion of Ukraine.
Back in Moscow, state media showed footage of the three leaders huddled together seemingly on loop — proof that Russia had regained what the Kremlin sees as its rightful place among global superpowers.
Ignored by Kremlin-friendly media were hints at more subtle power dynamics at play.
Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac personally — returning a gesture Trump had given the Chinese leader during his recent visit in Washington — while Putin received a more scaled down delegation upon arrival to Shenzhen.
Similarly, Trump was offered the top spot next to Xi during the APEC group photo and sat next to Xi during the APEC dinner reception — with Putin positioned at a separate table.
Was it a slight to Putin? A calculated attempt to flatter Trump? A reflection of Russia's vastly weaker economy? Whatever the answer, Xi wasn't ignoring his Russian guest entirely.
The two gathered privately for two hours on Wednesday — a sit-down China-Russia watchers estimated to be their 50th meeting all told.
Xi and Putin also echoed each other in their public speeches— both touching on familiar themes of the dawn of a new "multipolar world" and criticizing the use of sanctions as a sign of Western influence on the wane.
A new Yalta?
From the outset, critics of the summit voiced concern that Trump, Xi, and Putin would seek to carve the world into each country's perceived sphere of influence.
In Russia, the event was billed as a potential "new Yalta" — a reference to a moment in 1945 when the leaders of the U.S., Soviet Union, and United Kingdom hastily agreed to a post-World War II order for Europe.
Instead, the Shenzhen summit reflected the far more fragmented priorities of its participants.
Trump made no secret he hoped to include China in arms control talks — what Trump calls "denuclearization" — at a moment when key landmark nuclear treaties between Russia and the U.S. have all expired.
The catch: his Chinese hosts had little interest in the issue.
Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed U.S. attempts to include it in negotiations with Russia — noting that its arsenal remains far below those of Cold War-era rivals Moscow and Washington.
Differences also extended to the war in Ukraine, where Putin had hoped to press for U.S. and Chinese support for a settlement tilted in Moscow's favor — including a redrawn security map for Europe that would amount to a rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.
Xi has insisted Europe have a seat at the table in any negotiated settlement. Trump has largely relied on his trusted envoys — real estate developer Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner — to hash out the complexities of any peace deal.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 19 – Linda Mwananchi Movement leader Edwin Sifuna has announced plans to hold his first rally in Eldoret upon returning from a 10-day tour of the United States, where he is expected to engage Kenyans living abroad.
Speaking during an interview on Citizen Radio, Sifuna maintained that every Kenyan deserves an opportunity to understand the country’s political direction and the kind of leadership being proposed.
“Everyone is free to travel across the country seeking votes. Even me, when I return, I want my first rally to be in Eldoret,” he said.
“As I have told you, as a leader, I understand that I have a responsibility to explain our country’s political direction because this country belongs to all of us. There is no Kenyan who should be denied an opportunity to understand what the country would look like under your leadership,” the Nairobi Senator added.
Sifuna said the US tour would provide an opportunity to explain his political position and the movement’s vision through engagements with Kenyans living abroad.
“Our brothers and sisters living in the United States invited us. We will hold town hall meetings, which they particularly enjoy, to engage and have conversations with them,” he explained.
Sifuna has also released a detailed itinerary for the Linda Mwananchi Movement (LMM) diaspora tour, scheduled to run from November 21 to December 7, 2026.
The programme includes town hall meetings, church services, fundraising and community dinners, engagements with Gen Z groups and meetings with elected officials.
The tour comes as Sifuna steps up efforts to popularise the Linda Mwananchi Movement, following the rebranding of The Equitable Party (TEP).
The rebranding was approved during the party’s National Delegates Conference held on November 13, 2026, in an invite-only convention.
Sifuna took over the leadership of TEP on October 4, 2026, as part of efforts to establish a political vehicle for the Linda Mwananchi Movement.
The US tour will cover New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Texas, Washington State and California.
It will begin in Hackettstown, New Jersey, on November 21, with the official opening of the movement’s US office.
Sifuna will then travel to Allentown, Pennsylvania, on November 22, where he is scheduled to attend a church service before holding a town hall meeting at The Palace Center.
In Maryland and the Washington DC metropolitan area, the Nairobi Senator will hold a series of engagements between November 23 and 25, including a business community dinner, discussions on East African politics and policy, and meetings with elected officials.
The programme also includes engagements with the Afri Thrive organisation, as well as meetings with the 6.25 Movement and Gen Z representatives.
The delegation will proceed to Texas, where Sifuna is scheduled to attend a Thanksgiving dinner in Dallas on November 27 before holding a women’s caucus and a town hall meeting in Houston on November 29.
The tour will later move to Washington State, with engagements in Federal Way and Renton on December 3 and 4. These will include church services, a gala dinner and another town hall meeting with Kenyans living in the region.
Sifuna will conclude the tour in California, where he is scheduled to hold a town hall meeting in San Francisco and a gala dinner in Oakland on December 5, before attending a concluding dinner in Silicon Valley on December 7.
