Aston Villa vs Sunderland: Can Villa recover after sour note or will Black Cats begin to build?
Aston Villa left for the international break on a sour note after squandering a two-goal lead on two occasions at Old Trafford for their dramatic 4-4 draw against Manchester United.
Sunderland, meanwhile, secured a much-needed 1-0 win against Chelsea to relieve the pressure on Regis Le Bris.
His side remain in the bottom three because of their poor start to the season and a win at Villa Park is a big ask, especially given injuries to Granit Xhaka and Brian Brobbey, but it will be needed if talks of his departure are going to fizzle out.
The Black Cats have not travelled well this term with just one win on the road, which came in their narrow escape at Portuguese second-tier side Torreense, but Villa Park's crackling atmosphere has been dampened by the closure of the North Stand this season.
Injuries, storylines and ramifications. Plus, if it is anything like their last meeting at Villa Park, a dramatic 4-3 win for Villa courtesy of Tammy Abraham's injury-time winner, then this is one you will be wanting to follow along in the Sky Sports live blog.
Pat Rowe
Coventry vs Palace: Manager bounce or manager bump? Eagles might be in for a nasty surprise
The managerial merry-go-round is spinning again. Crystal Palace have jumped aboard, handing Thomas Frank the keys to Selhurst Park. New hope. But a new manager doesn't necessarily mean new results.
In fact, recent evidence suggests quite the opposite for teams in trouble.
The famous 'new manager bounce' is one of football's most romanticised theories. A fresh face walks through the door, standards supposedly rise overnight and points start rolling in.
Shame the numbers don't back it up.
Of the last six Premier League teams sitting in the bottom eight to change manager between November and March, five actually saw their points-per-game average drop across the following five matches.
Vitor Pereira at Nottingham Forest. Igor Tudor at Tottenham. Rob Edwards at Wolves. Graham Potter at West Ham. Ivan Juric at Southampton.
It's a fascinating trend that should serve as a warning to Palace supporters expecting Frank to arrive waving a magic wand.
The reality is that struggling teams usually have deep-rooted problems that can't be solved by a few tactical tweaks and an inspirational team talk. Confidence, structure and, ultimately, quality of players tend to outweigh a difference voice in the dugout.
Coventry are next up for Palace and Frank will be desperate to buck the trend.
But history suggests the bounce might be more of a bump.
Lewis Jones
Bournemouth vs Forest: Can Cherries pick up one more win to make club history?
Bournemouth couldn't buy a Premier League victory in the opening six weeks or so of the season, but over the last month they have looked like an unstoppable force. Now they can't stop winning.
Since a 3-0 win over Sturm Graz in the Europa League on October 15, the Cherries have won four in a row in the Premier League, three in a row in Europe and once in the Carabao Cup, booking a spot in the quarter-finals.
Eight wins in succession in all competitions; a club record equalled.
It's made even more astonishing when you realise Marco Rose has only been in charge for 16 games. And that it's the club's first ever season in Europe. And that those eight wins came within a period of just 25 days.
With the schedule that lies ahead, the run will naturally come under threat sooner rather than later, but where's the harm in trying to squeeze out one more win to make history?
Dan Long
Tottenham vs Ipswich: Stop Enciso, stop Tractor Boys?
Ipswich have a Julio Enciso problem. Not because the Paraguayan isn't delivering the goods. Quite the opposite. He's become so influential to their attacking output that stopping him is the key to stopping Ipswich.
Bournemouth certainly cracked it before the international break.
Their 2-1 victory over Ipswich was a tactical lesson in how to suffocate a team reliant on one creative spark. Cut off the supply lines into Enciso, deny him the space to weave his magic and ask the rest of the Ipswich attack to come up with the answers.

Max Verstappen has backed F1's plans to proceed with the final two races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi; the Red Bull driver had previously expressed doubt
items.text:
Max Verstappen says he trusts F1 bosses over plans to proceed with season-ending races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi amid conflict in Middle East
Max Verstappen has backed F1's plans to proceed with the final two races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi; the Red Bull driver had previously expressed doubts; watch the Las Vegas GP on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday
Thursday 19 November 2026 08:21, UK
Max Verstappen says he trusts Formula 1 to "make the right call" as the sport pushes on with plans to hold the final two races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi despite continued conflict in the Middle East.
F1 had to cancel races scheduled in April in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, but the Qatar Grand Prix from November 27-29 and Abu Dhabi Grand Prix from December 4-6 are currently set to go ahead.
While F1 bosses had maintained throughout the year that their intention was to proceed with the events as planned, it was only after the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on November 8 that a contingency plan to hold a season-ending race in Italy was aborted.

Therefore, Wednesday evening's media sessions ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, which forms a season-ending triple header with the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, was the first opportunity for the drivers to publicly react to the latest developments.
Red Bull's Verstappen, who had in September voiced his opposition to ending the season in the Middle East, appears to have changed his position.
The four-time world champion said on Wednesday: "I trust F1 and FIA to make the right call on that, right?
"I don't have all the intel. I'm not an officer. I just hope that they make the right call on that. And that's all that you can rely on, really.
"They also send over their findings and understanding. So I trust them."
While there haven't been notable recent incidents in Qatar or Abu Dhabi, a US military base in Bahrain was targeted over the weekend, and Houthi rebels in Yemen are advancing in their war against the country's Saudi Arabian backed government.
Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc acknowledged that the situation remains "tricky" but also expressed faith that F1 and the sport's governing body, the FIA, will act responsibly.
"It's a situation that is kind of tricky," Leclerc said. "At the same, I feel like we are up to date with whatever is organised, and I guess that on our side we have to trust the process, and that's what I'll do.
"I'm sure the FIA is taking everything seriously to make sure that everybody is safe. It's in the best interest of absolutely everyone.
"So, yeah, me as a driver, I'll just trust that process, and be in Qatar if it's safe to be there."
Norris, Russell reassured by friends in region
British drivers Lando Norris and George Russell both said they have been reassured by friends of theirs who live in the Middle East.
Russell often represents his rivals in his role as a director of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association (GPDA), but he explained that the seriousness of the situation has resulted in that organisation having little involvement.
"We're [the GPDA] not involved because it's way above our heads, and the truth is, we will be going if nothing is escalated," the Mercedes driver said.
"F1 is not making those decisions, it's the people in the high powers of politics.
"I trust in Formula 1. I'm not concerned. I know a lot of people who live in the region, and they say pretty bluntly, 'we're living there with our families, and if we didn't feel safe, we wouldn't be.'
"They feel safe as it is, and I'm sure and I hope everything will be ok."
Norris revealed that he will be attending a friend's wedding in Bahrain ahead of the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but said he was more concerned for members of his McLaren team than himself.
"I have my friend's wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there and then going on to Qatar and then Abu Dhabi," the 2025 world champion said.
"But it's not about me. It's a lot more people. It's the fans, it's the team personnel, so the question is for them, more than I would say it is for myself."

A skyscraper in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh was damaged on Thursday after the Gulf country reported new attacks by Yemen's Houthis. Witnesses said the city's Public Investment Fund Tower, which showcases Saudi Arabia'
items.text:
Skyscraper in Riyadh damaged as Saudi Arabia reports surge in new Houthi attacks
A skyscraper in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh was damaged on Thursday after the Gulf country reported new attacks by Yemen's Houthis. Witnesses said the city's Public Investment Fund Tower, which showcases Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions, was "damaged across several floors, with windows blown out".
A skyscraper in Riyadh housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund was damaged on Thursday, witnesses said, as the kingdom reported new attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited over the summer in neighbouring Yemen's civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.
In the early hours of Thursday, AFP journalists in the Saudi capital reported a powerful blast had been heard.
Around the same time, civil defence authorities issued a warning for "potential danger" but said minutes later that the danger had passed.
Read moreYemen: Why the Houthis may besiege Aden rather than storm it
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had "addressed a missile threat launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh".
"Initial assessment indicates the impact of debris, with material damage currently being surveyed," said coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki.
Witnesses later told AFP that Riyadh's Public Investment Fund Tower, which at 80 storeys, is the tallest in the city's financial district, had been damaged.
"The facade is damaged across several floors, with windows blown out," said one source who requested anonymity. Two other sources confirmed the damage.
Standing 385 metres high, the tower dominates King Abdullah Financial District, which acts as a showcase for Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions.
Read moreYemen's Houthis advance on Aden as government forces retreat to defend their capital
With imposing skyscrapers, luxury shops and green spaces, the district also hosts the headquarters of the Saudi stock exchange along with multinationals such as Goldman Sachs.
Chaired by Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the sovereign wealth fund is one of the largest in the world with more than $900 billion in assets under management.
It is also one of the main instruments for diversifying the kingdom's economy away from oil, plans which have been threatened by the latest fighting.
Deadly airport attack
Malki also said Thursday that the coalition had intercepted five ballistic missiles launched towards Saudi Arabia's southern region, which borders Yemen.
The Iran-backed Houthis have stepped up their attacks against Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, striking targets including airports, energy infrastructure, military sites and Riyadh's financial district.
In October, a deadly attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 14 people and injured hundreds, forcing the suspension of flights for two weeks.
In response, the Saudi coalition has been striking Houthi targets in areas of Yemen held by the group.
On Thursday, Houthi media outlets reported that Saudi Arabia had launched another attack on Yemen's capital Sanaa.
The Almasirah television channel said Saudi forces have "once again targeted the shoe and textile factory of the Alyateem Development Foundation", citing its correspondent in Sanaa.
The Saudi coalition said it had "destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Dhamar", a city about 100 kilometres (60 miles) south of Sanaa that was used by the Houthis to strike Riyadh.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.summary:
Why is Pete Hegseth strengthening US military ties with Venezuela?
Hegseth’s new military deal with Venezuela raises questions about US influence, regional security and Maduro’s removal.
Hegseth unveils new US-Venezuela military deal
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced a new c
items.text:
Why is Pete Hegseth strengthening US military ties with Venezuela?
Hegseth’s new military deal with Venezuela raises questions about US influence, regional security and Maduro’s removal.
Hegseth unveils new US-Venezuela military deal
United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced a new cooperation agreement with Venezuela’s interim government to facilitate military cooperation between the two countries.
The Pentagon chief’s announcement came during an unannounced visit to Caracas on Wednesday. The US says the agreement will help fight drug trafficking and improve security in the region. Venezuela says it will help strengthen its military without compromising its sovereignty.
But why is an agreement happening now, and what does each side stand to gain?
Here is what we know:
What is the new US-Venezuela military agreement?
The US and Venezuela have agreed to strengthen military cooperation in several areas, including joint training, intelligence sharing, military equipment and border security.
Hegseth met Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez and Defence Minister Gustavo Gonzalez Lopez in Caracas. He said the agreement would allow the two countries’ armed forces to work together to combat drug trafficking and armed groups operating in Venezuela.
Rodriguez described Hegseth’s visit as an extraordinary step in relations between the two countries.
She said renewed military cooperation would help improve troop training, modernise equipment and give armed forces access to new technologies.
Her government said the country’s armed forces, known as the Bolivarian National Armed Forces (FANB), would benefit directly from the agreement.
However, the full terms of the agreement have not been made public, including details of how the two countries would carry out joint military operations.
Why is the US strengthening military ties with Venezuela?
The Trump administration said closer military cooperation with Venezuela will help fight drug trafficking and armed groups, and improve security in the region.
Hegseth said the agreement should help Venezuela regain control of areas where armed groups and drug trafficking networks operate.
But political analyst Carlos Pina said the timing of the visit is important, particularly after the Democrats won the midterm elections in the US.
“I think many of the things happening between the United States and Venezuela are closely related to the November 3 election results,” Pina said.
He explained that the Democrats have already said they aim to increase scrutiny of US foreign policy towards Venezuela, including the agreements reached with Caracas during 2026, after US forces abducted then-President Nicolas Maduro and took him to New York. The US has since, in effect, taken control of Venezuela’s oil industry — the country has the world’s largest oil reserves.
Pina also pointed out the recent attempt to impeach Hegseth. “I think this Hegseth visit also falls within that framework, to get ahead of what will be the debate in the new US Congress.”
On November 10, the House of Representatives voted 211-204 against impeaching Hegseth for now, but Democrats could try again after January, with their new majority in the House.
The November resolution against Hegseth, introduced by Republican Thomas Massie, included eight articles of impeachment related to the US-Israel war on Iran, military strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats and the January operation that ousted Maduro from power.
Massie said Hegseth ordered an act of war against Venezuela without congressional authorisation. He argued that the operation went beyond arresting Maduro on drug trafficking charges and was also intended to give Washington control over Venezuela’s oil reserves.
“Secretary Hegseth executed unlawful orders effecting the removal of the President of a sovereign nation, placed boots on the ground, conducted preparatory bombardments, inflicted substantial casualties, and subsequently caused regime change, each of which constitutes acts of war,” Massie said in the impeachment resolution.
Pina believes Hegseth’s visit is partly aimed at defending Trump’s policy in Venezuela before Democrats take control of Congress in January.
“Hegseth goes to Venezuela, which is probably one of Trump’s few foreign policy successes, to show the American public that the plan they are carrying out in Venezuela benefits US national interests,” he said.
Why is Delcy Rodriguez cooperating with the US?
Rodriguez and her government welcomed the agreement, saying it will help strengthen the country’s forces and improve its training and access to technology.
Venezuelan officials have also stressed that the cooperation must respect the country’s sovereignty and constitution.
But analysts say the agreement may also signal Rodriguez’s efforts to remain in power following Maduro’s ousting.
“The simple answer is that they want to remain in power as long as possible,” Phil Gunson, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera.
He said Rodriguez’s government faces considerable pressure from Washington. “If they decline to cooperate, they have been told they will suffer the same fate as Maduro, or worse.”
He also pointed to Washington’s financial leverage over Caracas.
“The US currently controls most of Venezuela’s foreign earnings, in the form of revenue from oil sales, and can cut off the funds whenever it wishes,” Gunson said.
Since Maduro’s ousting in January, revenue from Venezuelan oil sales has been deposited into US-controlled accounts, with Washington supervising the release of funds to Caracas.
According to a Department of State report released on November 12, more than $12bn from Venezuela’s oil and other natural resources passed through these accounts between January and September.
The US government said nearly 99 percent of the money had been disbursed mostly to individuals and businesses in Venezuela through commercial banks. But the agreement means Caracas depends on Washin

Editor’s note: This article contains references to suicide and gra
items.text:
Gaza Syndrome: Why Israeli soldiers’ trauma erases Palestinian victims
In a new Al Jazeera Originals film directed by Awad Joumaa, Israeli soldiers describe the psychological toll of the genocide in Gaza, yet many express no remorse.
Editor’s note: This article contains references to suicide and graphic descriptions of combat.
If you or someone you know is at risk of suicide, support is available through international crisis helplines.
“I think our army is the most moral army in the world.”
Itay Sagi, a reservist in the Maglan unit, describes killing Hamas fighters inside Israel after October 7, 2023.
“I didn’t choose to kill people. I had to,” he says.
His grief is for his friends. Sagi wants to go back and fight. He does not mention the Palestinians killed in Gaza.
Boris Shtonda, who served with an Israeli special forces unit, lost a leg when an explosive device detonated inside a building in Gaza in November 2023, killing four of his friends.
“We lost our friends, we lost our families, we lost everything,” he says.
The Israeli soldiers in the film “Gaza Syndrome” speak of nightmares, panic, addiction and Israelis who died by suicide. They speak, too, of wanting to return to fight. In hours of testimony, the Palestinians of Gaza are almost entirely absent.
The overwhelming weight of Israel’s war has fallen on Palestinians in Gaza: their children, homes and hospitals. Israeli forces have killed at least 74,700 Palestinians, including more than 21,000 children, according to Al Jazeera reporting. In September 2025, an independent UN Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed genocide in Gaza. The soldiers in this film are part of those forces.
Guy Zaken, a military bulldozer driver, told an Israeli parliamentary committee that soldiers had to “run over “‘terrorists’, dead and alive, in the hundreds”. His co-driver, Eliran Mizrahi, spent 186 days in Gaza demolishing homes and died by suicide two days before he was due to return. “He got out of Gaza, but Gaza did not get out of him,” his mother told CNN.
The question is not whether the Israeli soldiers’ psychological injuries are real. It is what psychological injury means when it is joined to denial, impunity and the absence of remorse.
Psychological crisis
In The Wretched of the Earth, the mid-20th century psychiatrist and political philosopher Frantz Fanon observed that colonial violence inflicts severe psychiatric trauma on both the colonised and the perpetrators. When soldiers carry out systematic destruction and violence, the psychological toll cannot be separated from the political structure that enables and ignores it.
An Al Jazeera Investigative Unit examination of more than 2,500 Israeli soldiers’ social media accounts documented wanton destruction, abuse of detainees, and the use of Palestinian civilians as human shields.
The scale of the psychological crisis is growing. Nearly 30,000 Israeli soldiers and security personnel wounded since October 7 have entered the Defence Ministry’s rehabilitation system, the ministry said in October.
About 63 percent have psychological injuries, with thousands formally diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and acute stress reactions following prolonged combat exposure. The Israeli army says 22 soldiers died by suicide in 2025, one more than in 2024, up from 17 in 2023. An Israeli parliament Research and Information Center report recorded 279 suicide attempts between January 2024 and July 2025. Combat soldiers accounted for 78 percent of the deaths by suicide in 2024.
Mohanad Mustafa, a scholar of Israeli society, told Al Jazeera Israel faces “a psychological crisis among thousands of soldiers, but no moral crisis”.
He says many soldiers feel no remorse for violations of international law. “This indicates a very significant moral decline in Israeli society.”
Israel’s public culture has helped make that denial possible. Oren Ziv, an Israeli journalist with +972 Magazine, says soldiers he interviewed described “an atmosphere of revenge, that everything is allowed”. They could shoot if they saw movement, he says, or if they were bored, and “nobody will investigate it”.
Daniel Bar-Tal, a political psychologist, says soldiers in Gaza still confront Palestinian suffering “to some extent”, even when they deny it or refuse to see it.
This suppressed awareness, he said, creates a quiet, internal fracture, a psychological burden that deepens precisely because the trauma cannot be fully acknowledged or resolved without confronting the suffering of those they harmed.
Ashira Darwish, a Palestinian trauma therapist and survivor of severe trauma and torture who created Active Meditation to heal from full-body paralysis, believes Israeli soldiers can enter Gaza, shoot children and burn homes only by suppressing their own humanity. She and other trauma experts emphasise that returning reservists undergo a severe psychological transition when re-entering civilian life after engaging in continuous combat.
“Someone who can exterminate an entire people while sitting there laughing will carry a psychological impact.”
Darwish describes reservists returning from Gaza to a hospital, office or school within a week or two. She warns of anger, substance addiction, domestic conflict, and sudden outbursts of violence as untreated combat trauma manifests in everyday interactions. “Where are they supposed to go with everything they have done?”
Israel’s Observatory on Femicide recorded 34 femicides in 2025, a 48 percent rise from 23 in 2024. Firearms were the most common weapon for the first time. Women’s groups warned early in the war that combat trauma and expanded access to guns could heighten the risk of domestic violence. There is no official data proving that returning soldiers caused the rise, and the Observatory found no link between licenced guns and femicide. items.text:
How Premier League's big six keep getting richer
- Published
Ten games into the Premier League season, four of the top six spots are occupied by 'big six' clubs.
Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, and Premier League ever-presents Everton, have muscled their way in.
In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.
The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.
And the gap is growing. Every season.
BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.
Big six get richer and the gap grows
Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.
In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.
Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.
This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.
Let's look at how the gap has grown.
We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.
This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.
In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was £120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to £442m.
So what has driven this huge escalation?
In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.
Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.
"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.
"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."
Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.
It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.
For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.
But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.
Champions League widens the gulf
It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.
This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.
But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.
When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.
This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or £713m, for the historically most successful clubs.
At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned £37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool £35.5m and Chelsea £33.3m. Newcastle received only £13.6m.
The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.
Their value pillar is projected to be worth £25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.
The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.
Stamford Bridge - Chelsea's big problem
Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.
In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.
Not just by a small amount. They were £74m behind Tottenham, and £200m below Liverpool and City.
Chelsea's problem is simple - seats.
Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.
Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of £80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.
Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.
"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.
"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."
Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only £16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by £69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by £85m.
"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.
"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."
Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.
But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.
How new rules allow big six to spend even more
You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).
PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.
That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).

items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – Former Attorney General and National Assembly Speaker Justin Muturi has landed an international role after being appointed to the Commonwealth Election Observation Mission in The Gambia.
Muturi will join a team of election experts and prominent figures from different countrie
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 19 – Former Attorney General and National Assembly Speaker Justin Muturi has landed an international role after being appointed to the Commonwealth Election Observation Mission in The Gambia.
Muturi will join a team of election experts and prominent figures from different countries tasked with observing the electoral process in the West African nation.
The appointment was announced by the JB Centre, which said the former Cabinet Secretary had been selected by the London-based Commonwealth Secretariat in recognition of his experience in public service, parliamentary leadership and democratic governance.
“It’s an honor,” Muturi reacted to the appointment.
The mission will be led by former Lesotho Prime Minister Pakalitha Mosisili and will bring together experts from Nigeria, Saint Lucia, Sierra Leone, South Africa and Sri Lanka.
Other members include former ECOWAS Commission Director of Political Affairs Prof Aderemi Isola Ajibewa, constitutional governance scholar Prof Cynthia Barrow-Giles and Campaign for Good Governance Executive Director Marcella Samba-Sesay.
The team will assess the conduct of the elections against democratic principles, focusing on transparency, credibility and electoral integrity.
According to the JB Centre, the mission will work alongside international and regional stakeholders as part of efforts to support free, fair and transparent elections.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya,Nov 19 – Standard Chartered Bank Kenya recorded a 13 per cent year-on-year increase in profit before tax to Sh14.9 billion in the nine months to September 2026, on improved cost efficiency and stronger contributions from its wealth management and markets businesses.
The growth came despite an 18 per cent decline in net interest income, as lower interest rates and margin compression weighed on earnings from lending activities.
Operating income declined by six per cent during the period, with a 22 per cent increase in non-interest income providing a partial cushion against weaker interest earnings.
The growth in non-interest income was driven by stronger momentum in Wealth Solutions and Markets, signaling the bank’s increasing reliance on fee-based services and investment-related activities to diversify its revenue streams.
Operating expenses fell by 14 per cent, reflecting continued cost-control measures, while loan loss provisions declined by 62 per cent following recovery efforts and an improvement in the quality of the bank’s lending portfolio.
Standard Chartered Bank Kenya Chief Executive Officer and Head of Coverage Birju Sanghrajka said the performance reflected sustained business momentum and growth in non-interest income.
“We maintained strong momentum in the first nine months of 2026, delivering 13 per cent year-on-year growth in profit before tax to KSh14.9 billion, supported by growth in non-interest income,” he said.
The bank’s balance sheet expanded during the period, with net loans and advances to customers increasing by 16 per cent to Sh179.6 billion compared to December 2025.
Customer deposits grew by 18 per cent to Sh335 billion, largely supported by increased corporate deposits, while assets under management rose by 19 per cent to Sh361 billion, reflecting increased activity in its wealth management business.
Asset quality also improved, with the non-performing loan ratio declining by 130 basis points to 4.7 per cent, suggesting a lower proportion of the bank’s loan portfolio was classified as non-performing.
The lender maintained a liquidity ratio of 61.75 per cent, above the regulatory minimum of 20 per cent, while its Liquidity Coverage Ratio stood at 485 per cent against the required 100 per cent.
Its total capital ratio was 18.1 per cent, exceeding the regulatory minimum of 14.5 per cent.
Sanghrajka said the bank would continue focusing on client relationships and wealth management as it navigates changing economic conditions.
“We remain focused on supporting our clients in achieving their financial objectives while delivering sustainable growth.” he said.
The bank described Kenya’s economic environment as broadly stable, supported by a relatively stable currency and lower interest rates, although it noted that rising inflationary pressures and global geopolitical tensions continue to pose risks to energy markets, trade flows and investor sentiment.

items.text:
What makes 'Grand Theft Auto VI' more than just a game?
November 19, 2026
"Oh, it's so on now!" is the tagline in the latest trailer for the video game "Grand Theft Auto VI," or "GTA VI" for short.
"GTA VI" is a game of superlatives that's been crashing through records. The hype around it is unparalleled. No game in history has clocked so many pre-orders. It's thought that around 10 million people have already purchased it. There's no denying it: "GTA VI" is a global cultural phenomenon.
A few days before its release on November 19, fans can already start downloading the game. The file is so large that downloading it can take several days, depending on the internet connection. Providers have already registered a significant spike in data traffic.
As soon as the game is unlocked, players can start speeding through the fictional US metropolis of Vice City in a stylish sports car with criminal couple Jason and Lucia.
Miami gets cast as Vice City
To mark the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI," its real-life inspiration — Miami — is getting a full-scale "Vice City" makeover. This promotional push includes the Miami Heat basketball team stepping onto the hardwood in custom "Vice City" jerseys for a home game, a local festival featuring artists from the game's official soundtrack, and roadside "Vice City" signage installed across the area.
Expectations for "GTA VI" are sky-high. Nearly 5,000 people have been working on the game for more than 10 years. Development costs are estimated at around $1 billion (€900 million).
"Based on those figures alone — as well as the series' extremely successful and popular track record — this can certainly be described as a truly exceptional release," says Rudolf Thomas Inderst, cultural studies scholar and professor of Game Design and Game Studies at Germany's Neu-Ulm University of Applied Sciences.
When such an effort is put into a product, it's only natural for people to expect great things, he adds. Inderst is expecting "GTA VI" to showcase the absolute best of what modern gaming can do across gameplay, storytelling, visuals and tech.
Social satire and gameplay freedom
This video game series has been around for almost three decades, setting new standards through its different versions. A biting satire on US society and the American dream, "GTA" parodies politics, culture and the media.
The game is also renowned for its gameplay freedom and spectacularly staged chaos in a crazy world where players can do whatever they please. Shoot down helicopters with a bazooka, go to the hairdresser's, take a stroll on the beach, go to a nightclub, take part in car races and much more.
What makes it a standout among video games is how its NPCs — non-player characters, those not being controlled by a human player — are brought to life. They respond based on a player's interactions with them, displaying individualized behaviors and traits ranging from fear to hostility. "GTA VI" has an estimated 600,000 animations for the civilians in the fictional state of Leonida.
'Grand Theft Auto,' a long-running hit
"GTA VI" is essentially a huge adult playground, striking a chord across several generations. Millennials grew up with "Grand Theft Auto III," "Grand Theft Auto: Vice City," "Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas," and "Grand Theft Auto IV," while Gen Z grew up with "Grand Theft Auto V." Generation Alpha might still be too young for the latest edition, but will likely find ways to play it anyway.
Social media has certainly played a part in the series' ongoing success, particularly "GTA V" and its multiplayer spin-off, "GTA Online." Numerous content creators stream gameplay sessions on Twitch or YouTube, and particularly funny or crazy gameplay moments end up on TikTok.
At the same time, a dedicated role-play community has grown around the game. Players gather inside the world of "GTA" to act out specific characters, such as taxi drivers, judges or small-time criminals. They invent realistic backstories for their personas, and many even use accents to stay in character.
Perfectionism has its downsides
The hype surrounding "GTA VI" is not only good news for the game itself but could also boost the entire games industry by drawing more people back to their consoles. This is because the boom triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic was followed by studio closures and redundancies. Worldwide, it's estimated that 50,000 people in the games industry have lost their jobs since 2022.
But while publisher Rockstar Games is well-known for the meticulous polish of its titles and attention to detail, the perfectionism so prized by fans also has its drawbacks, especially for those working on the game. Rockstar, like many other game developers, has frequently faced major criticism regarding its labor practices.
Former developers report extremely long working hours and a heavy workload that resulted in health issues. Trade unions accuse company managers of employee surveillance, resulting in a culture of workplace stress and low morale.
Coinciding with the launch of Rockstar's largest game to date, the developers behind it are pushing for trade union recognition. That move would give them a collective voice to address working hours, pay, pensions and parental leave. If successful, their campaign could set a major precedent for the wider video game industry, which continues to face challenges around fair labor practices.
This article was originally written in German.

From Forest fringes to Glasner's go-to guy - the rise of McAtee
- Published
"James McAtee is probably one of the winners of this pre-season."
Oliver Glasner's immediate impression of his Nottingham Forest midfielder foretold the faith the head coach has shown in him.
Forest appear to have found their Elliot Anderson replacement from within as McAtee has become a key man for the Austrian.
After his £30m move from Manchester City in 2025, McAtee endured a difficult start to life at the City Ground.
Yet he played a key role as Forest toppled City and the returning Anderson before the international break for their first home win of the season.
There has been no clamour for an England call, but has Thomas Tuchel unfairly overlooked McAtee - and how has he gone from the Forest bench to indispensable?
The City academy graduate made only two Premier League starts last season, one of the bigger victims of Forest's revolving door as the club went through four managers.
Nine starts in Forest's run to the Europa League semi-finals could not hide a campaign of frustration.
It was supposed to be a platform after captaining England Under-21s to Euro 2025 victory, but he played only 289 minutes in the league.
The 24-year-old has already tripled those minutes this season after becoming a key player for Glasner, starting every top-flight game.
It followed the manager suggesting in the summer that McAtee could replace Anderson following his £116m move to City - something which left McAtee unsure.
"When I first came in and [Glasner] put me in the [number] six [role] on the second day in my head I was like: 'oh, he's not seeing me in his plans, I'm playing deeper'," he said at Forest's training ground.
"My confidence is growing, but not fully there yet, but I think we're on our way.
"I thought I had it in my locker, but I never thought he would actually try it out with me in pre-season.
"I think Ibra [Sangare] was injured at the time so I was thinking, I'm just going in for Ibra. But then as pre-season got on and I was playing there I felt more comfortable."
It was evidence of McAtee's work after he worked throughout the summer to return for pre-season.
He trained with former Plymouth, Leeds and Ipswich midfielder David Norris, now a personal trainer, and put on 2.5kg of muscle while losing 1kg of fat.
Weight sessions followed fitness work in the morning, which is what prompted Glasner to credit his summer of work.
The relationship with Glasner has been crucial. The Forest boss has offered clarity and calmness to a squad which endured the chaos last season.
A post-match inquest following the 2-0 defeat by Brentford sparked the right response from the squad, after a start which has left them 16th in the league.
After McAtee failed to find consistency and rhythm last season, Glasner promised him he would be afforded time and the benefit of the doubt if he had a poor game.
"I think [last season] was a me problem. I was struggling to get my chance," he said, having used a psychologist before the start of pre-season.
"I've never really had a season like that, I was always in and out. It was frustrating, but as frustrating as it was, it was a good lesson.
"As I saw my confidence kept going worse and worse and worse. As I've watched clips of me, I can tell when I was going a little bit under.
"This year, if I make a pass and I lose it, it won't bother me as much because I've been through that."
McAtee has always had supporters at the City Ground. All four managers were impressed by his training levels last season, but he was always under pressure to deliver when given a brief chance.
Forest technical director George Syrianos has also championed the calls internally for McAtee.
It has allowed McAtee - whose brother John plays for Bolton - to feel the faith, having learned from previous difficulties, with England on his mind.
He is eager to make the step up to Tuchel's senior side, and has supporters at the Football Association.
He prioritised playing for the U21s at Euro 2025 - captaining them to victory - over going to the Club World Cup with City, and underlined his determination to represent his country to manager Pep Guardiola and director of football Txiki Begiristain at the time.
Now, under Glasner, after a difficult first season, McAtee has that platform with Euro 2028 a realistic target.
"At this moment I need to have a good year for me to maybe be in with the chance of getting picked, but the competition in the position I'm playing is so high," he said.
"If I could add some goals, some stats, it could put me within a chance to be around that circle. The competition is very elite at the moment, but that's the aim, that's the goal."
Against City, he was moved further forward, with Ryan Yates coming in to add more bodies in midfield.
But the stats back up McAtee's improvement and he compares favourably to others.
He has made the most final-third passes for Forest (151) and has played the joint-most through balls with Morgan Gibbs-White (five). His 426 passes are behind only Murillo's 501, and he has created 18 chances - six short of Gibbs-White.
McAtee is only 29m behind Gibbs-White, having carried the ball 1,180m this season, but has made the most carries with 109 and has won possession back 63 times - winning 53% of his ground duels, indicating he has developed more of a mean streak in his game.
He has comfortably outperformed Everton's James Garner - one of his rivals for a place in the England squad - creating more chances, making more forward passes, winning more defensive duels and making more successful tackles.
McAtee has also made more recoveries, successful tackles, passes and clearances than Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton.
Now, having gone under the radar this season, come the next international break in March, Tuchel may not be able to ignore him.

items.title: ‘Too early’ to determine impact of US blockade on Iran, with Tehran defiant
items.summary:
‘Too early’ to determine impact of US blockade on Iran, with Tehran defiant
The US blockade of Iranian ports is having a crippling effect on the economy, but Tehran insists its economy can survive.
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s economy is expected to contract further due to the ongoing blockade of its ports
items.text:
‘Too early’ to determine impact of US blockade on Iran, with Tehran defiant
The US blockade of Iranian ports is having a crippling effect on the economy, but Tehran insists its economy can survive.
Tehran, Iran – Iran’s economy is expected to contract further due to the ongoing blockade of its ports by the United States, inflicting pain on tens of millions of Iranians. But experts say it is too early to tell whether Washington’s economic embargo on Tehran is having the desired outcome of either collapsing the Iranian government or forcing it to concede to US demands.
The US believes its naval blockade on Iran, overland trade disruptions and sanctions – part of its maximum pressure campaign on Tehran – are working. The US has also brought a third aircraft carrier into the region to support a potential military escalation, in what appears to be an attempt to force Tehran to capitulate further to its demands.
After a deadlock in the US-Israel war on Iran, which began with strikes that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on February 28, Washington has demanded Tehran reopen the Strait of Hormuz and curb its nuclear programme.
However, Iranian authorities insist they can withstand the economic pressure and have put forward their demands. Strikes on US interests in the region this week, including radar systems in Bahrain, have been viewed as a defiant response to the US military and economic pressure. But there are signs that the country’s economy and common Iranians are suffering from the current conditions.
Tehran-based economist Peyman Molavi said if current conditions persist, Iran’s inflation could rise considerably over the coming months.
“This will impact parallel markets like foreign currencies, gold, the stock market and housing,” he told Al Jazeera. “But it will unfortunately have the largest impact on the commodities market, from energy to agricultural products, metals, and industrial products.”
For decades, Iran’s governments have increasingly plugged their budget deficits by printing more money, which has saddled the country with a growing money supply, feeding chronic inflation. The foreign currency crunch from disrupted oil exports due to the US military blockade has only exacerbated the situation.
Molavi estimates that the year-on-year growth of the money supply in Iran could rise to 55-60 percent from its current figure of nearly 51 percent by the end of the Persian year in late March. Paired with negative economic growth, he said annual inflation could grow to about 85 percent, and point-to-point inflation to 100 percent.
‘Count your chickens’
Iranian Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati hit back at US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has led Washington’s sanctions regime against Tehran.
“Like I said, he must still count his chickens at the end of autumn before moving to winter,” he said in reference to an Iranian proverb – “It’s too early to talk about winter”.
Bessent has claimed the economic embargo will result in a 25 percent contraction of the Iranian economy by the year ending March 2027. Iran’s official figures indicated that the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 percent year-on-year between March 21 and June 20, the first quarter of the Persian calendar year.
Hemmati said the central bank has secured $30bn in foreign currencies to weather the pressure over the coming months, prioritising procurement of essential goods for its citizens.
“American officials believe they can achieve their goals through threats and raise something new each time; from the possibility of collapse to military threats and intensified economic pressure,” Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said on Sunday.
All overland routes to and from Iran, except for one with Iraq that was closed due to security reasons, remain open despite the US efforts to isolate Iran from its neighbours, Madanizadeh insisted.
For the seventh Iranian month of Mehr that ended on October 22, the 12-month average annual inflation was at 76.8 percent, according to the Statistical Centre of Iran. Point-to-point inflation, which compares just that month with the same month of the previous year, was at 88.7 percent.
Essential goods have already been experiencing triple-digit inflation for months, with the category of food, beverages and tobacco experiencing year-on-year inflation of 113.4 percent in October, the centre said.
Iranian social media is increasingly filled with personal stories of how most people in the country of about 90 million are rapidly losing their purchasing power.
“Everywhere you look, you could have bought the same commodity with one-fifth of the money last year,” one user wrote on X. “That’s no joke, millions of people have been crushed in between.”
Markets suffer
Saleh, a 37-year-old shopkeeper at Tehran’s Grand Bazaar who deals in electric motors for small industrial units, said both domestic and Chinese-made goods can still readily be found in the market. But supply and demand have decreased since US sanctions began to bite.
“The reason is that commodities are expensive, and there’s been a stagnation in the market and also uncertainty over what will happen next,” he told Al Jazeera, asking not to use his full name due to security reasons.
“Everyone’s looking at the dollar price, and manufacturers and clients are making their decisions based on price changes. If we sold 10 items before, now we’re selling three or four, but the price increase maintained some profit. I don’t see the market being near collapse, but there’s less business.”
Companies with an established client base are proving more resilient, he added.
Bessent hailed what is happening in Iran as “one of the fastest collapses in history”, and described the Trump-directed sanctions campaign against Iran as “the greatest economic isolation in the history of the world against a single country”.

items.title: Netanyahu’s last stand and the dangerous politics of survival
items.summary:
Netanyahu’s last stand and the dangerous politics of survival
Facing political oblivion, Netanyahu is playing a high-stakes game that could push Israel towards violence and chaos.
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the weeks since Israel’s October 27 election to launch a s
items.text:
Netanyahu’s last stand and the dangerous politics of survival
Facing political oblivion, Netanyahu is playing a high-stakes game that could push Israel towards violence and chaos.
Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the weeks since Israel’s October 27 election to launch a series of attacks on his opponents, and has called into question the legitimacy of the vote’s result.
The longtime Israeli leader is likely on his way out of power – as long as the country’s opposition, led by Gadi Eisenkot, can form a viable government.
That may involve leaning on parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, and Netanyahu has taken the opportunity to use that to tarnish the reputations of the Arab parties, and baselessly accuse them of cheating in the elections.
The environment that Netanyahu has helped generate has led to right-wing protesters threatening civil war, and critics have also accused him of deliberately fomenting war with Iran to retain office.
Separately, the Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency, led by Netanyahu’s ally David Zini, reportedly sought permission to tap the phones of five Arab lawmakers over suspected foreign interference, and to have politicians who are Palestinian citizens of Israel arrested on election day, requests the attorney general rejected.
Opposition leaders including Yair Lapid and Joint List chief Yousef Jabareen said the measures were evidence of an “attempted coup”. Meanwhile, law enforcement officials are said to be investigating whether the prime minister’s office itself fabricated the allegations of vote-buying.
For analysts and a number of Israel’s politicians, Netanyahu’s actions reflect an overriding determination to stay in power, or, failing that, engineer a government that is reliant on the support of him and his allies.
High stakes
Netanyahu faces numerous threats to both his legacy and even his freedom that, without the kind of influence he has wielded as prime minister, could prove far-reaching.
Calls for a state inquiry into Netanyahu and his government’s failings in the run-up to the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel have persisted for almost as long as the genocidal war Israel launched on Gaza in response. Those calls have grown more urgent following a series of reports suggesting that Netanyahu had been personally warned by senior Egyptian and Emirati officials about a potential attack. Establishing a state inquiry also featured prominently on the legislative slate of the parliament’s new session last week.
Similarly, both the war in Gaza and the constitutional crisis triggered by Netanyahu’s attempts to weaken judicial oversight over the government have provided useful cover against the corruption charges he has faced since 2019. Accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases, Netanyahu has seen his trial, running since May 2020, repeatedly delayed by his duties as prime minister. If found guilty, Netanyahu could face a prison sentence of up to a decade.
“Netanyahu is behaving like a wounded animal,” said Israeli analyst Ahron Bregman, of King’s College London. “For him, losing the elections is not just a political but also a personal matter, not least because of his corruption trial, which could result in him being sent to jail. Losing the premiership is losing his shield. Hence, for Netanyahu, nothing is off the table.”
Risk of violence
The chance of political violence in Israel has increased. In the days after the election, right-wing protesters gathered outside Eisenkot’s home, warning him not to form a government with the Arab-led parties, and calling him a “traitor”.
And in a letter shared publicly, Rabbi Gedalia Axelrod, a former head of Haifa’s rabbinical court, evoked the religious edict of din rodef, the “law of the pursuer”, the same principle invoked by Yigal Amir to justify his killing of former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in 1995 over the Oslo Accords agreement with the Palestinians.
“The longer it takes for Eisenkot to form a government, the higher the risk of political violence becomes,” said Ofer Cassif, a member of parliament representing the left-wing Hadash party. “Netanyahu is willing to do anything, and I mean anything, to stay in power. He’s a psychopath. People on the right talk about civil war, and I’m not ready to discount that … Netanyahu built a cult around him, and it may easily raise arms against his rivals.”
It remains unclear what, if any, immediate legal consequences Netanyahu may face for his alleged efforts to undermine the legitimacy of the election.
Aides accused of passing false information to the police on the eve of the election could face criminal scrutiny, while Shin Bet chief Zini could see both his agency’s independence and his own position fundamentally undermined by allegedly participating in efforts to subvert the democratic process.
“Netanyahu battles for his survival and doesn’t care if those around him disappear into oblivion, but he might not succeed this time,” said Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow at Chatham House. “He doesn’t care about them, or even his political legacy. All he cares about is survival, about fighting for the next day and trying to cling on, no matter what the cost.”

items.title: Bancroft speaks again after explosive Sandpapergate claims
items.summary:
Cameron Bancroft: Former Australia batter says he feels 'very free' after 'telling the truth' with Sandpapergate claims
Cameron Bancroft says he "never meant to point fingers or implicate others; "I just wanted to, for my own peace, to tell the truth;" in making his statement on the 2018 ball tamper
items.text:
Cameron Bancroft: Former Australia batter says he feels 'very free' after 'telling the truth' with Sandpapergate claims
Cameron Bancroft says he "never meant to point fingers or implicate others; "I just wanted to, for my own peace, to tell the truth;" in making his statement on the 2018 ball tampering scandal; meanwhile, Pat Cummins' manager says Test captain has been "consistent and adamant from day one"
Thursday 19 November 2026 07:58, UK
Cameron Bancroft says he feels "very free" following his explosive claims about the Sandpapergate scandal.
In a 4,000-word statement in The West Australian newspaper on Wednesday, Bancroft broke his silence on revelations in Usman Khawaja's new book, claiming that Cummins' press conference denying the allegations was the "final straw" for him, revealing that the entire bowling unit maintained full knowledge of the extensive use of sandpaper.
Bancroft saw his career turned upside after being suspended for his part in the 2018 incident alongside then captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner. Those were the only three players to be punished.
Speaking to local media on Thursday, Bancroft said: "I never meant to point fingers or implicate others; I just wanted to, for my own peace, to tell the truth.
"This has been a burden that I've carried with me for such a long period of time but I feel very free and I feel very happy that I've been able to do that."
Footage on social media on Thursday also showed Cummins being approached for comment by local TV reporters when leaving his house for training with New South Wales. The Australian Test captain declined to address Bancroft's remarks.
A statement from his manager, Neil Maxwell, said: "Pat's position hasn't changed in eight years. He's been consistent and adamant from day one.
"Pat feels for Cam [Bancroft] of course. He has been through a lot. We would urge people to again read Pat's interview transcript. There is nothing he hasn't answered. And that includes in response to what Cam has now said."
Bancroft's statement has heaped pressure on Test captain Cummins, with Australia's next red-ball series against New Zealand beginning on December 9.
The claims come in the wake of a furore of discussion around the 2018 scandal, with Khawaja's book first bringing to light claims that the entire team knew about the use of sandpaper.
Khawaja also alleged that discussions about ball-tampering had been held "openly and lightheartedly" across the entire squad, involving not just the batters, bowlers and coaching staff but the wider team.
Cummins dismissed Khawaja's claims as "complete and utter nonsense" during a sensational 68-minute press conference last Friday.
Bancroft's statement came just after Cricket Australia announced an independent forum to explore the scandal, stating that players could share their version of events without fears of reprisals - a decision which Khawaja and David Warner have questioned.

items.text:
Vote for the first BBC Men's Footballer of the Year
- Published
Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.
Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.
The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.
The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.
Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.
"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.
"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."
The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.
The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).
Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.
Jude Bellingham
Age: 23 Country: England
Club: Real Madrid Position: Midfield
Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.
In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.
That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.
Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.
The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.
Harry Kane
Age: 33 Country: England
Club: Bayern Munich Position: Forward
In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.
His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.
Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.
Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.
Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.
Kylian Mbappe
Age: 27 Country: France
Club: Real Madrid Position: Forward
Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.
The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.
Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.
It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.
Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.
He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.
Rodri
Age: 30 Country: Spain
Club: Barcelona Position: Midfield
Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.
By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.
His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.
Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.
His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.
Lamine Yamal
Age: 19 Country: Spain
Club: Barcelona Position: Forward
Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.

items.text:
Formula 1 drivers back return of 'very cool' V8 engines in the future ahead of Las Vegas Grand Prix
Several Formula 1 drivers have backed the possibility of V8 engines returning to the sport as early as 2030; watch the Las Vegas GP weekend on Sky Sports F1, with Friday's practice sessions at 12.30am and 4pm
Thursday 19 November 2026 06:47, UK
Formula 1's drivers appear to be unanimous with the prospect of V8 engine returning to the sport in the 2030s.
Earlier this week, ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem teased the possibility of V8 engines with the sound of a screaming F1 car with a caption: "You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon."
The FIA also published graphics on social media which suggested an agreement in principle had been reached by themselves, Formula 1 management and the engine manufacturers for V8 engines to return from 2030, but the post was deleted.

The current regulations are set to run until 2031, which could be an explanation for the deleted post, while further details of the overall power unit, including whether an electrical element and a turbo will remain, need to be finalised.
"I'd love to see it. When I look at the old videos of the old engines, they give me goosebumps," said Mercedes driver George Russell.
"I think it's about just that high-pitched squeal that I'm missing from this era. The purists will say take away all electrical power, but I think when you look at how a lot of these cars have evolved in recent years, and the power output from some of these electrical motors these days, Formula 1 is going to continue to be the fastest race cars on the planet, you need to have it, that's just the reality.
"You need to have some sort of hybrid, because the power you get, you can't really produce that just solely on internal combustion.
"If we go back to V8s, having some sort of electrical power as well, to give you that extra 400, 500 kilowatts to bring the cars to 1000+ horsepower, that's what we want.
"I think it's worth remembering as well actually, the final V8 era, they sounded awesome, but the cars, they actually weren't very fast. I don't think many people realise that."
New world champion Kimi Antonelli agreed with his Mercedes team-mate and claims "many people would look forward" to the return of V8 engines.
"It's going be very cool to go back to more old style. Also, the cars will get lighter even further, probably 70kg, which is immense," he said.
"Definitely, I think it's a very exciting regulation change. Of course, we have got to first do well in this one."
Verstappen: F1 going in the right direction
Max Verstappen has been critical of the current power units which are around 53 per cent battery powered and led to an unusual style of driving and racing at some tracks, with the drivers sometimes unable to push flat out in a traditional manner.
Verstappen, who warned driving in Las Vegas will be "painful" due to the long straights, feels the FIA have listened to the drivers and realised the 2026 regulations are "not what you want".
The four-time world champion stated he would get rid of the turbo in future power unit regulations, and effectively have a fully normally aspirated engine.
"In some tracks then you're not allowed to race because it will be too loud because if it's up to me I would take the turbo off," he explained.
"I would get rid, maybe you can use it as a push to pass, but not too much of the battery side. But then on some tracks, you're not allowed to race, so fuel consumption goes up a lot without a turbo, so you need a bigger tank if you don't want to do refuelling in the races, so I understand that you want to have a turbo.
"If it's fully up to me, of course you go back to like a V10 or whatever. That sounds even better, but I know that not something realistic.
"This [news] is good. This is for sure in the right direction, but again, it's not confirmed yet. So there's still a few things I guess that they need to agree on."
Lewis Hamilton, Fernando Alonso, Nico Hulkenberg Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas are the only drivers who drove in the previous V8 era which ended in 2013.
Alonso said it's "frustrating" F1 has not had V8 engines since 2014, while Hamilton is keen to know more details about the proposed return of V8s.
"I think it's ultimately dependent on… it's all well going to V8. It depends on how they design it, regulation-wise, and going back to the good sound because that's I think been lacking since we've been in the V6 era," he said.
"Yeah, bring back the smaller exhaust and get that sound back.
"But you could have that, and as long as we don't have the engine dying halfway down the straight, then I think that'd be better."

items.text:
Could Trump, Putin and Xi end the nuclear age?
Their meeting in China could revive the dream of nuclear disarmament that Reagan and Gorbachev nearly realised 40 years ago.
Excitement abounds around the possible tripartite meeting in Shenzhen, China, between Presidents Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, and Donald Trump during the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
Some are calling it Yalta 2.0. We’d rather think of it as Reykjavik 2.0, while also welcoming some of the broader diplomatic breakthroughs and global reordering achieved at Yalta almost 82 years ago.
Dmitri Trenin, who directed the Carnegie Moscow Center for many years and is now president of the Russian International Affairs Council, wrote encouragingly: “The US president has mentioned that an unprecedented trilateral meeting… would make sense if it were focused on denuclearisation.” Trenin wrote this in Al Jazeera while explaining why Russia could play a helpful role in negotiating a new nuclear agreement between its Iranian ally and the United States.
While anything that might help end the dangerous, destructive, and potentially apocalyptic conflagration in Southwest Asia would be more than welcome, we think the leaders can and should aim even higher: Why not rekindle the spirit of the 1986 meeting between US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, at which they came within a hair’s breadth, arguably one word, of agreeing to eliminate not only all ballistic missiles, as Reagan originally proposed, but all nuclear weapons, as Gorbachev countered. Reagan replied, “Yes, all”, and Secretary of State George Shultz agreed. “Let’s do it,” he said.
The chance to achieve the most extraordinary diplomatic breakthrough in history slipped through Reagan’s grasp when he insisted on unlimited testing of his Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) fantasy rather than limiting SDI to the laboratory for 10 years. The world’s hopes were dashed, and we have not come close since.
Sure, we’re up against obstacles, and the odds are long. Trump has responded to the midterm shellacking by appointing Stephen Miller as chief of staff, in effect giving the middle finger to those who didn’t support the Republicans, which is not a hopeful sign. Putin knows that much of Russia’s power comes not from its economic prowess or its conventional military but from possessing the largest nuclear arsenal in the world. And Xi has made it clear that China won’t engage in arms control talks until the largest nuclear arsenals are reduced – meanwhile, China has been rapidly increasing the size of its arsenal.
That said, there are good reasons why all three could support this proposal. After his party’s midterm defeat, Trump, probably the most recalcitrant of the three, may be desperate for an achievement that could cement at least a piece of a positive legacy – and in this case a very big piece, a resounding piece. And he has been all over the map on the nuclear issue. In February 2025, he said, “There’s no reason for us to be building brand-new nuclear weapons. We already have so many. You could destroy the world 50 times over, 100 times over. And here we are building new nuclear weapons, and they’re building nuclear weapons.” He also said, “We’re all spending a lot of money that we could be spending on other things that are actually, hopefully, much more productive.”
This is apparently something he’s been contemplating for many years. In 2016, he told Maggie Haberman and David Sanger of The New York Times: “I personally think it’s the biggest problem the world has, nuclear capability. I think it’s the single biggest problem… Power of weaponry today is beyond anything ever thought of, or even, you know, it’s unthinkable, the power… And to me, it’s the single biggest, it’s the single biggest problem.” He credits his “very brilliant” MIT physicist uncle, John Trump, with making him aware of this danger.
In 1986, he sought the advice of Bernard Lown, cofounder of International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War (IPPNW), which won the Nobel Peace Prize, on negotiating nuclear disarmament with Gorbachev. He told Lown he would get Reagan to send him to Moscow and that he would secure disarmament and end the Cold War in one hour. Lown commented, “I sat there dumbfounded. ‘Who is this self-inflated individual? Is he sane or what?’”
On January 23, 2025, Trump told the World Economic Forum in Davos: “And I will tell you that President Putin really liked the idea of – of cutting way back on nuclear. And I think the rest of the world, we would have gotten them to follow. And China would have come along too. China also liked it. Tremendous amounts of money are being spent on nuclear, and the destructive capability is something that we don’t even want to talk about today, because you don’t want to hear it. It’s too depressing. So, we want to see if we can denuclearise, and I think that’s very possible. And I can tell you that President Putin wanted to do it. He and I wanted to do it. We had a good conversation with China. They would have been involved, and that would have been an unbelievable thing for the planet.”
Whether Trump is sane is even more heatedly debated today than it was 40 years ago, but the possibility that he is iconoclastic enough to take a dramatic step that reverses the course of history should not be in doubt. The question is whether he’s capable of taking such a step in favour of humanity rather than against it.
The same is true of Putin. Putin told a meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club in Sochi in 2017, “Should you ask me if nuclear disarmament is possible, I will tell you: Yes, it is possible. Does Russia wish to achieve universal nuclear disarmament or not? The answer is in the affirmative, too. Yes, it does, and it will be working for it.”
