Chelsea 1-0 PSG: Veerle Buurman scores late winner as Sonia Bompastor's side go top of Women's Champions League table
Match report as Chelsea snatched a late 1-0 win against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League; Veerle Buurman bundled her effort home from close range in the 88th minute; Chelsea now move to the top of the Champions League table with one league phase game to play
Wednesday 18 November 2026 22:12, UK
Veerle Buurman's late winner snatched a late 1-0 win for Chelsea against Paris Saint-Germain to move them to the top of the Champions League table.
Sonia Bompastor's side looked as if they were heading to back-to-back goalless draws, following the 0-0 draw with BK Hacken last time out in Europe, until Buurman was able to bundle her effort home at the near post in the 88th minute.
- Got Sky? Watch WSL games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream WSL games with no contract📺
The hosts had been the dominant side throughout but were thwarted by Katarzyna Kiedrzynek on more than one occasion.
Alyssa Thompson had come close to breaking the deadlock just before the break after seeing her initial shot and follow-up effort smothered by Kiedrzynek.
The corner for Buurman's timely winner arrived after the PSG goalkeeper got down well to her right to keep Sjoeke Nusken's header out.
Lucy Bronze's delivery and a slight touch on the way through sparked panic among the PSG defence and it was Buurman who reacted first to sweep home the winner, sending her side to the top of the table with one league phase game to go.
The Blues remain unbeaten in Europe, winning three of their five games so far, and are well placed to qualify for the last 16 through the top four automatic qualification spots. They face OH Leuven in their final game, where they will go into it as strong favourites.
Bompastor praises resilient team performance
Chelsea boss Sonia Bompastor speaking to UEFA:
"I like the resilience from my team. Believing until the end of the game we could score that important goal and it was really important for us to win tonight.
"What I like in my team and squad is the fact they are really flexible; they are really open-minded to changing systems sometimes, adapting to what is happening on the pitch.
"They understand really quickly. I think it was good for us to be able to change, to go to a back four. We wanted to have the width to destabilise them more than we did in the first half."
On her side potentially finishing in the top four: "We knew we had two games left and getting two wins will help us to probably secure top four.
"So we still have things under control and that was why it was really important for us to win."
Buurman on 'important' win for Chelsea
Chelsea defender Veerle Buurman speaking to Disney:
"It was really important we scored the goal. Winning and three points was really important, especially after the last Champions League game where we drew against Hacken.
"A good team performance. We tried really hard and that I can score a goal is really important for the team."
Walsh: We are in a good place in WCL
Chelsea midfielder Keira Walsh speaking to UEFA:
"We spoke about it before the game about wanting to finish the evening on top. We are in a good spot going into the last game.
"It was a massive win. It was tough for us tonight. They defended really well and they're aggressive.
"It was a difficult game physically but to get the win was really important. Hopefully it will push us into the top four."
Key moments from The Cherry Red Records Stadium
43: SO CLOSE! Thompson has an initial shot and a second effort saved by Kiedrzynek from close range.
53: SAVE! Kanjinga makes space to shoot, but Hampton keeps her effort out at the near post.
67: CLOSE! Buurman meets the corner and glances her header towards goal but it is saved by Kiedrzynek again.
86: ANOTHER SAVE! Nusken's header looks destined for the bottom corner until Kiedrzynek dives to claw it away.
87: GOAL! Chelsea finally break the deadlock as Buurman scores late winner at the near post.

items.text:
During Nvidia’s quarterly call on Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim-CEO Colette Kress dropped this little oddity: She said Nvidia wouldn’t be immediately filing its quarterly results report, known as a 10-Q, with the SEC. “We plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks.” And she offered no reason why.
The delay was widely noticed. Among the many comments on X about it, economic and investment analyst Edward Dowd called it a “red flag.” Nvidia has typically filed the 10-Q the same day it reports results.
The 10-Q offers far more detail about a company’s operations than an earnings press release, including sections that disclose “legal proceedings,” which include lawsuits that could affect the company; and “risk factors,” which cover other potentially business-impairing items.
The announcement of the delay was so unusual that UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked about it after the public earnings call. Nvidia told him the delay was related to whether the company would need to disclose additional information about its ongoing investigation into Huang in the 10-Q.
“The company announced that the 10-Q will be filed ‘in the coming weeks’ – later than usual. When queried on our callback, management indicated this was related to the ongoing investigation and whether any additional risk factors would need to be added to the filing,” Arcuri wrote in his research note. (Arcuri still rates the stock a “buy” by the way, although he did lower his price target to $220 from $240. The stock is now trading around $150).
Notably, on the same day that Nvidia reported earnings, The Wall Street Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors.
So the mystery thickens: What will Nvidia disclose? We’ll have to wait and see. (Nvidia has not yet responded to our request for comment.)
The delay suggests the company may have more to say about its mounting legal troubles. Nvidia is now facing multiple federal investigations over allegations that its partners were selling restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. So far, the scrutiny has come from a number of congressional committees; the Department of Justice looking into Megaspeed, the company run by a woman with whom Huang had an affair and who is also suspected of being a Chinese spy; and now, reportedly, the SEC.
Additionally, Nvidia is conducting its own internal investigation into Huang after he admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang (the Megaspeed executive), and allegations surfaced that he also had affairs with other Nvidia employees.
There’s little doubt that Wall Street will scrutinize that 10-Q once it’s finally filed. The intrigue brings to mind the old saying: “Doctors bury their mistakes. Lawyers put theirs in prison. And accountants hide theirs in the footnotes.”

Addressing the recent spate of tech outages, the Oculus founder and Anduril Industries co-founder argued that older systems are
items.text:
AI-powered cyberattacks are moving faster than outdated technology systems can defend against them, Palmer Luckey warned at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. Addressing the recent spate of tech outages, the Oculus founder and Anduril Industries co-founder argued that older systems are struggling to keep pace with the new hacking capabilities enabled by AI and warned it was time to quicken the pace of securing our defenses.
“We’re seeing the natural effects of a lot of these advanced AI tools allowing for the creation of various exploits,” he said.
While government officials largely attributed the latest set of technical issues to companies rushing to patch their systems to protect against the new vulnerabilities AI has discovered, Luckey focused on the underlying security challenges facing organizations using outdated technology.
Luckey explained that U.S. adversaries are currently exploiting the mismatch between new attack capabilities and our defense capabilities. These attacks are being carried out for both strategic and financial reasons, and North Korea was particularly involved, he added.
The interviewer, Andrew Ross Sorkin, noted that U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance had canceled his appearance at the Times’ conference this week because of the recent tech outages, saying he now had to attend meetings about the matter.
Given the situation, Sorkin asked Luckey how worried we should be about all this.
“It depends on how well prepared you are,” was Luckey’s answer. (He then ominously warned, “You guys are going to find out what’s going on soon enough.”)
The tech executive argued that AI could ultimately give defenders the upper hand, but they’d have to move more quickly.
“In the long run, the advantages are going to accrue to the side that is most effectively using AI for defense,” Luckey said. “With the people who say that everything can be hacked — they are right, for now. That actually may be the case with certain new techniques that are coming along. But as of right now, there’s a mismatch between the attackers who are very fast-moving and using technology and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed,” Luckey continued.
“And I think … people are going to have to pick up the pace,” he said. “It’s time to start running.”

items.title: Palmer Luckey thinks China is ‘thrilled to have Jensen out,’ so he wants the ousted Nvidia CEO reinstated
items.summary:
Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey thinks Nvidia’s board is giving China exactly what it wants by removing the company’s longtime CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang.
Nvidia, the leading semiconductor designer whose chips power much of the AI industry, is undergoing a critical, unexpected leadership change. Hua
items.text:
Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey thinks Nvidia’s board is giving China exactly what it wants by removing the company’s longtime CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang.
Nvidia, the leading semiconductor designer whose chips power much of the AI industry, is undergoing a critical, unexpected leadership change. Huang, who led the company for 33 years, stepped down last week amid several controversies, including his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy who has been investigated for possibly smuggling Nvidia chips into China to circumvent U.S. export restrictions.
“China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” Luckey said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, repeating a statement he posted on X last week. “They’re thrilled to have Jensen out… There’s a reason it’s knocking a trillion dollars off Nvidia’s market cap. They know it makes America weaker to knock him out.”
Luckey disagrees with Huang’s longstanding position that Nvidia should have more leeway to export chips to China. But he also recognizes that China stands to benefit if its domestic chipmakers can challenge Nvidia’s dominance.
“China doesn’t want Nvidia to sell GPUs to Chinese companies,” Luckey said. “There are Chinese companies that want to buy Nvidia GPUs… China will not give them an import permit because they want to build an internal domestic processor industry… not build one that is dependent on the United States.”
Nvidia has said as much itself — the U.S. government granted the company license to ship some of its powerful H200 chips to certain Chinese customers, but those sales were restricted by the Chinese government. Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress said during the company’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday that it will no longer sell H200 chips in China at all.
Luckey is far from alone among industry peers in his defense of Huang.
More than 200,000 people — including Elon Musk and the CEOs of Y Combinator, Databricks, Epic Games, Shopify, and Replit — have signed a petition calling for Nvidia to reinstate its founder. But Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that the company does not have plans to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return.

- Published
On-loan Tottenham winger Mykhailo Mudryk says he blames the administration of the Ukraine national team for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban from football.
The 25-year-old, on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from
items.text:
Ukrainian FA to blame for failed drugs test - Mudryk
- Published
On-loan Tottenham winger Mykhailo Mudryk says he blames the administration of the Ukraine national team for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban from football.
The 25-year-old, on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 until July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium, which he believes entered his system while on international duty.
Having initially faced a four-year ban from the Football Association (FA), his appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport was successful.
He returned to football after accepting he had breached anti-doping rules and agreeing to a suspension equivalent to the time he had already served.
After appearing for Chelsea during a pre-season tour of Asia, Mudryk joined Tottenham on transfer deadline day to reunite with his former Shakhtar Donetsk manager Roberto de Zerbi.
In a lengthy interview with the Ukrainian YouTube channel Guest of Gordon, Mudryk was asked who he blamed for his absence from the game.
"The environment, the situation in the Ukrainian national team," he replied. "It should never have existed. I probably haven't said it publicly yet, but I'm saying it now.
"I had never heard of a drug like meldonium. It is a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe. It could only have got into my body in Ukraine. There is no such drug in England."
He explained how he had only been in Ukraine to be with the national team and "it points to the fact it was in a national team camp".
Asked specifically whether he blamed the national team, Mudryk replied: "Yes, exactly."
He also said Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) president Andriy Shevchenko offered little support, blamed the association for leaks that emerged during the case and claimed its handling of the matter delayed his return to football.
Mudryk also said he spent millions of pounds on legal fees, coaching, pitch hire and private physiotherapy while being unable to access services at Chelsea.
He added: "It was a bolt from the blue. I couldn't believe it [the positive test] was true.
"It was like falling off a skyscraper. In a dream you would hit the ground. In life, I just kept on falling. It hit me very hard, mentally."
Mudryk said he cried and drank alcohol after the initial suspension but never doubted that he would eventually return to top-level football.
BBC Sport has contacted the UAF for comment.
Last year a UAF spokesperson told BBC Sport it was "in close contact with Mudryk's lawyers" but had not been contacted by the FA about the case.

items.title: Strasbourg appoint Swansea boss Matos
items.summary:
Strasbourg announce appointment of Swans boss Matos
- Published
Strasbourg have announced the appointment of Swansea City's Vitor Matos as the club's new head coach.
The French top-flight side made the announcement on Wednesday evening, but there has been no official confirmation of Matos' departure
items.text:
Strasbourg announce appointment of Swans boss Matos
- Published
Strasbourg have announced the appointment of Swansea City's Vitor Matos as the club's new head coach.
The French top-flight side made the announcement on Wednesday evening, but there has been no official confirmation of Matos' departure from the Swans.
Strasbourg are expected to pay Swansea compensation thought to be in the region of £5m in order to secure his services.
Matos, 38, spent just under a year at Swansea having left his role at Maritimo to succeed Alan Sheehan as the Championship club's head coach in November 2025.
Four members of Matos' coaching team - Diogo Medeiros, Toze Mendes, Goncalo Ricca and head of goalkeeping Pedro Pereira - are also expected to leave Swansea.
Ex-captain Ashley Williams is set to return to the club to join an interim coaching team also featuring fellow former players Kristian O'Leary and Leon Britton.
O'Leary and Britton are set to be the only remaining members of Matos' Swansea staff.
Alongside Williams, they will lead Swansea while the club searches for Matos' permanent successor.
Their first game will be at home to West Bromwich Albion on Saturday.
Swansea go to Middlesbrough next Tuesday before hosting rivals Cardiff City on Sunday, 29 November.
Matos moves on despite agreeing an extended Swansea contract running until 2030 in July.
Swansea were 20th in the second tier when the former Liverpool coach took over, but he leaves a team lying only three points off the top of the table in sixth.
Matos led Swansea to an 11th-placed finish last season, and has raised hopes of a potential promotion push in 2026-27 thanks to an encouraging start to this campaign.
But he told Swansea he wanted to move on after Strasbourg, who have the same ownership group as Premier League side Chelsea, made their move last weekend and he said goodbye to players and staff on Tuesday.
Having finished eighth last season, Strasbourg are 13th in Ligue 1 having won only three of their 10 league games under Hugo Oliveira, who was only appointed in the summer after Gary O'Neil departed to take over at Ipswich Town.
Matos was touted as a contender to take charge at Crystal Palace earlier this season - the Eagles have since appointed Thomas Frank - while he had also been linked with a return to Portugal on the back of his impact at Swansea.
When asked in October about the Palace links, Matos said: "I'm Swansea manager. I love being here, love my players, love the staff, so my focus is always on the next game and what we can do better."
In an interview last week, Swansea chief executive Tom Gorringe acknowledged that Matos' impact will not have gone unnoticed at other clubs.
But Gorringe played down the idea of Matos being lured away, saying: "The reality is there'll always be interest in anyone performing well in any role on and off the pitch.
"That's one of the outcomes of being successful - we're aware of that.
"[But] we're all quite happy. We've all agreed to go on this journey together and we hope that Vitor is here a long time."

items.title: FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on
items.summary:
FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on
- Published
The Football Association has considered challenging Gianni Infantino's eligibility to run for a fourth term as Fifa president, BBC Sport can reveal.
But it believes any attempt to prevent him from standing in the election in March is li
items.text:
FA explored legal challenge to Infantino staying on
- Published
The Football Association has considered challenging Gianni Infantino's eligibility to run for a fourth term as Fifa president, BBC Sport can reveal.
But it believes any attempt to prevent him from standing in the election in March is likely to fail.
Infantino oversaw the introduction of a three-term limit when he replaced Sepp Blatter as leader of world football's governing body.
However, Fifa's council agreed in 2022 that his first period in office from 2016 to 2019 should not count as it was the remainder of his predecessor's interrupted final term.
Earlier this month, human rights campaign group Fair Square wrote to the FA claiming that the decision is open to legal challenge and was "contrary to the spirit and purpose" of Fifa statutes.
It urged the FA to ask Fifa's governance committee to bar Infantino from the election in March because he has already served the maximum three terms.
FA chair Debbie Hewitt has now replied, telling Fair Square that the governing body "has explored the possibility of challenging Mr Infantino's eligibility to run for a further term as the Fifa president but does not consider that such a challenge would secure the outcome sought".
In correspondence seen by the BBC, Hewitt adds: "Ultimately the process followed Fifa's governance and led to an outcome where Mr Infantino's part term was disregarded for the purposes of maximum term limits.
"Having considered the process in detail, we do not believe that a challenge would succeed."
In a statement, Fair Square said: "It's understandable that the FA has no faith in Fifa's internal processes to hold Infantino accountable for serious breaches of the rules, but it's a mistake to abandon these channels, not least because it sends a signal to Infantino that he can do whatever he likes.
"We will encourage the FA to leave its options open where this matter is concerned not least because Debbie Hewitt's position on the Fifa council puts her in a very strong position to demand clear answers on why Fifa discounted Infantino's first term."
Miguel Maduro - a former head of Fifa's governance committee - has said a national association or confederation may need to challenge Infantino's eligibility at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).
The FA was among a number of national associations to withdraw its support of Infantino in the wake of the crisis sparked by his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors.
European confederation Uefa has backed rival candidate Philippe Diallo, the president of the French Football Federation.
Hewitt, who became a member of Fifa's council in 2023, also told Fair Square that the FA "remains opposed to Mr Infantino's re-election and is committed to providing its full support to Philippe Diallo as our preferred candidate in the upcoming Fifa presidential election".
Fifa has been approached for comment.
It has previously referred to the fact that in 2022 its council "unanimously confirmed its agreement with the view of the governance, audit & compliance committee that the period between 2016 and 2019 does not count as a term of office for the current Fifa president, who is therefore about to end his first term".
The FA declined to comment.

Cadillac have confirmed Valtteri Bottas will stay on at the team for the 2027 Formula 1 season, ending speculation about the Finnish driver's future.
Bottas returned after a year's absence from the grid for this season, Cadillac's first in the sport, as one of two hugely experienced drivers for the all-new American team's first line-up alongside Sergio Perez, who signed a contract extension last month until at least 2029.
But, Bottas' future has been up in the air recently as Cadillac pushed for American Formula 2 driver Colton Herta to earn a Formula 1 super licence, which he secured two weeks ago, by running him in practice sessions.

The team have committed to Bottas for another year though, citing the 37-year-old's "extensive Formula 1 experience, technical insight and race-winning pedigree to the team".
"To whom it may concern, I'm staying!" said Bottas, in reference to his team radio after winning the 2019 Australian Grand Prix with Mercedes.
"I'm excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027. We knew building a new Formula 1 team from the ground up wasn't going to be easy, but that's exactly what makes this challenge so special.
"We've laid the foundations, we're learning and improving, and there's still plenty more to come, I'm hungry for more, and I believe in what we're building together. The story is only just getting started."
Newcomers Cadillac are yet to score a point in their maiden campaign but Bottas is ahead of Perez in the Drivers' Championship due to countback, as his 13th place result at the Chinese Grand Prix is the team's highest result.
But, Perez has generally outpaced his team-mate which, with the links of Cadillac potentially keen for an American driver in Herta, led to speculation about Bottas' future.
Cadillac F1 CEO Dan Towriss said: "Valtteri's experience, perspective and commitment are important strengths for our team.
"Continuity gives us a strong platform as we continue developing the team and working toward our ambitions in Formula 1. On the eve of the Las Vegas GP, everyone in the team is pleased to have Valtteri locked in for 2027 alongside Checo and look forward to the next stage of our journey together."
Cadillac say they will announce their 2027 F1 reserve and test drivers in "due course".
Just one seat left to be filled on 2027 F1 grid
With Bottas' future secured and Racing Bulls confirming last week that Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will be their line-up once again in 2027, only Haas are yet to complete their driver pairing for next year.
Last month, Haas announced Rafael Camara will drive for the team in 2027, having already made an early F1 debut in Brazil and will compete again this weekend in Las Vegas, after Esteban Ocon was dropped following a dispute at the Mexico City Grand Prix.
But, Oliver Bearman has not been confirmed, although is expected to keep his seat once a "few bigger-picture things that we're working on" have been resolved according to the British driver.
Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu furiously dismissed reports claiming that contract extension talks with Bearman are being held up by the British driver demanding a £5m annual salary.
"I have no idea where that comes from," he said in Mexico.
"I've experienced this sometimes this season as well. People say there's no smoke without fire but really some people will invent a story."

items.title: Sam Altman says his life is so weird that he’s unfazed by Andrew Garfield portraying him in upcoming movie
items.summary:
Hollywood has found plenty of material and cinematic inspiration from a string of Silicon Valley scandals and power struggles in recent years.
“You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, smashed box office expectations, and Netflix’s limited series “The Altruists” comes out Thu
items.text:
Hollywood has found plenty of material and cinematic inspiration from a string of Silicon Valley scandals and power struggles in recent years.
“You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, smashed box office expectations, and Netflix’s limited series “The Altruists” comes out Thursday to tell the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the downfall of FTX.
As the founder and CEO of OpenAI, one of the most influential companies of the century, Sam Altman isn’t going to escape the Hollywood treatment, either.
In “Artificial,” a biographical comedy-drama opening in theaters on Christmas, the lauded actor Andrew Garfield will portray Altman in a film that chronicles OpenAI’s rise and the internal turmoil that erupted when he was briefly ousted in 2023.
“If you had told me 20 years ago that someone was going to make a movie about me, I think that would have struck me as … that would have been a very weird thing,” Altman said onstage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. “Now it doesn’t feel like it’s in like the top 10 weirdest things about my life.”
Garfield is best known for his role as Spider-Man, but his big break came in 2010, when he played Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” alongside Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg. (That film also had a sequel of sorts this year called “The Social Reckoning,” but it bombed at the box office.)
So, if Altman isn’t fazed by the looming release of “Artificial,” what’s actually the weirdest thing in his life?
“The fact that we are ushering in this technology that we have all of these very real concerns about, and that we have, we find ourselves in a role of such significance and such responsibility to make that go well,” Altman said. “That’s a crazy situation to find yourself in.”
Sure, that is pretty weird, Sam. It’s also weird that you use ChatGPT for parenting advice and don’t respect olive oil. But I’d wager to say it’s even weirder that there’s an upcoming film about the time your colleagues briefly ousted you because they were concerned that you can’t be trusted.
Say what you want about Mark Zuckerberg (I certainly have), but at least he’s honest about what he thinks about “The Social Network.”
“It was weird, man,” Zuckerberg reflected on a podcast last year. “They got all these very specific details of what I was wearing, or these specific things correct, but then the whole narrative arc around my motivations and all this stuff were like, completely wrong … The whole arc is like, I’m somehow motivated by trying to find a girlfriend, [but] I was dating Priscilla [Chan] before I started Facebook.”
Zuckerberg said he knew his employees would be tempted to see the movie, so he organized a company outing when it was released, even though the film hardly paints a flattering portrait of him.
Zuckerberg even had enough of a sense of humor to buy a prop from the film at auction. He owns an Ardsley High School T-shirt that Eisenberg wore in the movie and even wore it himself in a video with YouTubers Colin and Samir.
Eisenberg hasn’t been particularly complimentary of Zuckerberg, saying that he doesn’t want to think of himself as “associated with somebody like that.” And while “Artificial” hasn’t hit theaters yet, Garfield doesn’t seem to have a much more favorable opinion of the tech founder he portrays.
“I don’t know Sam Altman. I’ve never met him,” Garfield told Esquire. “But I think anyone who takes on that level of responsibility for a company or technology that you know is going to do a hell of a lot of damage to the soul of humanity [must have] a certain ability to dissociate.”

items.title: ‘An honour’: Pochettino up for challenge of leading Manchester United revival
items.summary:
Mauricio Pochettino said it was “an honour” and “a privilege” to be the new Manchester United head coach after arriving in England on Wednesday.
Pochettino flew from Cincinnati to Manchester overnight after overseeing the USA beating Haiti in his final game in charge. Members of Pochettino’s staff l
items.text:
Mauricio Pochettino said it was “an honour” and “a privilege” to be the new Manchester United head coach after arriving in England on Wednesday.
Pochettino flew from Cincinnati to Manchester overnight after overseeing the USA beating Haiti in his final game in charge. Members of Pochettino’s staff landed earlier in the week to begin work at Carrington, laying the foundations as United seek to turn their season around. His right-hand man, Jesús Pérez, the goalkeeping coach Toni Jiménez and the fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino, who continues to work with his father, have already taken training with those not on international duty.
Those away with their national teams will return to the club on Thursday, when they are expected to meet Pochettino for the first time and hold meetings. Conversations have also been held with various departments within the club, as Pochettino sought to learn about the squad’s health as he seeks areas of improvement.
Pochettino’s first challenge will be at Anfield on Sunday, when 18th-placed United take on Liverpool. The 54-year-old has his eyes set on rattling Manchester City after being told on TNT Sports that “Manchester’s blue and always will be blue” by DaMarcus Beasley, who once had a loan spell with City. Pochettino responded: “No way. You will see. Give me time … give me time and that is going to start to change.”
Speaking about joining United, Pochettino said: “It’s a big challenge but at the same time, it’s adrenaline that you want to feel because I think we are going to have a different job. But I think one of the things that is important is that we have the experience to deal with that, and I think we need to add our common sense and the way we are going to approach all the things.
“We know that the situation is not a situation that a club like Manchester United deserves,” Pochettino added. “The fanbase is amazing and after we signed here in America, of every 10 people I crossed in the street, nine are Manchester United fans. It’s amazing.”
Pochettino is also reunited with the strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya, the analyst Alec Scott and his long-term assistant, Miki D’Agostino, at Old Trafford.

items.title: Snapchat now lets developers build AR Lenses with AI assistants like Claude Code and Cursor
items.summary: Snapchat announced on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let users alter their appearan
items.text:
Snapchat announced on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let users alter their appearance, add digital objects to their surroundings, or interact with animated experiences through the camera.
The company is introducing Easy Lens CLI, which builds on its existing Easy Lens tool, which lets creators generate Lenses from a single prompt on the web and mobile. Easy Lens CLI brings that same idea into developers’ existing workflows, allowing AI assistants to handle the technical work while creators focus on the vision for the Lens itself.
The launch indicates that Snapchat is looking to lower the barrier to creating AR content, while making its platform more accessible to developers who are increasingly using AI coding assistants. Instead of requiring creators to learn how to use Snapchat’s own development tools, the company is bringing Lens creation into the AI coding workflows they already use, which could in turn expand the pool of people who build for Snapchat.
Developers enrolled in Snapchat’s Lens+ Payouts program can earn from the Lenses they create with Easy Lens CLI. Snapchat says it paid out $1.8 million to Lens+ community creators last month.
Lens creators can describe the Lens they want in plain language, and their AI assistant handles the process from start to finish, Snapchat says. That includes building with more than 100 AR building blocks and 50 AI asset generators, generating previews, and publishing them to Snapchat and tracking their performance.
With Easy Lens CLI, Snapchat says developers can create everything from Web Lens games with leaderboards to camera effects and beauty filters.
AI assistants can generate assets, build and test Lenses, address errors, and send updated versions directly to the creator’s phone. The new capability can take a game from an initial idea to a published Lens in a single day, without developers having to write code themselves, Snapchat says.
The tool is aimed at different types of creators. The company notes that game developers can bring existing browser games to Snapchat as Web Lenses, while AI creators can use assets from their preferred tools to build Lenses in their own style. Additionally, agencies and brands can turn existing campaign videos, images, and other brand assets into AR experiences with less production time.
Easy Lens CLI runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.

Brooks Koepka has dubbed his 2026 season a "a disappointment" but insists he is hungry to secure a spot on Team USA's 2027 Ryder Cup squad.
The American returned to the PGA Tour via the one-time-only Returning Member Program in January following his LIV Golf exit at the end of 2025, a decision he said he was "beyond happy with".
After being welcomed back to the tour with open arms, Koepka made his return at the Farmers Insurance Open in February. He'd go on to make 16 starts on the PGA Tour this year but would miss the cut at five events and record only one top-10 finish.

Koepka, who was not selected as one of Keegan Bradley's captain's picks for the 2025 Ryder Cup and was also omitted from Brandt Snedeker's President's Cup team in 2026, hopes to raise his game and earn a spot in the roster for next year's Ryder Cup.
"Adare Manor is a big goal of mine," Koepka said. "But this year has just been a little bit of a disappointment, so I know I need to pick it up a little bit.
"It's something I don't enjoy, sitting back watching the Presidents Cup.
"I know I've only played in one [2017], a lot of those [omissions are due to] injuries. But those team events are a lot of fun, I really enjoy them.
"Getting to be around the guys and representing your country is pretty cool.
"So, anytime you can do that, or you have the opportunity to, and you're not able to go play, it kind of infuriates me sitting on the sidelines."
The 36-year-old has featured in four Ryder Cup's in the past, notably helping Team USA to victory in at Hazletine in 2016 and Whistling Straits in 2020.
He boasts an overall individual record of 7-6-2.
'The reception was fantastic from the players'
Koepka was the lone player to elect to sign up to the PGA Tour's Returning Member Program, with Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith all snubbing the deal, instead choosing to remain at LIV Golf in 2026.
However, following the dissolution of the formerly Saudi-backed breakaway league, Rahm, DeChambeau and Smith have all elected to rejoin the DP World Tour for the 2027 season, along with multiple other former LIV Golf players.
Koepka, meanwhile, was asked ahead of this week's RSM Classic whether he felt back at home after returning to the PGA Tour, replying: "Yeah, I felt very at peace with coming back.
"The reception was fantastic from all the players, caddies, just everybody on tour.
"I think I kept a good relationship with everybody even when I left.
"I think that played probably a huge part in that.
"Everybody was really receptive. I loved the conversations that I've had just throughout the year, just guys asking what was going on, thought process and how things went and the decisions made to get back here.
"Everything was great. I'm beyond happy with my decision."
Can Koepka win the RSM Classic? Watch the first round of the PGA Tour event live on Sky Sports Golf from 1.30pm on Thursday.

items.text:
President Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler. As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song.
Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
Facing opposition at home, Trump is eyeing the former US colony to build chip fabs and data centers.
Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
Facing opposition at home, Trump is eyeing the former US colony to build chip fabs and data centers.
Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — saying “Trump out.” Others say “Reject Pax Silica,” the name for the US-led international initiative to secure chips and critical minerals used in the hardware fueling the AI boom.
Peace and prosperity for whom?
“Pax” comes from the Latin word for “peace, stability, and long-term prosperity,” the Pax Silica website proudly says. Yet the unspoken question — peace and prosperity for whom? — explains the whiplash between the Philippine government’s warm welcome of Trump and the public fury raging outside.
Trump says he wants to “win AI” — whatever that means. As such, the US needs data centers full of GPUs to do it. With Americans increasingly opposed to data centers and chip factories being built in their communities, the US is now recruiting less affluent nations to take up some of the slack. Lawmakers from both the US and the Philippines are promising a slice of the riches that advances in generative AI are supposed to create. And that’s supposed to be worth the land razed, homes destroyed, and natural resources lost in the name of technological progress. In the Philippines, that’s taking the shape of a proposed 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) hub for chip factories, processing plants for critical minerals, and data centers.
At least two dozen countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative, and Trump was expected to pressure more to join while in the Philippines for events related to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. With Pax Silica, the US aims to insulate itself from China’s dominance in manufacturing semiconductors and processing critical minerals needed to make those chips. Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen to meet with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.
Philippine and US officials are expected to sign a framework agreement by the end of the year for the jointly developed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone. The details are still murky and shrouded in NDAs. The Philippines’ Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) overseeing the plan expects an economic boom from minerals processing and chip manufacturing, with perhaps a data center or two on site. Meanwhile, human rights advocates who oppose the project warn that it will displace Indigenous residents, cutting them off from water resources on which they rely.
“How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood?”
“We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.
The Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.”
The agency says the project will be located on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.
There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here
The BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he said, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf.
He did mention, however, that an American energy company was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.
Bingcang said in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley.

items.title: What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat
items.summary:
If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.
What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat
I want you
items.text:
If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.
What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat
I want you to understand just how much money this company rakes in.
What’s next for Nvidia? Whatever doesn’t rock the mind-bogglingly profitable boat
I want you to understand just how much money this company rakes in.
It’s easy to look at Nvidia, a company that just lost its visionary founder CEO due to a series of scandals, and think that the company and maybe the entire AI industry are in terrible trouble. Perhaps so?
But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful company that might tempt a new CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.
It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.
If you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but shows you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.
TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.
Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering company is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.
Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.
Maybe that’d make people feel differently about data centers?
But even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.
And make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the company’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she announced. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.
Nvidia isn’t the only company whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.
But while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.
In the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.
On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.
Asked how things might change under new management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-important firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.
“Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”
Nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress said Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.
In other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the plan.
Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

items.title: Emma Hayes to assist in US Soccer hiring process for next USMNT coach
items.summary:
The US women’s national team head coach, Emma Hayes, said she was “confident in the group that is being put together” to select her next counterpart for the men’s team – a group that includes her.
Speaking after announcing her team’s squad for the Concacaf championship and World Cup qualifier, Hayes
items.text:
The US women’s national team head coach, Emma Hayes, said she was “confident in the group that is being put together” to select her next counterpart for the men’s team – a group that includes her.
Speaking after announcing her team’s squad for the Concacaf championship and World Cup qualifier, Hayes shed light for the first time on her role in searching for Mauricio Pochettino’s replacement after the Argentinian decamped to Manchester United. US Soccer had previously said Hayes – alongside the federation CEO, JT Batson, the chief operating officer, Dan Helfrich, and Oguchi Onyewu, the vice-president of sporting – would assist with the search.
“Listen, I’m very embedded into the federation, and I work really closely with JT, in particular, and even more so with Dan as we’re growing to develop the American soccer movement,” Hayes said. “And you know, JT asked if I would be involved as a technical voice to be involved with the process. And I feel confident in the group of people that have been put together to create a thorough process to select the next men’s national team coach – my role is merely to support that through a technical lens, knowing I do this job … albeit with the women’s team, and that I’ve coached for a number of years, and can offer some of that insight into the application of what to look for and why.”
Hayes résumé spans 25 years and is distinguished, having coached at the very highest level for club and country alike. The Englishwoman, who took over the US team in 2024, moved from being the assistant coach at Arsenal to taking charge of the Chicago Red Stars in Women’s Professional Soccer in 2008, and later moved to Chelsea, winning the Women’s Super League seven times. Since accepting the US job, she has guided the women to an Olympic gold medal and taken on an expansive role at the federation as it looks to overhaul and grow the women’s game.
“I think it will be a very thorough process,” Hayes said. “I think that’s the most important part of it. I feel very embedded in what we’re doing with the federation, so it doesn’t feel unusual to me [to help with the search]. So, like I’ve said many times, let’s build off the good work that Mauricio has done. I think that’s the important part, and let’s get it right.”
Hayes offered a heartfelt goodbye to Pochettino on the TNT broadcast of the his final match with the USMNT on Tuesday night, a 2-0 victory over Haiti in their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final. “I just want to say thank you on behalf of all of us at US Soccer, it’s been a privilege to work with you here, see the amazing work you’ve done with the team,” she said. “I think you’ve left an amazing foundation for someone to come in and build on that great work and the good feeling and certainly the good habits you’ve left with the team. You’ve left a lasting impression on the American people.
Pochettino replied on the broadcast, saying: “I admire a lot Emma. She is a wonderful coach, and a wonderful person. It was an honor to share [this experience] with her.”

The former Aston Villa manager replaced Eileen Gleeson at the h
items.text:
Ward close to new deal as Noonan returns to squad
- Published
Republic of Ireland manager Carla Ward says she is close to agreeing a contract extension, as she named her squad for their 2027 Women's World Cup play-off final with Poland.
The former Aston Villa manager replaced Eileen Gleeson at the helm in January 2025 and has led the side to promotion to League A in the Nations League and their highest ever position in the Uefa rankings.
The Republic of Ireland have lost just one of their past six games and now face Poland in a play-off for a spot at the World Cup in Brazil next summer.
Ward's side travel to Gdansk for the first leg on 1 December before the reverse fixture four days later at Dublin's Aviva Stadium.
The 42-year-old's current deal expires at the end of the 2027 World Cup qualification cycle.
Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said earlier this month that there were "live conversations" around Ward's contract.
"I want to get one thing straight - last time I said I wanted to focus on the next four games," said Ward.
"What I mean by that is, I want the focus to be on the players and certainly not myself.
"But what I can say to everybody is, I think you all know that I love being here. I want to be here. I have absolutely no intention of going anywhere.
"Thankfully, the FAI feel the same. So yes, just to echo David's words, we're close. And look, we're happy. I'm happy. So, yeah, I'm sure you'll have me for a little bit longer."
- Ward in talks over Republic of Ireland contract extension 
  - Published7 November
- Two down, two to go - Irish target back-to-back World Cups 
  - Published14 October
- Republic of Ireland to 'lock in' for World Cup dream 
  - Published13 October
Saoirse Noonan returns to the Republic of Ireland squad for the Poland games after sitting out the play-off semi-final victory over Kazakhstan because of an ankle injury.
The Watford forward comes in for Jess Ziu, who has a shin injury, in the only change to the squad.
Ward said that "now is not the time for trying new things" with the squad, which includes Crystal Palace midfielder Shanade Hopcroft after her first call-up for the Kazakhstan games.
Republic of Ireland secured 3-1 and 1-0 victories over the Poles when the sides met in World Cup qualifiers in April.
Poland edged out Belgium on penalties in their semi-final and Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor poses a dangerous attacking threat.
"They're a top side, they're a really good side," added Ward.
"They've proven that. They've got arguably one of the best forwards in the world and I think that their performance against Belgium was superb, home and away. I think they were excellent.
"They created a lot. We're under no illusions that this is going to be easy because we've won two games of football against them.
"I think both sides will tweak a few things naturally because we'll both want to try and win the game. But I go back to if we focus on us, what we're good at, if we execute our game plan and everything we want to do, then I think that we can win the game."

items.title: How fallen giants and their fans bounce back from scandal -- and relegation
items.summary:
What does it feel like to realize the club you love is stuck in a doom spiral of its own making?
Whether due to cheating, financial mismanagement or general ineptitude, some of Europe's greatest teams have suffered the ignominy of relegation by means of punishment -- and their supporters have watche
items.text:
What does it feel like to realize the club you love is stuck in a doom spiral of its own making?
Whether due to cheating, financial mismanagement or general ineptitude, some of Europe's greatest teams have suffered the ignominy of relegation by means of punishment -- and their supporters have watched it unfold. From Juventus and Fiorentina in Italy to Rangers in Scotland, fans have seen offices stripped bare and managers and players scrambling for places on the first boats off the sinking ship.
But a crisis offers the chance for heroes to drag their team out of the deep while suits swap seats in the boardrooms. And amid schadenfreude, anger and denial, supporters of flawed giants find unity through their morbid, self-deprecating humor and fortitude in their situation.
As Manchester City's fans await the results of their appeal and the level of punishment for their 114 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, they might find some small comfort in seeing how others have bounced back from the depths of despair ... or renewed dread at the tribulations that could lie ahead.
Fleeing for greener pastures
By the time manager Fabio Capello had sprinted to Real Madrid in 2006, taking stars Emerson and Fabio Cannavaro with him, Juventus' offices had already been ransacked.
The "Calciopoli" scandal started as a doping investigation into Juventus, but instead found evidence of attempted match-fixing by executives who manipulated referees and their bosses -- a scandal that also implicated Fiorentina, AC Milan, Reggina and Lazio. Papers, contracts and hard drives were seized by the Guardia di Finanza (Financial Police) on May 18, 2006.
The original swath of punishments was handed out just six days after Italy won the 2006 World Cup. Juventus were hammered the hardest; they were kicked down to Serie B and stripped of their 2005 and 2006 league titles, triggering a flurry of expedited exit strategies.
"This world had been turned upside down," Ibrahimovic wrote in his 2011 autobiography. "It wasn't possible to take it all in. We'd won two titles in a row -- were we going to lose everything? One after one the players got away ... every one of us who were left called our agents: 'Sell us, sell us.'
"Uncertainty and desperation hung in the air ... No way was I going to sacrifice a year in the second division. My best years were in danger of being wasted; I told [agent Mino Raiola], 'Do whatever it takes, just get me out of here.'"
Ibrahimovic watched teammates Lilian Thuram and Gianluca Zambrotta join Barcelona, while Patrick Vieira headed to Internazionale. Didier Deschamps took charge, though he couldn't persuade Ibrahimovic to stay. Ibrahimovic said he'd train but wouldn't play in matches, leading to the striker refusing to get on the bus for a preseason game -- instead, he hid in his room and played video games, eventually joining Vieira at Inter.
"In the years following the scandal, any player who had left Juventus and came back to play would get booed. The fans felt betrayed," Lorenzo Bettoni, Football Italia editor, told ESPN. "Even today, if they come back to the Allianz Stadium, they'll still get booed."
Gianluigi Buffon, Alessandro del Piero, Pavel Nedved and David Trézéguet remained and guided Juventus through Serie B. "We chose to stay together to honour a shirt, a club, a fanbase," Buffon wrote in a column for La Stampa in 2017. "We lost everything to gain things which aren't measurable and can't be bartered: respect, affection."
AC Milan's players feared relegation, too. "The whole thing was an absolute shambles," Andrea Pirlo wrote in "I Think Therefore I Play." "One thing I was sure of, though: I would never drop down to Serie B. And if I had to leave, I wouldn't feel like a traitor. You always want to be ambitious and play for a noble cause. There was no way I was going to pay for other people's sins, if that's what they turned out to be." Ultimately, Milan received a hefty points deduction but remained in Serie A.
Choosing to stay
While some players seek the nearest exit option, others choose to stay. Their club's careworn fans hold them close as symbols of hope and rare loyalty.
When Fiorentina were declared bankrupt due to unpaid debts and wages and dissolved in summer 2002, the club restarted in the fourth tier as a brand-new entity. Italy international Angelo Di Livio, then 36, refused to flee and joined the phoenix club Associazione Calcio Fiorentina e Florentia Viola. On June 18, 2002, Di Livio was a second-half substitute as Italy were knocked out of the World Cup by South Korea. Three months later, he started for the reformed Fiorentina team as they drew 1-1 at Sangiovannese in the fourth tier of Italian football.
"My other teammates left, but I stayed in [Florence] for a few days to reflect with my family," Di Livio said in an interview with La Nazione. "Then I called [sporting director] Giovanni Galli and said, 'If you want, count on me. I'm staying.'
"I owed it to the Viola fans. In this city there has always been a true, authentic passion. And there was a great desire for rebirth." His 2003 memoir -- part of a great swath of Fiorentina-related literature -- was called "Io resto qui" ("I'm staying here").
"It was a horrible time for Fiorentina fans," Lorenzo Lepore, Fiorentina fan and owner of SV Media, told ESPN. "The club is part of daily life in Florence. It was very hard for Fiorentina fans to accept -- the club hadn't cheated, instead it was the owners who let us down." For Fiorentina, gone were the trips to AC Milan and Inter Milan as they rebuilt, instead they planned for car rides to Aglianese and Poggibonsi.
The scene that greeted players and management on their first days back in as Fiorentia Viola was grim. "I arrived on August 13, but there was nothing," then-manager Pietro Vierchowod said in a 2017 interview. "With sporting director Giovanni Galli, I went to a shop to get balls and shirts, and at the first training sessions I only had five Primavera players.

items.title: Banned Springboks coach Erasmus invites fans to watch along of Ireland game
items.summary:
Rassie Erasmus: South Africa coach invites fans to watch-along of Springboks clash vs Ireland following six-match ban
Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was handed a six-match suspension for comments he made about referees following South Africa's Nations Championship defeat by France; South Africa Rug
items.text:
Rassie Erasmus: South Africa coach invites fans to watch-along of Springboks clash vs Ireland following six-match ban
Springboks coach Rassie Erasmus was handed a six-match suspension for comments he made about referees following South Africa's Nations Championship defeat by France; South Africa Rugby have requested a full hearing into his ban
Wednesday 18 November 2026 17:44, UK
Rassie Erasmus has invited fans to join a live watch-along online of South Africa's clash against Ireland, after the Springboks coach was suspended for six matches for comments he made about match officials.
Erasmus had questioned whether there were double standards in the officiating of South Africa's 21-19 defeat to France during a press conference earlier in the week, prompting an investigation from World Rugby, who later said that the coach had "disrespected the authority of the officials".
He will now be unable to have any match-day involvement in his side's Nations Championship match against Ireland on Saturday, or their Nations Championship Finals match, commencing the following week.
South Africa have requested a full hearing in response to the sanction and on Wednesday, Erasmus broke his silence, inviting members of the public to join him to watch Saturday's game via a live stream.
"Can sit and moan or make the best of it," the Springboks coach wrote in a post on X.
"I'll be watching the match at the hotel. Not keen to watch [it] on my own.
"So, let's give it a go and hope I get the 'tech' sorted = TV on, My Laptop camera on, and you're welcome to join me.
"Sign up here (adults 18+): http://watchwithrassie.com. This is personal, not official."
On his streaming website, Erasmus has embedded a video of a flying South Africa flag, with a link to sign up to watch.
The 54-year-old, who guided South Africa to back-to-back Rugby World Cups in 2019 and 2023, provided some more details on the webpage about how the live stream would work.
"We each watch on our own TV, and I'll be on camera so you can see me watch it too. Send me a message and I'll read some out."
A disclaimer on the page read: "This is me personally, Rassie. It is not an official team or Springbok channel."
It is unclear when Erasmus will be able to return to coach South Africa, but he is expected to be available for the 2027 Rugby World Cup.
On Tuesday, World Rugby confirmed an independent panel had reviewed the comments made by Erasmus under World Rugby's Match Official Abuse Sanction Process, a framework that was introduced in July.
"The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials," the governing body said in a statement.
"In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity."
Erasmus: Manipulation of the game or the result?
On Monday, Erasmus claimed France should have been given three yellow cards for illegal tackles as he leapt into a rant criticising referees.
"Let's say 11 of those were at least a penalty and three I thought were at least three yellow cards. And not one was sanctioned and not one was shown out or cited," Erasmus said.
"I'll send you the playlist, but I'll get into trouble… So I can't send the playlist to anybody and we can only send five clips to World Rugby. So we'll probably query it, but the answer will probably be: 'Yes, it was a mistake; it should have been penalised'.
"On numerous times we mentioned to the referee 'we think there's a knee-drop tackle'. I'm saying to you, my feeling is that knee-drop tackles is out. They happened 17 times in our game. Not one was penalised.
"And if the TMO didn't see it, then maybe technology must be better. If he saw it and ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result? Or players getting injured?
"So, all I'm asking is don't take the TMOs out and discourage them from getting involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."
World Rugby has since received backlash on social media in the wake of Erasmus' ban, and South Africa Rugby has condemned the abuse.
"SA Rugby unequivocally condemns any form of intimidation, threats or personal attacks. Such behaviour has no place in rugby and is entirely contrary to the values upon which our game is founded."

items.text:
ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz defies injury concerns to continue flawless run with win vs Daniil Medvedev
Carlos Alcaraz continued his perfect run at the ATP Finals with a win over Daniil Medvedev; the Spaniard called for his physio after appearing to pull up with a hamstring problem; watch the ATP Finals live on Sky Sports
Wednesday 18 November 2026 18:22, UK
Carlos Alcaraz kept up his strong end-of-season form with a 6-2 6-4 victory over Daniil Medvedev at the ATP Finals on Wednesday despite taking a medical timeout and getting his left thigh strapped.
Seven-time Grand Slam champion Alcaraz extended his winning streak to 11 matches as he seeks a third consecutive indoor title after trophies in Vienna and Paris.
He will now qualify for the semi-finals of the elite eight-man event if Frances Tiafoe wins a set against Flavio Cobolli in the other group match later.
- Keep track of the full tennis schedule live on Sky Sports
- Download Sky Sports app for analysis, news and video 📺
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW📱
Alcaraz conceded only four games to Tiafoe in his opener.
World No 1 Medvedev moves to a record of 1-1 for the tournament after he beat Cobolli on Monday.
Alcaraz's win was his fifth in six matches against top-five players this year. His lone loss came against Jannik Sinner in the Monte Carlo Masters final.
Alcaraz 'feeling OK' despite medical timeout
After breaking Medvedev twice in the first set, Alcaraz was forced to call for treatment in the second set.
"I was playing great and suddenly I felt a little problem in my hamstring," Alcaraz said.
"But just a little bit. I mean, I could play really good tennis since that moment until the end of the match.
"I was trying to stay relaxed, to move not too aggressively.
"Right now I'm just feeling OK. We will see with my team, with my physio, but I think the rest of the day and tomorrow is really going to be important."
Alcaraz missed this year's French Open and Wimbledon after he was ruled out for four and a half months due to a right wrist injury.
Henman: Injury proves no distraction for Alcaraz
Sky Sports Tennis' Tim Henman said:
"I don't expect, even at this stage, he [Alcaraz] knows how serious this [injury] is.
"Whether he has been compensating, trying to protect his knee and now it's gone to his hamstring, his quad on the other leg.
"What could have been a distraction, just didn't really materialise, because his tennis is faultless.
"Where do you attack? He's so fast from the back of the court and is so good off both wings. He changes direction. You hit a great shot; he hits a slice back. He can stay in the rally and defend. His serving has been so consistent.
"We've seen him play like this on other surfaces; outdoors hard, on clay, on grass.
"But this level indoors is even new for him."

items.summary:
Alexander Zverev notified of lawsuit by former partner in abuse case during middle of ATP Finals
Alexander Zverev has been notfied about a lawsuit filed by his ex-partner during ATP Finals; world No 1 advanced to the semi-finals of the season-ending tournament on Tuesday night
Wednesday 18 November
items.text:
Alexander Zverev notified of lawsuit by former partner in abuse case during middle of ATP Finals
Alexander Zverev has been notfied about a lawsuit filed by his ex-partner during ATP Finals; world No 1 advanced to the semi-finals of the season-ending tournament on Tuesday night
Wednesday 18 November 2026 18:41, UK
World No 1 Alexander Zverev was officially notified of a lawsuit filed by his former partner during the middle of the season-ending ATP Finals on Wednesday.
The latest legal case brought by the mother of Zverev's former partner alleges the tennis player violated the terms of an out-of-court settlement between the pair after the woman accused him of assaulting her.
The lawsuit brought by Brenda Patea in Germany takes issue with Zverev reportedly saying in an interview with French sports news outlet L'Equipe earlier this year that "it has been proven that the accusations were false" and "my innocence has been proven."
Zverev's Berlin-based lawyers, Christian Schertz and Anna Sophie Heuchemer, confirmed in a statement shared with The Associated Press that they were formally served with Patea's lawsuit on Wednesday.
"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit," Zverev's lawyers said. "If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion" protected by the German constitution.
They said there had been no breach of any contractual obligations.
Patea's lawyer, Michael Scheele, told The Associated Press that Zverev's claim over his innocence "triggered a veritable storm of criticism against our client."
He said the backlash was damaging to her business as an influencer and that she also felt her honour had been violated.
"Quite apart from the fact that Zverev's claim is false, he was not permitted to make any public statements whatsoever, in any form," he said. "Both Brenda Patea and Alexander Zverev had agreed to this in a settlement."
Patea is seeking that Zverev be ordered not to repeat such comments and that he be fined up to £208,484 €250,000 euros every time if he does.
Zverev faced a charge of causing bodily harm to Patea during an argument in Berlin in May 2020. He always denied any wrongdoing.
The case ended in a district court in Berlin in 2024 after the settlement. Zverev agreed to pay fines to the state and charitable organisations.
Zverev this month ascended to the No 1 ranking for the first time. He also won his first two Grand Slam titles this year and is competing this week at the ATP Finals in Turin.
Zverev has not commented on the lawsuit.
He previously denied abuse allegations from another former girlfriend, Olga Sharypova, who first made the accusations in 2020 and followed up in 2021 with a detailed account in a Slate.com article that was taken down because of a preliminary injunction issued by a German court. Slate said it stood by the article.
The allegations prompted the men's professional tennis tour, the ATP, to investigate her claims. It ended 15 months later, in January 2023, with the ATP saying there was "insufficient evidence" to substantiate the claims.

items.summary:

But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the
items.text:
The tightest survival scrap for years? Why it's not too early to worry
- Published
Despite being only 10 games into the season, sitting in the relegation zone even at this early stage is more worrying than you might think.
But with how tight the Premier League table is, this could also be one of the fiercest relegation battles we have seen in a long time.
Two of the current bottom three, Crystal Palace and Manchester United, will resume their campaigns at the weekend with new managers after appointing Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino respectively.
Sunderland, sandwiching the pair in 19th, have not pressed the panic button and have kept faith with Regis le Bris.
But is it too early to worry? We look at what the stats tell us about relegation battles in the past and what we can learn for the months ahead.
The bottom three may already be taking shape
Looking at every Premier League season since it changed to a 20-team league in 1995-96, the current bottom three have cause to be concerned.
In 19 of the previous 31 seasons (61%), only one of the bottom three sides after 10 games managed to avoid relegation.
For fairness and accuracy, the 'bottom three' are the three sides with the worst record after 10 games, not simply those in the relegation zone after matchweek 10, since in some seasons a team had played nine games by that point.
Only in 10 seasons (32%) have two or more of the bottom three stayed up - and that has not happened in any of the past eight campaigns. The last time more than one team avoided the drop was in 2017-18, when all three survived.
That has only happened twice, although only twice have all three sides been relegated.
Overall, of the 93 previous teams in the bottom three after 10 games, 41 survived and 52 were relegated - a survival rate of 44%.
It's not all bad news for the bottom three
This is the third time that Palace have been bottom after 10 games. On both previous occasions, they did not just survive but thrived, finishing 11th.
They did so under Tony Pulis in 2013-14 and under Roy Hodgson in 2017-18. Both managers, like Frank, were appointed early in the season following poor starts under Ian Holloway and Frank de Boer respectively.
The 2013-14 season is the only previous time that Sunderland and Palace were the bottom two at this stage. The Black Cats also survived thanks to a great, late escape under Gus Poyet.
This is the first time United have been in the bottom three after 10 games of a Premier League season.
Given the size and resources of the club, it is unlikely they will go down, although the team in 18th place at this stage have been relegated in each of the past six seasons.
Fans of all three clubs will hope for a repeat of 2017-18, when not only Palace but the bottom three improved significantly to finish comfortably mid-table.
Tight at the bottom - and in the middle
While history suggests only one of the bottom three will survive, there is also evidence to suggest that this might not be a standard Premier League season.
Palace have seven points, which is the most the bottom side after 10 games have had for 24 years. The bottom three all had eight points in 2002-03.
Sunderland's eight points is also the most the side in 19th place have had for 16 years. Wolves had nine points in 2010-11 and survived in 17th.
In fact, only five points separate the bottom half of the Premier League, with Tottenham in 11th on 12 points and Palace bottom with seven – the smallest gap at this stage for 24 years.
The highest that a team in the bottom three after 10 games have finished the season is eighth - Bolton in 2003-04, Tottenham in 2008-09 and Everton in 2017-18 - which suggests it will be Conference League at best for United next season.
Then again, the table is so tight that only nine points separate Chelsea in fifth and Palace - the smallest gap at this stage for 16 years.
Given that fifth place has been enough to qualify for the Champions League in recent seasons, optimistic United fans may not be ruling it out just yet.
That means even sides who have started well could be involved in the relegation battle.
The most points a team have had after 10 games of a 38-game season and been relegated is 14 - Joe Royle's Manchester City in 2000-01.
The most recent team to start well but be relegated were Eddie Howe's Bournemouth in 2019-20, who were sitting pretty in ninth with 13 points at this stage but went down on the final day.
As mentioned, this season has both the 'best' bottom side in terms of points and the most compact bottom half of the table that we have seen at this stage since 2002-03.
That season West Ham were relegated on the final day with 42 points - the most a side have been relegated with in Premier League history.
Given the way this season is shaping up, 40 points might also not be enough to survive.
