items.title: USWNT squad: Emma Hayes names veteran group for Concacaf championship and World Cup qualifier
items.summary: In the two years since the Paris Olympics, Emma Hayes has thoroughly tested fresh faces and new combinations, gathering a considerable amount of data about the US women’s national team. It’s been a thorough process, with 33 players earning their first caps since Hayes assumed the post, to bring her
items.text:
In the two years since the Paris Olympics, Emma Hayes has thoroughly tested fresh faces and new combinations, gathering a considerable amount of data about the US women’s national team. It’s been a thorough process, with 33 players earning their first caps since Hayes assumed the post, to bring her roster of options to 61 players.
At last, the main event is nearing. On Black Friday, the United States will enter the Concacaf W Championship with a clear objective: beat El Salvador. Winning the whole thing is nice, of course, and the USWNT have done so in nine of its 11 installments to date. But by far the most important game on that journey is the first one, a 27 November quarter-final date with clear stakes: overcome El Salvador or rely on a playoff to reach next summer’s World Cup.
Hayes’s 23 selections for the tournament suggests what her preferred core may look like for the remainder of the cycle. Only four field players on her roster arrive with fewer than a dozen caps: midfielder Croix Bethune (seven), who sent the Kansas City Current to the NWSL championship last weekend with a brilliant curling free-kick, plus defenders Kennedy Wesley (nine), Kate Del Fava (one) and Evelyn Shores, who becomes only the second uncapped USWNT player selected for a World Cup qualifier (following Taylor Flint, née Kornieck, 2022).
Eight players from Hayes’s Olympic gold medal squad remain in the fold, including the star attacking trio of Trinity Rodman, Mallory Swanson and Sophia Wilson. Sam Coffey returns after an injury prevented her from joining the team in the previous window, while Naomi Girma misses out due to persistent muscle issues. Claudia Dickey, Mandy McGlynn and Phallon Tullis-Joyce will continue to vie to start in goal, continuing their open competition following Alyssa Naeher’s retirement. The average age of this roster is 26.1, with only two players (Lindsey Heaps and Rose Lavelle) at least 30.
The Concacaf W Championship doubles as qualifying for both the 2027 Women’s World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. All four semi-finalists will be guaranteed a spot in the World Cup field, and the top three finishers will also join the Olympic field. (The US have qualified for the Olympics automatically as hosts). The losing teams in the quarter-finals will compete against each other for Concacaf’s two spots in the inter-confederation playoffs, which are scheduled for February in Morocco.
This story will be updated with remarks from Hayes’s presser on Wednesday morning.
US women’s national team squad
Goalkeepers: Claudia Dickey (Seattle Reign), Mandy McGlynn (Utah Royals), Phallon Tullis-Joyce (Manchester United)
Defenders: Tierna Davidson (Gotham), Kate Del Fava (Utah Royals), Emily Fox (Arsenal), Avery Patterson (Houston Dash), Tara Rudd (Washington Spirit), Evelyn Shores (Angel City), Gisele Thompson (Angel City), Kennedy Wesley (San Diego Wave)
Midfielders: Croix Bethune (Kansas City Current), Sam Coffey (Manchester City), Lindsey Heaps (Denver Summit), Claire Hutton (Bay), Rose Lavelle (Gotham), Lily Yohannes (OL Lyonnes)
Forwards: Michelle Cooper (Kansas City Current), Trinity Rodman (Washington Spirit), Ashley Sanchez (North Carolina Courage), Mallory Swanson (Chicago Stars), Alyssa Thompson (Chelsea), Sophia Wilson (Portland Thorns)

items.title: CME Group Tour Championship: Can Hull and Woad stop Korda?
items.summary:
CME Group Tour Championship: Field, format, prize money as Nelly Korda, Charley Hull, Lottie Woad battle for win at LPGA finale
Key questions about the CME Group Tour Championship, as the LPGA Tour’s 2026 season-long points race comes to an end; watch all four rounds live on Sky Sports
Wednesday 18
items.text:
CME Group Tour Championship: Field, format, prize money as Nelly Korda, Charley Hull, Lottie Woad battle for win at LPGA finale
Key questions about the CME Group Tour Championship, as the LPGA Tour’s 2026 season-long points race comes to an end; watch all four rounds live on Sky Sports
Wednesday 18 November 2026 16:28, UK
Who will be crowned the LPGA Tour’s Race to the CME Globe Champion? Who can stop Nelly Korda from winning? Can Brits Charley Hull and Lottie Woad claim victory? We get you up to speed ahead of this week’s LPGA Tour 2026 season finale, live on Sky Sports.
What is the CME Group Tour Championship?
The CME Group Tour Championship is the final event in the LPGA Tour's season-long points race.
Throughout 2026, players have competed in the LPGA Tour's points competition, the Race to CME Globe.
- Latest LPGA Tour headlines and results
- Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
- What golf is live on Sky Sports and when? Full TV listings
The top 60 players on the Race to CME Globe Points List are invited to feature at this weekend's event and the player who wins the 2026 CME Group Tour Championship will be crowned the Race to CME Globe champion.
Where is the CME Group Tour Championship held?
The tournament is held at the Tiburon Golf Club at the Ritz-Carlton Golf Resort in Naples, Florida.
The course has hosted the tournament since 2013.
Who can beat Korda?
It is the second time in consecutive years that Korda has arrived at the CME Group Tour Championship sitting at the top of the Race to CME Globe standings.
The American has already been crowned the Rolex Player of the Year, with three events to spare, but has never won the Race to CME Group Tour Championship. A first title this week would see her qualify for the LPGA Hall of Fame.
Standing in her way is a field of the LPGA Tour's best players, including two-time CME Group Tour Championship winner Jeeno Thitikul, who arrives in Florida having won four times on the LPGA Tour this season.
Miyu Yamashita, who has three wins on the LPGA Tour in 2026, enjoyed a strong finish to her season, winning twice while placing inside the top 10 three times in her last six events.
Haeran Ryu, who clinched back-to-back majors at The Amundi Evian Championship and the KPMG Women's PGA Championship, also comes into this event off the back of a fine vein of form, finishing tied-second and tied-third in her last two starts.
What Brits are playing?
Hull clinched the first LPGA Tour title of her career at this event back in 2016, so she certainly knows how to win at Tiburon Golf Club.
It's been a great year for Hull, who won the Solheim Cup with Team Europe in September and placed inside the top 10 at five LPGA Tour events. She'll no doubt want to end the season in style with a win.
Woad is the only other English player in the field. She too has enjoyed an excellent year, winning the Kroger Queen City Championship in May and finishing tied-ninth at last week's The ANNIKA, marking her seventh top-10 finish of the season.
What's the prize pot?
A total prize purse of £8.33m ($11m) is up for grabs, with the winner set to take home a £3.03m ($4m) cheque, the biggest cash prize in the history of women's golf.
The runner-up is also set to receive £757,423 ($1m).
What other end-of-season awards are up for grabs?
The LPGA Tour will also award the golfer with the lowest scoring average across the 2026 season with The Vare Trophy.
While Korda holds the lowest average score for the year, she has not played enough rounds to qualify for the award, meaning Yamashita, who has a scoring average of 69.50 and Thitikul, who follows her at 69.87, will battle it out to win The Vare Trophy.
How to watch the CME Group Tour Championship?
Sky Sports will be showing all four rounds of the CME Group Tour Championship live.
The first two rounds of the tournament will be shown live on Sky Sports Mix from 7pm on Thursday and Friday, with the action also live from 8pm on both days.
The third round coverage starts at 6pm on Saturday on both Sky Sports Mix and Sky Sports Golf, while Sunday's action is also live from 6pm on Sky Sports Golf and Sky Sports+.
Coverage of the final round will begin at 6pm on Sky Sports+.

PLANES, CLAIMS AND AUTOMOBILES
With his team mired in the relegation zone and a massive match at Liverpool this weekend, Mauricio Pochettino has been understandably busy since being appointed head coach of Manchester United. Unfortunately for Old Trafford regulars, the small print of his contract meant the Argentinian was tied up masterminding victory for USA USA USA in the second leg of their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti when he ought to have been in Carrington moving red magnets around a tactics board in front of Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Harry Maguire.
The match in Cincinnati was ostensibly a dead rubber, given the hosts kicked off with a 6-0 lead. However, the conditions of Pochettino’s release clause dictated he had to remain in charge until finishing his post-match media duties at the TQL Stadium. Like an errant spouse having one last dinner with their put-upon partner while their lover waits outside the restaurant with the engine running, Pochettino was unable to make his excuses and leave until the bill was settled. It was no surprise that his new role came up during his exit interview. In a playful exchange with DaMarcus Beasley, who spent a season on loan at Manchester City during the (Ben) Thatcher era, something of a gauntlet was thrown down to the departing boss. “Manchester is blue, it will always be blue,” honked the former international, who may be unaware of his former club’s disgrace and potentially imminent relegation to the North West Counties League.
“No way, you will see,” chuckled Pochettino by way of response. “Give me time. Give me time and that is going to change, for sure.” While the future colour scheme of football in Manchester almost certainly lies more in the hands of the three-person independent panel who will decide City’s fate after finding them guilty of industrial scale financial shenanigans, Pochettino assured fans he and his staff will do their bit to ensure the city will be painted red. “We are excited because the new challenge is a big challenge,” he whooped. “But at the same time, it’s the adrenaline that you want to feel. We are going to have a different job, but we have the experience to deal with that. We know that it is not a situation that deserves to be at a club like Manchester United and for the fanbase. The fanbase is amazing.”
Considering they’ve been flirting with Pochettino for nine years, most United fans will be unconcerned by his eventual arrival being delayed by an extra couple of days but, with that game against Liverpool to prepare for, the 54-year-old wasted little time in hightailing it to the airport and boarding a private jet for his new home. Upon arrival, he is expected to oversee his first training session, an event Sky Sports News has melodramatically anticipated using a serene, high-budget cinematic aesthetic that captures our Argentinian hero gazing longingly into a Manchester sunset. It’s a majestic, blockbuster shot that has rightfully become the subject of no end of online mockery. Football Daily wonders if we’ll see a contrasting shot on Sunday, when the Sky cameras cut to Pochettino staring in wide-eyed horror as Liverpool spank yet another goal past his side’s hapless defence.
LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE
Join Sarah Rendell at 8pm GMT for updates on Chelsea 2-0 PSG in Women’s Bigger Cup.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“It’s wicked, the stuff I’ve done … going to Milan fashion week, being taken to Paris with brands like Christian Louboutin is a level I never thought I would reach or be possible when I first started it. Some of the people I’ve met doing it … when I walked for Burberry I met Kanye West … just celebrities and people that I grew up listening to and I feel like without that it probably wouldn’t have happened” – Omar Sowunmi gets his chat on with Will Unwin about his dual life as a top, top model and no-nonsense centre-back with Bromley.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 Thanks for drawing my attention to the ‘Pierre Sage playbook for unfussed continental coaches’ (yesterday’s Football Daily). Any info about where to order a copy? I’m asking for a newly-employed friend in Manchester” – Mike Wilner.
 When I first skimmed over mention of BigShoe (yesterday’s Still Want More? – full email edition), I was shocked to think the likes of Clark’s, Kickers and Bull Boys (signed by him, Alan Hansen) had formed a global order à la Big Tech, Big Pharma and (possibly) Big Website. Thankfully, it’s a rather life-affirming organisation. Kudos to them and all involved” – Martin Clifford.

items.title: Divide and conquer - now maverick Erasmus plans online watchalong
items.summary:
Divide and conquer - now maverick Erasmus plans online watchalong
- Published
Having been banned from the touchline for six matches, you will not find Rassie Erasmus at the Aviva Stadium when his South Africa side face Ireland.
Instead he will be hosting an online watchalong of Saturday's match, cou
items.text:
Divide and conquer - now maverick Erasmus plans online watchalong
- Published
Having been banned from the touchline for six matches, you will not find Rassie Erasmus at the Aviva Stadium when his South Africa side face Ireland.
Instead he will be hosting an online watchalong of Saturday's match, courtesy of a swiftly purchased domain name.
The South Africa head coach plans to stream his reactions live while watching on television from his team's Dublin hotel.
It is typical Erasmus. An unapologetic, unabashed show of defiance in the face of the authorities.
And he will not be short of virtual company.
Because, while Erasmus has run low of advocates elsewhere, his compatriots have rushed to his defence.
"Rassie was just asking questions," said former South Africa hooker Hanyani Shimange in the wake of Erasmus' ban for a scattergun series of complaints about the injustices suffered by his side.
"But you have to look at the facts. Where was the accountability for that refereeing performance [in the loss to France]?"
Naas Botha, legendary South Africa fly-half turned pundit, described Erasmus' punishment as a "debacle". "You can't tell me [officials] are untouchable," he said.
Supersport, which broadcasts South Africa's games domestically, published an article accusing Erasmus' critics of "pearl clutching", external and "shooting the messenger" with regards to the game's faults.
Despite slurring officials with a suggestion of match-fixing, Erasmus has the support of South Africa.
It is not surprising.
His feats with the team are astonishing.
South Africa were ranked sixth in the world when he took over in March 2018.
He arrived after a November tour in which they lost to Wales and were thrashed 38-3 by Ireland. New Zealand had racked up a record 57-0 win a few months earlier.
Erasmus turned the team around at speed, marrying their trademark up-front power with pace out wide.
They won the 2019 World Cup. The defended their title in 2023. They will go into the tournament in 2027 aiming for an unprecedented hat-trick. And few would bet against them achieving it.
Erasmus is relentlessly innovative.
Long before the sport's data revolution, he was coding game footage, picking up the technique from a friend who worked in the military. He has since developed Outfox, his own software which allows his teams to run through moves virtually on a screen away from the pitch.
Tactically, he has also been ahead of the curve. He pioneered the use of forward-heavy replacement benches, giving his team an edge in the final quarter of the match.
He saw the game-breaking potential of diminutive Sevens specialist Kurt-Lee Arendse and moulded Andre Esterhuizen into a genuine hybrid player, capable of playing in the back row and the backline.
Trick plays - forcing a scrum with a deliberate infringement off kick-off, or setting up a line-out in the middle of the pitch - have been part of Erasmus' arsenal.
Legally, he is across every possible loophole.
There was controversy before the match against France last weekend when he made use of the Nations Championships' looser regulations to swap his starting front row just over an hour before kick-off.
Previously, he demoted himself to water boy so he could run the touchline during the 2021 series win over the British and Irish Lions.
Former Springbok wing Bryan Habana worked under Erasmus at the Stormers in Cape Town.
"He is one of the master tacticians the game has ever seen," Habana told BBC Sport's Ireland Rugby Social.
"I don't always agree with how Rassie comes across, but I understand he wears his heart on his sleeve. He has got incredibly high standards.
"He's willing to be in the firing line to defend what he believes is right."
But there is no doubt, by the letter of the law, that Erasmus is wrong - certainly in terms of the platform and terms he chose for his complaints.
In July World Rugby introduced new rules around criticism of officials. It specifically targeted "comments which, viewed objectively, a reasonable person would conclude were an attack on the credibility or competence of the match officials".
Mentioning "match-fixing" undermines the officials in exactly that way.
Considering Erasmus' previous, including an hour-long monologue bemoaning officiating of a first-Test defeat by the Lions in 2021 and a series of tweets after a loss to France a year later, he may be fortunate to only be banned for six matches.
World Rugby, perhaps pre-empting the reaction in South Africa, was clear that it was not punishing Erasmus for asking questions.
"Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches," it said in its judgement.
"Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."
For many South Africans, though, Erasmus is still an outlaw hero.
World Rugby, based in Dublin, is seen by them as tilted towards the north.
Australian Brett Robinson, the current chairman, is the first figure from outside the Six Nations countries to hold the organisation's top job since it became an elected position.
The World Cup has been lifted by South Africa on four occasions, but held there only once.
Japan coach Eddie Jones, Erasmus' fellow maverick, recently suggested Ireland's political clout, external was behind his team's home game being staged in Australia rather than Tokyo.
South Africa were a powerful voice against the possible moves to "depower" the scrum - a key part of the Springbok game - at a February conference to discuss future law tweaks.
Erasmus' public pronouncements have fuelled conspiracy theories weaved from those threads. They have also made an all-time great team harder for outsiders to love.
Whether it is a deliberate ploy is hard to tell.
Certainly Erasmus is a repeat offender, but his offences have also come in his second language. He is an Afrikaans speaker.

items.title: Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
items.summary:
Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
- Published
Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens continue to struggle with the high cost of living.
The $60m (£46m) French-made Falcon 6X has sparked political row
items.text:
Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
- Published
Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a new presidential jet amid criticism over its cost, as many citizens continue to struggle with the high cost of living.
The $60m (£46m) French-made Falcon 6X has sparked political row, with opposition politicians accusing President John Mahama's administration of misplaced priorities.
But the government says the purchase is justified, arguing that Ghana's improving economy makes the aircraft affordable and is needed to replace an ageing presidential jet.
The controversy comes as Mahama's administration seeks to demonstrate an economic recovery after years of financial difficulties that forced Ghana to seek IMF assistance.
- Can Ghana's new president meet the voters' high expectations? 
  - Published7 January 2025
Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.
Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.
The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase.
While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.
Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high.
"What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added.
He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.
Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.
The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs.
"This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted.
But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.
Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle.
Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties.
"We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.
He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF.
"The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.
Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.
Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.
He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation.
"When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.
The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.
But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air".
"There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.
He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.
The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.
The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.
Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.
Additional reporting by Thomas Naadi in Accra

items.summary:
Nigeria approves law allowing states to run their own police
- Published
Nigeria has moved a step closer to introducing state police system after all 36 states approved a motion to create and operate their own police force alongside federal police.
The resolution, which seeks to amend the constituti
items.text:
Nigeria approves law allowing states to run their own police
- Published
Nigeria has moved a step closer to introducing state police system after all 36 states approved a motion to create and operate their own police force alongside federal police.
The resolution, which seeks to amend the constitution, now requires President Bola Tinubu's assent to become law. It also requires further federal and state legislation for state police to become operational.
The move comes amid persistent security crises across Nigeria, including banditry, mass kidnappings and communal violence, which the federal security forces have struggled to contain.
But critics fear that governors could use the forces to intimidate political opponents, suppress dissent or influence elections.
There are also concerns about the shortage of police officers, who rights groups say are often poorly equipped, inadequately trained and vulnerable to corruption in a country of more than 200 million people.
Nigeria currently has a centralised police system, with the federal government controlling the police under 1999 Constitution.
Supporters of the state police argue that decentralizing law enforcement would allow authorities to respond quickly to security threats and better understand local conditions.
On Tuesday, the Clerk to the National Assembly, Kamoru Ogunlana, said his office had completed the verification of resolutions submitted by state legislatures in support of the constitutional amendment.
He described the unanimous backing as 100% approval, exceeding the legal requirement of at least 24 states.
Under the proposed two-tier system, the federal police would retain responsibility for enforcing federal laws and protecting national institutions, as well as tackling threats such as terrorism, cybercrime and border security.
State police would be responsible for enforcing state laws, maintaining public safety and preventing and investigating offences within their jurisdictions.
The federal police would, however, be allowed to intervene in a state on some occasions including serious breakdown of public order or human rights violations.
Such intervention will however require presidential authorisation and will be subject to judicial review.
The proposed law includes safeguards intended to prevent political interference and abuse of power.
Governors would be prohibited from ordering officers to unlawfully arrest or detain individuals or groups.
Independent state police commissions would oversee hiring, discipline and accountability. Their officials would be appointed by governors on the recommendation of the federal National Police Council.

items.title: Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
items.summary:
Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
- Published
As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.
She
items.text:
Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
- Published
As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.
She is thinking about getting around more easily.
The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.
For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.
"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.
But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.
It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.
Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.
The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.
The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.
But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?
The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.
Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.
"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza
"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."
DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.
A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.
The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.
The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.
The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.
At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.
When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.
The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.
Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.
LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.
For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.
"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.
Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.
But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.
"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."
Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.
"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.
The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.
Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.
"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.
But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.
The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.
"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."
For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.
State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.
LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.
"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.

items.text:
Senegal become first side to book Afcon 2027 spot
- Published
Senegal became the first side to qualify for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) after Mozambique secured a 1-0 win away against Ethiopia.
That result means the Teranga Lions, who beat Sudan 4-2 on Monday, are guaranteed a top-two finish in Group J with two rounds of fixtures to play.
Eight more sides, including Morocco, Cameroon and Ivory Coast, could join Patrick Vieira's side in booking a spot at next year's finals as the fourth round of fixtures culminates on Tuesday.
Egypt could have qualified with an away win over Malawi but were held to a goalless draw after an inspired second-half showing from Flames goalkeeper George Chikooka.
After Mohamed Salah had hit the outside of the post from a tight angle, Chikooka denied Trezeguet and Haissem Hassan before also making fine stops from Mohamed Hany and Ibrahim Adel in stoppage time in Lilongwe.
The Pharaohs are now two points behind Angola in Group B after Miro's first-half effort secured a 1-0 victory for the Palancas Negras in South Sudan.
Meanwhile, Nigeria's hopes of progressing suffered another blow as the Super Eagles failed to beat tournament co-hosts Tanzania.
With the East Africans already assured of a spot at the finals, Nigeria are competing with Guinea-Bissau for just one qualification spot available in Group L.
A 0-0 draw in Zanzibar means the three-time continental champions could find themselves three points behind Guinea-Bissau if the Djurtus win away against Madagascar later in the day (16:00 GMT).
Elsewhere, Lesotho recorded a surprise 2-1 win over Gabon in Group A, leaving Morocco needing just a point from their match against Niger to go through.
The final two rounds of qualifiers will be held in March next year, with Afcon 2027 scheduled to be held in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July.

items.title: South Africa head coach Erasmus banned for six matches
items.summary:
South Africa head coach Erasmus banned for six matches
- Published
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has been banned for six matches by World Rugby over comments he made about match officials in his side's Nations Championship defeat by France last week.
Speaking at a news conference conference
items.text:
South Africa head coach Erasmus banned for six matches
- Published
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has been banned for six matches by World Rugby over comments he made about match officials in his side's Nations Championship defeat by France last week.
Speaking at a news conference conference in Dublin on Monday before the Springboks' match with Ireland, Erasmus questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: "is that not match-fixing?".
The two-time Rugby World Cup-winning coach was referencing the implementation of new rules surrounding hip-drop and knee-drop tackles, and felt the laws were not being applied correctly.
It comes after Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast became the first player to be cited for a hip-drop tackle in Ireland's win over Fiji on Saturday, which was not penalised in-play by referee Angus Gardner and television match official [TMO] Mike Adamson.
World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments "suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match".
In response, South Africa Rugby said it has requested a full misconduct hearing and an opportunity for Erasmus to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".
It is the third time Erasmus has been sanctioned by World Rugby over his comments about match officials.
When he was South Africa's director of rugby, he was suspended for two months by World Rugby after he posted an hour-long video criticising the refereeing in the Springboks' opening Test defeat by the British and Irish Lions in 2021.
World Rugby found the video contained "multiple abusive and insulting comments and attacks on the officials".
In 2022, he received a two-match ban for a series of tweets criticising officials in a defeat by France.
Erasmus' latest ban has been imposed under World Rugby's match official abuse sanction process, which was introduced by the governing body in July.
If the suspension is upheld, Erasmus will miss Saturday's game with Ireland in Dublin (16:40 GMT), next week's finals weekend fixture at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium and the start of his side's Rugby Championship campaign next summer.
- 'Is that not match-fixing?' - Erasmus questions officiating 
  - Published17 hours ago
- Nations Championship final round - who needs what? 
  - Published23 hours ago
- Prendergast cited and could miss South Africa game 
  - Published1 day ago
Erasmus said that 17 hip-drop or knee-drop tackles had been missed in South Africa's 21-19 defeat in France by match officials. Andrea Piardi was the referee for the Stade de France fixture, while Matteo Liperini was the TMO.
Erasmus added that if TMOs were not intervening for reviews to limit the number of interruptions during a match then it was "manipulation", before he added that his comments were "not an accusation".
"I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" Erasmus added.
"If the TMO didn't see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result or injured players getting injured.
"So all I'm asking, don't take TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."
'Unacceptable attack on credibility and competence of match officials'
In a statement on Tuesday, World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments had met "the threshold for serious misconduct".
World Rugby confirmed the ban will stop Erasmus having any match day involvement for six matches, which includes coaching, direct or indirect contact with the team management or players on match days, entering the stadium, coaches' box, playing enclosure or technical area.
"The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials," its statement said.
"In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity.
"Therefore, the panel reviewed a number of elements of the commentary including the timing and reach of the statements, combined with the allegations of bias or bad faith, and found that the comments attracted a six-match automatic suspension."
World Rugby added that "respect is fundamental to rugby, and match officials are central to the sport".
"Protecting their wellbeing and integrity, and their right to perform without abuse or intimidation, is a responsibility World Rugby and unions take seriously," their statement added.
"Coaches, players, unions and everyone in the game must uphold these standards.
"Robust, respectful debate is natural, but teams have access to well-established and supported channels and protocols for raising officiating matters before and after matches. Challenging a decision is not the same as questioning an official's integrity or making comments that expose them to personal abuse."
In the same news conference, which lasted more than half an hour at the Springboks' team hotel, Erasmus also questioned what he felt were double standards in terms of sanctions.
The outcome of the citing has yet to be released, but he predicted that Prendergast will be available to play against South Africa due to a "technicality", and also questioned the decision not to ban Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong for an alleged groin grab while playing for Leinster ahead of the November Tests.
Last year, South Africa prop Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-match ban

items.title: Mozambique opposition leader faces trial over deadly 2024 election unrest
items.summary:
Mozambique opposition leader faces trial over deadly 2024 election unrest
- Published
Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.
Ven
items.text:
Mozambique opposition leader faces trial over deadly 2024 election unrest
- Published
Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.
Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges, including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience, over protests that left hundreds of people dead. He denies any wrongdoing.
Security has been tightened around the Supreme Court, where Mondlane is due to appear on Tuesday, with authorities fearing a fresh wave of demonstrations by his supporters.
Police have appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly and avoid actions that could threaten public order.
The trial is widely seen as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after disputed elections triggered some of the country's deadliest political unrest in decades.
"The trial is a real test for Mozambique. It is is an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone," said Luis Nhachote, a political analyst.
Mondlane, who challenged the presidential election results that declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner, accused the authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages.
The demonstrations continued for months, with rights groups accusing security forces of using excessive force against protesters.
Amnesty International, citing local civil society organisations, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, which was one of the country's worst post-election crises since independence.
Mozambican police put the death toll at 96, including 17 police officers.
- Children shot dead after joining pot-banging protests in Mozambique 
  - Published23 November 2024
European Union election observers also reported irregularities in the October 2024 vote, raising questions about the credibility of the results.
Prosecutors accuse Mondlane of encouraging demonstrations that disrupted public services, damaged property and threatened public security.
The charges include publicly glorifying criminal acts, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to commit crimes and offences linked to terrorism.
He could face up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge.
Mondlane has rejected the accusations, insisting that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency rather than encouraging violence.
His party, the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), has described the prosecution as politically motivated.
The Supreme Court has denied allegations of political interference in the proceedings.
A heavy deployment of police has been seen patrolling around the Supreme Court and major streets in Maputo ahead of the trial.
In a statement issued on Monday, Mozambique's police appealed to citizens to "preserve tolerance and peaceful coexistence," adding that the right to demonstrate must be exercised strictly within the limits of the law.
Police also pledged to protect people and property while acting preventively and proportionately in accordance with the rule of law.
The court has only granted access to selected media organisations, sparking criticism from journalists and press freedom campaigners.
Court officials say the restrictions are necessary because of limited seating capacity in the courtroom, but critics argue they undermine transparency in a case of significant public interest.
The proceedings are expected to be heard by five judges, with witnesses called by both the prosecution and defence.
Political observers warn that the trial could reignite tensions in a country still struggling to recover from the violence and deep political divisions that followed the 2024 elections.

items.title: Nigerians among 12 suspects arrested in $4.5m Canada luxury car theft syndicate
items.summary:
Nigerians among 12 suspects arrested in $4.5m Canada luxury car theft syndicate
- Published
Canadian police have arrested 12 suspects, including eight Nigerians, in an investigation into an alleged car theft syndicate.
They are accused of stealing luxury vehicles and shipping them to West Africa.
Po
items.text:
Nigerians among 12 suspects arrested in $4.5m Canada luxury car theft syndicate
- Published
Canadian police have arrested 12 suspects, including eight Nigerians, in an investigation into an alleged car theft syndicate.
They are accused of stealing luxury vehicles and shipping them to West Africa.
Police in Peel, Ontario said they had recovered 96 high-value vehicles concealed in shipping containers. The vehicles, valued at $4.5m (£3.4m) were destined for export via Canadian ports.
The suspects face 231 charges, with arrest warrants issued for others. Police say some of the accused may face deportation after their criminal proceedings are concluded.
The arrests followed months of what police described as an "extensive auto theft investigation".
The investigations began in March in partnership with Canada's border agency after police identified a warehouse allegedly being used to store stolen vehicles.
Investigators believe the network was led by five people who coordinated the theft, transportation and export of the stolen vehicles, with the others playing supporting roles.
"Together, investigators linked the network to loading sites, container movements and the transportation of stolen re-VINed vehicles," the police said in a statement.
Re-VINing is the illegal practice of altering the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) to conceal its identity and make it harder to trace.
Canadian authorities have described organised vehicle theft as a growing threat, saying it was linked to wider criminal networks.
"Organised auto theft is a predatory business model run by transnational syndicates that terrorise families and fund broader criminal enterprises," Peel Regional Police Deputy Chief Nick Milinovich said.
The trafficking of vehicles from North America and Europe to African countries has been a long-standing concern for law enforcement agencies.
Last year, Interpol said more than 100 luxury vehicles stolen from Canada and European countries had been recovered, exposing a network involved in trafficking stolen cars to West Africa.
In a separate operation the same year, Ghanaian security authorities recovered 43 luxury vehicles stolen from Europe and North America.
They attributed the success of the operation to improved cooperation between national and international law enforcement agencies.

items.text:
Kidnap, child marriage and poverty: Why millions of Nigerian children can't go to school
- Published
As she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school.
"Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says.
One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village.
"They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says.
Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married.
"It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains.
Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home.
Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced.
Hadiza is one of nearly 19 million children in Nigeria who are missing out on an education, according to estimates shared by Unesco in 2024. That's about one in four of the country's school-age children.
Against this backdrop, the BBC World Service has launched Dars Hausa, an educational programme in the main language spoken in northern Nigeria, as well as neighbouring Niger, Cameroon and elsewhere in West Africa.
It brings English, maths and science lessons to children across West Africa, via social media, local television partnerships and radio. Many people in the region get their news from the radio and nearly half of households in Nigeria have one, according to the charity Save the Children.
Dars means "lesson" in Pashto and Dari, and it was first launched in those languages in 2023 for Afghan children barred from attending school. An Arabic version followed in February 2025.
The reasons why so many Nigerian children are out of school are numerous and complex. Like Hadiza, 12-year-old Rukayya also lives in the displacement camp in Goronyo.
"It pains me to see other children studying and going to school while I cannot," she says.
As the eldest child, each day Rukayya goes out to gather firewood to sell and to beg so that her younger siblings can have something to eat.
"If my father was alive, I wouldn't have to go out and beg," she explains, saying some people mock her "but it doesn't stop me because it is our only way to survive."
Bandits killed her father about a year ago in front of her, she says, and her family fled from their home to the camp.
She and Hadiza are among 670,000 people in north-west and central Nigeria who have been forced from their homes by armed robbery and kidnappings, according to the International Organization for Migration.
- Three Girls: Lessons in Limbo features the stories of Hadiza and Rukayya - you can watch the full film on YouTube, external
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by criminal gangs, known in Nigeria as bandits, who steal, kill and kidnap.
The school that Hadiza once attended in Goronyo is the only one serving children in the camp and typically has about 50 students in each class.
One of the teachers, Kamilu Sulaiman Jakada, says that even though lessons are free, only a tiny portion of the children attend, and even then sporadically, because parents tell him that "it is the children that are the breadwinners" and they need to earn money to eat.
He says the school does not have enough teachers or classrooms, explaining that funding is inconsistent and often comes from individuals or organisations rather than the government.
The other challenge is the bandits. A gang once came to the school on motorbikes, shooting in the air, he says, and although no-one was hurt, many parents were scared and withdrew their children. That has been parents' reaction to attacks in some other parts of the country too.
Every Nigerian child is meant to get nine years of free, compulsory education - six in primary and three in secondary school. Responsibility is shared between federal, state and local governments.
But many schools are facing shortages and poorer families who cannot afford private education can struggle to pay for uniforms, books and transport.
The crisis has built up over decades, with successive governments struggling to address chronic underfunding and poor oversight of resources.
In addition, many children in the traditional Almajiri system, which provides Islamic education, are not taught subjects such as maths and science, and are considered by Unicef to be out of school.
Minister of State for Education Prof Suwaiba Sa'id believes the number of children out of school is lower than has been reported, but admits that with Nigeria's growing population "the proper investment, the proper oversight, has not been done… I will not mention the names, but we know of two states that did not recruit a single teacher for eight years".
She says that education is the government's "number-one priority" and initiatives such as Lumina are designed to help address "decades of neglect". Lumina aims to support one million girls by 2030, providing an accelerated learning programme for older girls who have missed years of formal education.
She also says that "the government is doing everything possible" to deal with bandits and that "we have seen children that should be at school but are engaged in this banditry".
In the meantime, it is children like Hadiza and Rukayya that the BBC World Service Dars Hausa programmes aim to help. Hadiza says she still has a dream to one day become a doctor "to help my fellow women".
Dars Hausa will air on BBC News Hausa radio on Sundays at 06:45 West Africa Time, with a repeat at 20:45. The programme will also be available via BBC News Hausa's digital platforms, including YouTube, Facebook, X and Instagram.

items.text:
Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
- Published
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024.
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said the plan to open a centre in Rwanda had no "future or humanity", according to AFP news agency.
"I don't see any future or humanity in that. It's not the solution," Sanchez told the Spanish broadcaster Telecinco, AFP reported.
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".
Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.
Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".
He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".
Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.
The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.
"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".
With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.
Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries.
Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.
"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."
The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.
The agency added that unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, which the Dutch government has confirmed will not take place.
According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.
In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

items.text:
Cameroon, Senegal and Benin close in on Afcon 2027 qualification
- Published
Nicolas Jackson was on target again as Senegal, Cameroon and Benin moved to the brink of qualification for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) with away victories.
After Aston Villa striker Jackson had opened the scoring, Senegal gave up a 2-0 lead against Sudan before two late goals sealed a 4-2 win, while five-time Afcon winners Cameroon cruised to a 3-0 triumph over Namibia.
A goal in second-half stoppage time from Ede Oloko sealed a 1-0 success for Benin against Central African Republic.
All three sides are on 10 points in their respective groups after four rounds of matches and will progress to next year's finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda if other results go their way on Tuesday.
Elsewhere, Jordan Ayew's first-half penalty was enough for Ghana to register back-to-back victories over Somalia in Group C.
The Black Stars had home advantage for what should have been an away tie, with the game played in Sekondi-Takoradi because the Ocean Stars do not have a stadium fit for international football.
Ayew had a penalty saved as Ghana beat Somalia 2-0 in the reverse fixture last Thursday, but the Sheffield United forward kept his composure when he sent the goalkeeper the wrong way in the 36th minute after Brandon Thomas-Asante had been pulled down in the box.
Ghana, who parted company with Carlos Queiroz after losing their opening two fixtures, move level in the table with The Gambia, with both sides on six points.
- Salah scores twice as Egypt and Nigeria win Afcon 2027 qualifiers 
  - Published2 days ago
- Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years? 
  - Published30 October
The Gambians are themselves three points adrift of group leaders Ivory Coast before they host the Elephants on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, Guinea moved to the top of Group D after Yakhouba Barry scored twice in their 3-1 away win over Eritrea in neutral Cairo.
The West Africans lead South Africa, who travel to Kenya on Tuesday, by two points in a group with only one qualification spot available because the Kenyans are assured of a spot at the finals as co-hosts.
And Zimbabwe beat Equatorial Guinea 3-0 in Harare to go two points behind Group E table toppers DR Congo.
Thando Ngwenya, Tawanda Chirewa and Tawanda Maswanhise were all on target for the Warriors before Equatorial Guinea's Josete Miranda had a penalty saved and Saul Coco was sent off for the visitors late on.
The National Thunder were without first choice goalkeeper Jesus Owono after he asked not to be selected following his involvement in a collision with Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died the day after the incident.
DR Congo, Ivory Coast, Mali and Morocco can all book their tickets to the tournament when the fourth round of fixtures culminates with 18 matches on Tuesday.
The final two rounds of qualifiers will be held in March next year, with Afcon 2027 scheduled to be held in East Africa from 19 June to 17 July.
Teranga Lions leave it late
Patrick Vieira's Senegal survived a scare in neutral Juba after Jackson's early goal put the Teranga Lions ahead and a low strike from Brentford left-back El Hadji Malick Diouf made it 2-0 midway through the first half.
Sudan hit back through Al-Gozoli Nooh and Salah Adel to level proceedings with 15 minutes to play, but Pathe Mboup's lob made it 3-2 in the 87th minute and Paul Mendy made the points safe for the West Africans in the first minute of added time.
Senegal are still awaiting the outcome of their appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport over the destination of the 2025 Afcon title.
The Teranga Lions beat Morocco 1-0 after extra time in January's final, but a Confederation of African Football appeals board stripped them of the title two months later, decreeing Senegal had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them.
Mahamadou Nagida opened the scoring for Cameroon against Namibia in neutral Botswana with a stunning volley from outside the box in the 12th minute, and Ryan Fosso's deflected effort doubled the lead just before the hour mark.
Saidou Alioum made it 3-0 with a fine first-time volley with 19 minutes remaining, and David Pagou's men will be assured of a place at Afcon 2027 if Congo-Brazzaville fail to beat Comoros on Tuesday.

Somalia 0-1 Ghana (Group C)

items.text:
Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 17 dead
- Published
South African police are investigating the murders of 17 people in two separate shootings on Sunday night.
Eight men were fatally shot in a minibus in KwaZulu-Natal province. Police declared them dead when they arrived at the scene. Hours later, nine people were found shot dead inside a shack in western Pretoria.
Police say the two incidents are unrelated. The motive for the shootings has not yet been established.
South Africa is struggling to contain violent crime, including gang-related killings. The country has one of the world's highest murder rates.
Police say they responded to reports of a shooting outside Pietermaritzburg town in KwaZulu-Natal and found a white seven-seater vehicle riddled with bullet holes.
Inside were eight men with multiple gunshot wounds.
"It has not been established how the incident happened, and police are collecting pieces of evidence to determine the possible motive of the killings and the identity of the suspects," police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said.
The police have launched a manhunt for the suspects.
In a separate shooting in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria, police found the bodies of six men and three women.
They are believed to have been killed inside a four-room shack between 22:00 and 23:00 on Sunday. The bodies were scattered across the rooms, with several spent cartridges discovered outside the shack.
Community members initially mistook the gunshots for thunder and lightning.
"The provincial commissioner of police in Gauteng [province, which includes Pretoria] has mobilized the necessary resources, including the crime intelligence and the deputy provincial commissioner tracking team to search for the suspect," police spokesperson Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.
It's not the first mass shooting in the area. In January, five men were shot dead outside a local shop in broad daylight.
Illegal firearms are widespread in South Africa, where gun violence remains a persistent problem, increasingly involving mass shootings.
In September, 28 people were killed in two separate cases.
Eighteen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar near Johannesburg and opened fire on 25 September. Fourteen others were injured.
In a separate shooting the following day, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town. A further 11 were injured.
Much of the violence has been linked to turf wars between gangs involved in drug trafficking and illegal mining.
In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa described organised crime as "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".
Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police to five provinces with the highest murder rates, including Gauteng, in an effort to tackle armed violence.
According to the latest police statistics, 5,427 people were murdered nationwide between April and June 2026, an average of about 60 killings a day. This was a 6% decline compared with the same period a year earlier.
Additional reporting by Christian Parkinson in Johannesburg

items.text:
US basketball player arrested with 34kg of cannabis at Nigerian airport
- Published
A basketball player from the US has been arrested in Nigeria with 33.95kg (75lbs) of cannabis in his luggage at the main airport in Lagos.
The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) identified the player as Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, from the US state of Georgia, who it said had arrived from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.
According to the agency, the suspect said he had been playing professional basketball in Thailand and was visiting to Nigeria to "build networks" for his career. He has not publicly commented on the allegations.
The agency said an examination of the suspect's phone had pointed "to his knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity".
In statement on Sunday, the agency said he was arrested on Wednesday after airport officials noticed him abandoning his two checked-in bags and attempting to leave with his carry-on bag.
The two bags, which bore his name, contained 32 packs of the drug known as "Loud", a potent strain of cannabis, the agency said.
A tracking device was also recovered from the bags, the agency added.
The International Basketball Federation (FIBA) lists a player by the name Damonte Greene, with the most recent appearance at the Phuket Elite Cup in Thailand, on 26 September.
Nigeria, once regarded primarily as a transit hub for drug trafficking, has increasingly become a producer, consumer, and distributor of illegal drugs, according to the UN.
Recent NDLEA operations have uncovered several industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratories, raising concerns about links between Nigerian drug producers and Mexican cartels seeking to manufacture and export the drug.
In September, the agency said it had dismantled a meth lab and arrested a Mexican suspected drug kingpin who was allegedly attempting to flee Nigeria through Lagos.
Methamphetamine, commonly known as meth, is a highly addictive synthetic drug that can cause severe psychosis, heart attacks or stroke.
In August, a social media influencer suspected of links to an international drug trafficking network was arrested after the authorities seized cocaine worth nearly $28m (£21m), which was destined for the UK.

Town destroyed by flood rebuilt by Libya's strongman - but questions remain

Just three years ago he
items.text:
Town destroyed by flood rebuilt by Libya's strongman - but questions remain
- Published
"It was joy when I moved in. I could finally relax," says Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious new apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna.
Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him.
Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a new, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya.
It is part of a rapid $2bn (£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country currently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge.
The money comes from the state coffers of the oil-rich country, allocated by its parliament. But there are no published records of how it has been spent, raising questions about accountability and possible corruption.
Damdoum, like many flood survivors, simply thanks the head of the Development and Reconstruction Fund, Belkacem Haftar, for what has been achieved since the early hours of 11 September 2023, when lashing rain from Storm Daniel burst two dams above Derna, sending a wall of water 7m (23 ft) high cascading down onto the sleeping city.
The exact death toll will probably never be known. Some estimates have been as high as 6,000, though 4,000 now seems a more likely figure. Many bodies are still unidentified.
In a city of about 100,000 people, that means almost everybody lost someone they loved. The 14 relatives and neighbours on the roof with Damdoum – including his father, brother and sister - all drowned.
He survived, but his home was destroyed, and he had to find temporary accommodation. "It was rent, rent, rent," he says. "Now, no-one can take this [new flat] from me. I thank Engineer Belkacem. God sent this person who picked the city up from disaster."
Portraits of Belkacem, widely known simply as "the Engineer", his younger brother Saddam, a military chief also involved in reconstruction, and their father Khalifa are on hoardings all over Derna and the region.
"Since 2011, Libya has not built big projects like this," says Hussein el-Mansory, project manager of the "2,000 Apartments" complex where Damdoum now lives. "I feel very happy and proud and I'll tell my children: 'I made this.'"
The complex includes a new mosque, hospital, shopping mall and schools. New roads, bridges have also been built in Derna. But while many survivors have been rehoused, some are still waiting.
Among them is Izz al-Nasr Ibzeou, a marine science lecturer at the university. His wife Salima, her mother Mouna, and all the couple's seven children, aged between one and 11, drowned.
His family home was ruined, but the authorities have not yet fully restored it because Ibzeou also has an undamaged apartment in another part of town.
He returns every day to his old house, now an empty shell, to see his children's possessions, which he has kept in dust-covered piles.
"This is my son Moez's bike. He played with it every day. And this is my daughter Fawzia's dress. She wore it whenever she went to a wedding," Ibzeou says. "Even if I decide not to come to remember them, my feet will bring me here of their own accord."
To this day, he has not found their bodies. In Derna's vast new flood cemetery, most graves are marked only by numbers, not names, because the process of matching survivors' DNA with corpses is still not completed.
"I go to the cemetery and try to guess where my family are," he says. "This has burned my heart too much. Thank God, I'm patient, but I'm still waiting just to read the Qur'an [at their graves] and say hello to them."
Belkacem Haftar has now extended the work of his reconstruction fund to Libya's second city, Benghazi, and other parts of Libya his father controls.
Libya's parliament, based in the east, last year allocated him a further sum of nearly $11bn, to be spent over three years, in addition to the $2bn it had already given him specifically for Derna.
Building in Benghazi has included new skyscrapers, hospitals, housing developments and a refurbished football stadium that last year hosted a friendly between Inter Milan and Atlético Madrid. Officials have talked in the past about turning the city into a version of "Dubai on the Mediterranean."
Belkacem tells the BBC he has accomplished more than any previous Libyan administration.
"Libya went through the Gaddafi era, 40 years of neglect and poverty," he said. "The interim governments [post-Gaddafi, based in Tripoli] wasted a lot of money without providing anything the people could touch. I have never made promises to the people. But I have provided them with what they need."
International human rights organisations have repeatedly accused the authorities in eastern Libya and Libyan Arab Armed Forces headed by Khalifa Haftar of serious abuses, including secret executions, arbitrary detentions and forced disappearances.
The Haftars and the Benghazi-based government deny the allegations. Belkacem told the BBC there was complete freedom of speech in eastern Libya.
Critics also say the Haftars have a top-down approach to development, with little public participation in planning decisions, and no transparency.
"There is absolutely zero accountability. We've never seen any financial statements of the Reconstruction Fund, for even the legal on-the-table disbursements of funds," says Claudia Gazzini from the International Crisis Group (ICG) think-tank.
Belkacem says the fund is independently audited and that all contracts are drawn up to high international standards. Dismissing concerns about transparency, he says: "What we've done in Derna was almost impossible. What we care about is the reality, what we do on the ground."
He agreed to show the BBC the audits. Bu

items.text:
AS FAR retain Women's African Champions League title
- Published
Moroccan club AS FAR became the first team to retain the Women's African Champions League title with a hard-fought 3-1 win over Mamelodi Sundowns.
Imane Touriss put the North Africans ahead in the 23rd minute in Ismaila, Egypt, when her early shot from outside the box caught out Sundowns goalkeeper Andile Dlamini.
But the South African side levelled two minutes later through a stunning effort from Refilwe Tholakele, who flashed a right-footed shot from a narrow angle across goal and inside the right-hand post.
Seventeen-year-old right-back Hiba Youssoufi restored the lead eight minutes before half-time when her shot from 12 yards was deflected in off Sundowns defender Asanda Hadebe.
And, as the Brazilians pushed forward in search of an equaliser, an unmarked Touriss made it 3-1 with 13 minutes remaining with a low first-time finish from the middle of the area after fine work down the right flank by Fatima Tagnaout.
Ronnel Donnelly had scored a hat-trick for Sundowns in their semi-final victory over Kawempe Muslim Ladies but was largely kept quiet by the AS FAR defence.
The closest the Brazilians came to an equaliser in the second half was when substitute Nthabiseng Majiya had an effort deflected wide, and they failed to test AS FAR goalkeeper Khadija Er-Rmichi after going two goals down.
AS FAR, who had surprisingly lost their opening game at the finals to Ugandan outfit Kawempe Muslim Ladies, are the first side to win the Women's African Champions League title three times and also take home $600,000 (£449,000) in prize money.
The side representing Morocco's armed forces add to their triumph in 2022, when they beat Sundowns 4-0, and last year's victory over ASEC Mimosas of Ivory Coast.
Sundowns have claimed the title twice themselves, winning the inaugural competition in 2021 and lifting the trophy again two years later.
AS FAR players scooped the individual awards, with Touriss winning the golden boot with four goals, captain Ghizlane Chebbak named the player of the tournament and Er-Rmichi awarded the golden glove.
